sights.blurb: A four-way arch of Constantine's time, inside a medieval farmhouse, with the marks of the stripped marble clamps still on it.
sights.when: Opens on a monthly calendar and event days; reach it on the Roma–Nord line to Sacrofano (check dates first).
sights.q: Arco di Malborghetto, Via Barlassina 1, Roma

sights.name: Palazzo di Giustizia (the Palazzaccio)
sights.blurb: Calderini's law courts of 1889–1911, an early reinforced-concrete building behind travertine, with a missing third floor.
sights.when: Exterior; inside only by the Court of Cassation's rules.
sights.q: Palazzo di Giustizia, Piazza Cavour, Roma

sights.name: Where Lazio was founded
sights.blurb: Piazza della Libertà, where S.S. Lazio was founded on a bench on 9 January 1900, with flares lit on the anniversary.
sights.when: Street.
sights.q: Piazza della Libertà, Roma

sights.name: Ponte del Risorgimento
sights.blurb: A 1910–11 bridge with a single 100 m arch only 10 m high, the longest concrete span in the world when it opened.
sights.when: Street; the inscriptions are at mid-span.
sights.q: Ponte del Risorgimento, Roma

sights.name: Piazza Mazzini fountain
sights.blurb: De Vico's 1927 garden fountain with Luppi's sculptures, fed by the Acqua Vergine.
sights.when: Garden free; fountain restored. Pin from Google Places.
sights.q: Fontana di Piazza Mazzini, Roma

sights.name: RAI headquarters, Viale Mazzini
sights.blurb: Berarducci's RAI building of 1965–66 with Messina's dying horse at the entrance.
sights.when: Exterior.
sights.q: RAI Viale Mazzini 14, Roma

sights.name: Mercato Trionfale
sights.blurb: A large covered market (270+ stalls) with colour-coded counters and Diavù's portraits of Anna Magnani on the stairs.
sights.when: Mon–Sat 7–14; Tue and Fri until 19. Closed Sun.
sights.q: Mercato Trionfale, Via Andrea Doria 41, Roma

sights.name: Antico Falcone
sights.blurb: A 15th-century posting station on the road to the north, an osteria since 1877, under Strozzi arms and octagonal brick piers.
sights.when: Google (Nov 2026): closed Tuesday, open other days 12:30–15 and 19:30–23; older sources say closed Sunday evening. Phone 06 3973 6404.
sights.q: Antico Falcone, Via Trionfale 60, Roma

sights.name: San Lazzaro on Via Trionfale
sights.blurb: A chapel with a surviving wall of a medieval leper hospital that carries the double cross of Santo Spirito.
sights.when: Sunday Mass.
sights.q: San Lazzaro, Via Trionfale, Roma

sights.name: Monte Mario Observatory
sights.blurb: Villa Mellini's astronomical museum with Mercator and Cassini globes, and the solar tower; the site of Italy's old zero meridian.
sights.when: Open by booking and at outreach events (Google lists daily hours; check). Pin from Google Places.
sights.q: INAF Osservatorio Astronomico di Roma, Viale del Parco Mellini 84, Roma

sights.name: Prime meridian of Italy (Roma 40)
sights.blurb: The belvedere on the Parco della Vittoria marking the origin of Italian longitudes until 2011, with a view of St Peter's.
sights.when: Free viewpoint, open day and night; the park is run-down. Pin from Google Places.
sights.q: Belvedere Primo Meridiano d'Italia, Roma

sights.name: Monte Mario fossil sands
sights.blurb: Pleistocene shell-rich sands over Pliocene clays on Via del Farneto, with cold-water shells that show the sea was once colder here.
sights.when: Reserve open; exact outcrop points not confirmed. Map pin approximate.
sights.q: Via del Farneto, Monte Mario, Roma

sights.name: Zodiaco belvedere
sights.blurb: A viewpoint from the Alban Hills to Monte Soratte; the restaurant is shut and the site run-down.
sights.when: Viewpoint open.
sights.q: Belvedere dello Zodiaco, Monte Mario, Roma

sights.name: Rome Cavalieri
sights.blurb: The 1963 hotel (formerly Hilton) with a zigzag plan and brown brick chosen to hide its bulk on the hill.
sights.when: Lobby only; hotel. Pin from Google Places.
sights.q: Rome Cavalieri, Via Alberto Cadlolo 101, Roma

sights.name: French military cemetery
sights.blurb: A quiet cemetery for the French soldiers who died in the Italian campaign of 1943–44.
sights.when: Mon–Fri 8–16, Sat 8–13.
sights.q: Cimitero Militare Francese, Vicolo dei Casali di Santo Spirito 70, Roma

sights.name: Villa Madama
sights.blurb: Raphael's villa of 1518, with a loggia and the elephant fountain made for Hanno, Leo X's pet.
sights.when: Closed to tourists; view only from the road.
sights.q: Villa Madama, Roma

sights.name: Fornace Veschi
sights.blurb: The last of Valle Aurelia's brick kilns, shut in 1960, with an oval kiln, umbrella roof and chimney beside a shopping mall.
sights.when: Visible from outside; restored then vandalised. Pin from Google Places.
sights.q: La Vecchia Fornace Veschi, Valle Aurelia, Roma

sights.name: Viadotto del Gelsomino
sights.blurb: An eight-arch viaduct of the Vatican railway (1929–34) with a pedestrian path running beside the St Peter's station.
sights.when: Street; the path is open. Pin from Google Places (Passeggiata del Gelsomino).
sights.q: Passeggiata del Gelsomino, Roma

sights.name: Monte Ciocci greenway
sights.blurb: An 8 km path on a former rail line, with an old tunnel under a seminary and a hill with a view of the dome.
sights.when: Park open (Google shows odd Tuesday hours). Pin from Google Places.
sights.q: Parco di Monte Ciocci, Via Anastasio II, Roma

sights.name: Primavalle borgata
sights.blurb: A 1936–39 borgata of comb-plan gallery blocks built for people evicted from the Spina di Borgo, with a mural mapping the original plan.
sights.when: Street. Map pin approximate. Google's pin for Via Federico Borromeo is in a different part of the quarter.
sights.q: Via Federico Borromeo, Primavalle, Roma

sights.name: Santa Maria della Salute, Primavalle
sights.blurb: Guidi's 1960 church that closes the borgata's axis, with a 35 m travertine-clad bell tower.
sights.when: Mass hours.
sights.q: Santa Maria della Salute, Primavalle, Roma

sights.name: Forte Braschi
sights.blurb: An 1877–81 fort that has housed Italy's military intelligence since 1925, now the headquarters of AISE.
sights.when: Closed military site; the surrounding Pineto park gives views. Pin from Google Places.
sights.q: Forte Braschi, Via della Pineta Sacchetti 73, Roma

sights.name: Torrevecchia towers
sights.blurb: Four 15-storey IACP towers from 1978–84 around a piazza on a raised pedestrian deck.
sights.when: Street. Map pin approximate. The designer is probably Barucci with Passarelli and Vittorini (unconfirmed).
sights.q: Via di Torrevecchia 871, Roma

sights.name: Insugherata nature reserve
sights.blurb: A reserve where cork oaks grow on warm slopes and hornbeam and chestnut on cool ones, with 44 plants found nowhere else in Rome.
sights.when: Open (Google shows 24 hours); some entrances overgrown, so wear long trousers. Pin from Google Places.
sights.q: Riserva Naturale dell'Insugherata, Via Augusto Conti, Roma

sights.name: San Pio X alla Balduina
sights.blurb: A 1957–61 church by Ressa with Morbiducci's crucifix and a crypt reached from the piazza.
sights.when: Mass hours.
sights.q: San Pio X, Via Friggeri 87, Roma

sights.name: Ipogeo degli Ottavi
sights.blurb: A 3rd-century family tomb with a fresco of a six-year-old girl in the Elysian Fields, now in Palazzo Massimo, and her father's sarcophagus in place.
sights.when: Free, by booking (06 47788343); a restoration is planned. Pin from Google Places.
sights.q: Ipogeo degli Ottavi, Via della Stazione di Ottavia 73, Roma

sights.name: Borgo Clementino fountain and wash-house
sights.blurb: An 1866 fountain and wash-house by Sarti on a branch of the Acqua Paola, below road level on Via Trionfale.
sights.when: Street.
sights.q: Borgo Clementino, Via Trionfale, Roma

sights.name: Pastificio Cerere
sights.blurb: A 1905 pasta mill turned into artists' studios in 1973, with the courtyard in Francesca Woodman's 1977–78 photographs.
sights.when: Foundation gallery Tue–Sat 15:00–19:00 (Google), free during shows; the studios are private.
sights.q: Pastificio Cerere, Via degli Ausoni 7, Roma

sights.name: Prima Casa dei Bambini
sights.blurb: The building where Maria Montessori opened her first school on 6 January 1907, still a nursery today.
sights.when: Street only; it is a working nursery, not a museum. A 2026 bilingual QR plaque marks it.
sights.q: Via dei Marsi 58, Roma

sights.name: 19 July 1943 in San Lorenzo
sights.blurb: Plaques and scars from the first Allied raid on Rome, at the Verano gate and in the streets around it.
sights.when: Street. Map pin approximate.
sights.q: Piazzale del Verano, Roma

sights.name: Bar Marani
sights.blurb: A 1928 bar with a covered pergola and home-made gelato, in the street of San Lorenzo's 1970s radicals.
sights.when: Closed Mon; Tue–Sat 7:30–13:00 and 16:00–21:00, Sun from 8:00 (Google). Cash only, per a recent reviewer.
sights.q: Bar Marani, Via dei Volsci 57, Roma

sights.name: Torrione Prenestino
sights.blurb: An Augustan mausoleum 41 m across, left standing in a small park and recently restored down to its ancient floor level.
sights.when: Park open 24 h (Google). The register records a 2026 reopening after PNRR works with free visits on set days; the interior is usually closed. Check dates.
sights.q: Parco del Torrione Prenestino, Via Prenestina 77, Roma

sights.name: Via Fanfulla da Lodi: Accattone
sights.blurb: The street of Pasolini's first film, Accattone (1961), with the murals that now commemorate it.
sights.when: Street. Google gives the street, not the bar.
sights.q: Via Fanfulla da Lodi, Roma

sights.name: Banglatown, Via della Marranella
sights.blurb: Rome's Bengali quarter on the Torpignattara edge: shops, money-transfer offices and, behind garage doors, prayer rooms.
sights.when: Street; shops open daytime. Prayer rooms are private places: stay outside unless invited.
sights.q: Via della Marranella, Roma

sights.name: Parco Sangalli and the Aqua Alexandrina
sights.blurb: A stretch of the Alexandrine aqueduct (AD 226) inside a small park, its arches scarred by the shacks that leaned on them until the 1970s.
sights.when: Park open 24 h (Google); the surrounding streets are rough, so go in daylight.
sights.q: Parco Giordano Sangalli, Roma

sights.name: Villa De Sanctis and the quarries below
sights.blurb: A public park that sits on pozzolana quarries (the 'Labirinto Casilino') and, above ground, on land cleared of car-breakers' yards in 1994.
sights.when: Park daily about 8:00–21:00/23:00 (Google), free. Underground tours by Roma Sotterranea, about €15 (register); dates unconfirmed.
sights.q: Villa De Sanctis, Via dei Gordiani 5, Roma

sights.name: Villa Gordiani: Tor de' Schiavi
sights.blurb: A 17.7 m domed Roman tomb with a barrel vault on one central pillar, in a park of cisterns and a medieval tower.
sights.when: Park 7:00–18:00 (Google); interior usually shut.
sights.q: Mausoleo di Tor de' Schiavi, Via Prenestina 351, Roma

sights.name: Casilino 23
sights.blurb: A 1960s public-housing estate planned by Quaroni and others, 29 slab blocks fanning round four centres.
sights.when: Street; people live here. Google's pin is the estate's covered market (mornings; to 19:30 Tue, Thu, Sat; closed Sun).
sights.q: Casilino 23, Via Francesco Ferraironi, Roma

sights.name: Centocelle: Italy's first airfield
sights.blurb: The field where Wilbur Wright made 67 flights in April 1909, now a park whose old runway is a coloured sports track.
sights.when: Park open 24 h (Google). The new park opened 22 Sep 2026.
sights.q: Parco Archeologico di Centocelle, Via Casilina 761, Roma

sights.name: Alexandrine arches on Viale Togliatti
sights.blurb: Arches 20–25 m high carrying the AD 226 aqueduct across the Fosso di Centocelle, with a tiny chapel in the hollow beside the viaduct.
sights.when: Street. Map pin approximate.
sights.q: Viale Togliatti, Via dei Pioppi, Roma

sights.name: Il Quagliaro
sights.blurb: A family trattoria (1958) in Quarticciolo whose house dish is quail roasted with mushrooms.
sights.when: Lunch and dinner; Mon dinner only, Sun lunch only (Google). Book at weekends.
sights.q: Il Quagliaro, Largo Mola di Bari 17, Roma

sights.name: Pietralata borgata
sights.blurb: A 1922 settlement for war veterans, one of Rome's official borgate, whose streets are named after stones.
sights.when: Street. Google gives Via Feronia.
sights.q: Via Feronia, Roma

sights.name: Santa Maria del Soccorso, Tiburtino III
sights.blurb: A church of 1937–38 by Tullio Rossi in the Tiburtino III borgata, with a frieze reading 'Sancta Maria succurre miseris'.
sights.when: Open 24 h Mon–Fri on Google; Sat closed; Sun 10:30–12:30. Treat as Mass hours.
sights.q: Chiesa Santa Maria del Soccorso, Via del Badile 1, Roma

sights.name: Biblioteca Vaccheria Nardi
sights.blurb: A public library in a former dairy farm, with reading tables under a holm oak.
sights.when: Mon, Wed, Thu 9:00–19:00; Tue, Fri 9:00–15:00; closed Sat–Sun (Google).
sights.q: Biblioteca Vaccheria Nardi, Via di Grotta di Gregna 37, Roma

sights.name: Museo di Casal de' Pazzi
sights.blurb: A museum built over a 200,000-year-old Aniene riverbed, with the tusks of the straight-tusked elephant found here.
sights.when: Free; book via 060608. Google lists Tue–Fri 9:00–14:00, Sat–Sun 10:00–14:00. The register says the outer walkway and garden shut in July 2026 and may be open again.
sights.q: Museo di Casal de' Pazzi, Via Egidio Galbani, Roma

sights.name: Casa Pasolini, Rebibbia
sights.blurb: The small flat where Pasolini lived while writing Ragazzi di vita (1951–54), restored and open free.
sights.when: Thu–Fri 9:00–14:00, Sat–Sun 10:00–18:00; book on the Musei Italiani app; max 15 people.
sights.q: Casa Pasolini, Via Giovanni Tagliere 3, Roma

sights.name: Complesso Giorgio Morandi
sights.blurb: A 1970–79 public-housing estate of 504 flats round a central court, designed as a racetrack loop.
sights.when: Street, daytime. Map pin approximate: Google's nearest point is at Viale Morandi 199.
sights.q: Viale Giorgio Morandi, Roma

sights.name: Torre della Cervelletta
sights.blurb: A 13th-century 30 m tower and a Borghese farmhouse of 1630 at the edge of a nature reserve.
sights.when: Exterior only: closed for risk of collapse, still unrestored. Reserve paths and a summer cinema are open.
sights.q: Castello della Cervelletta, Roma

sights.name: San Basilio
sights.blurb: A 1940 village for large families, rebuilt in 1953–58, and the scene of the revolt of 8 September 1974.
sights.when: Street; people live here. The pin is Google's Via Recanati.
sights.q: Piazza Recanati, San Basilio, Roma

sights.name: Acqua Vergine springs, Salone
sights.blurb: The springs that have fed the Trevi Fountain since 19 BC, still run by Acea and still gravity-fed.
sights.when: Outside only. Google pins the Acea plant ('Source of the Virgo Aqueduct').
sights.q: Sorgenti Acqua Vergine, Via Collatina, Roma

sights.name: Castello di Lunghezza
sights.blurb: A castle on a tufa crag over the ancient town of Collatia, restored by Munthe in 1881 as a clinic, now a theme park and TV set.
sights.when: Open on event days only; Google lists daily 10:00–19:00 and the register says a Christmas season starts mid-November. Check first.
sights.q: Castello di Lunghezza, Via della Tenuta del Cavaliere 230, Roma

sights.name: Ponte di Nona
sights.blurb: A seven-arch Republican bridge, 72 m long and 16 m high, which still carries traffic on the Prenestina.
sights.when: View from below along the Marrana, and from the road. Google gives no hours.
sights.q: Ponte di Nona, Via Prenestina, Roma

sights.name: Gabii
sights.blurb: A Latin city older than Rome, on the rim of a drained volcanic lake, built of lapis gabinus.
sights.when: Google lists Sat–Sun 9:30–13:00; a reviewer found the gate locked at 8:00 and others report 'open on demand'. The register says events only. Check before travelling. The manual check puts it in Municipio VI; Google's address says Monte Compatri.
sights.q: Area archeologica di Gabii, Via Prenestina Nuova km 2

sights.name: Santa Maria Causa Nostrae Laetitiae, Torre Gaia
sights.blurb: A Rococo-style church by Tullio Rossi (1939–41) for a workers' village.
sights.when: Mon–Thu mornings and some afternoons; Sun open (Google). Mass hours.
sights.q: Piazza Siderea 1, Roma

sights.name: Palazzina Mancioli I
sights.blurb: Ridolfi and Frankl's 1952–54 apartment house on a garage, with a concrete band at the join and a perforated-brick crown.
sights.when: Street view only.
sights.q: Palazzina Mancioli, Via Lusitania 29, Roma

sights.name: Palazzina Mancioli II
sights.blurb: Ridolfi's last Roman palazzina (1958–60).
sights.when: Street view only.
sights.q: Via Vulci 9, Roma

sights.name: Santi Antonio e Annibale Maria
sights.blurb: A 1955–66 church of travertine that copies Bolsena's Santa Cristina in neo-Romanesque style.
sights.when: Open for prayer (Google); check Mass hours.
sights.q: Piazza Asti 10, Roma

sights.name: Ex STEFER depot, now Happio
sights.blurb: The tram depot of the Castelli line (1903–80), now a shopping centre; trams had to be pushed in because the depot had no turning loop.
sights.when: Mall open daily 10:00–20:30 (Google).
sights.q: Happio, Via Appia Nuova 448, Roma

sights.name: Tombs of Via Latina
sights.blurb: Roman tombs, mostly 2nd century, along a surviving stretch of the basalt Via Latina.
sights.when: Ticketed (register); the Appia park ticket also covers Sette Bassi and the Quintili. Reviewers say entry is free: check.
sights.q: Parco delle Tombe di Via Latina, Via dell'Arco di Travertino 151, Roma

sights.name: Tomb of Annia Regilla
sights.blurb: The two-colour brick tomb of Annia Regilla, about AD 160, long called the Temple of the god Rediculus.
sights.when: Exterior only.
sights.q: Sepolcro Annia Regilla, Via della Caffarella 15, Roma

sights.name: Sant'Urbano alla Caffarella
sights.blurb: A 2nd-century temple turned into a church in the 9th century, with 11th-century frescoes and a small crypt.
sights.when: Closed except for rare special openings (one on 13 June 2026 under the PNRR programme).
sights.q: Sant'Urbano alla Caffarella, Roma

sights.name: Cava romana dell'Appia Antica
sights.blurb: 1.5 km of Roman quarry galleries inside the park, with a mushroom farm, a WWII shelter and a reconstructed mithraeum.
sights.when: Weekend tours only: Google lists Sat–Sun 9:30–18:00, a sign says Sat 16:00 and Sun 11:00. Book first; reviewers report unanswered emails.
sights.q: Il Labirinto di Roma, Via della Caffarella 44, Roma

sights.name: Casale della Vaccareccia
sights.blurb: A Caffarelli farmhouse round a medieval tower, with a flock of about 1,000 sheep and a farm shop selling pecorino and ricotta.
sights.when: Farm shop; reviewers note it can be closed.
sights.q: Casale della Vaccareccia, Via della Caffarella 40, Roma

sights.name: Nymphaeum of Egeria
sights.blurb: A 2nd-century nymphaeum with a headless statue of the river-god Almo in its back niche, once used as an osteria.
sights.when: Always open, free; PNRR maintenance in 2026.
sights.q: Ninfeo di Egeria, Via della Caffarella, Roma

sights.name: Fonte Acqua Egeria
sights.blurb: A naturally fizzy spring where you fill your own bottles; bottled since 1948.
sights.when: Mon–Sat 8:00–17:30, Sun 8:00–13:30 (Google); weekend farmers' market. Reviewers report about 9 cents a litre; unconfirmed.
sights.q: Egeria - L'Acqua Santa di Roma, Via dell'Almone 111, Roma

sights.name: Porta Furba
sights.blurb: An arch of Sixtus V's Acqua Felice over Via Tuscolana, with Clement XII's 1733 fountain of a bat-like winged mask spouting into a shell.
sights.when: Street. Google's 'Porta Furba' is the metro station, not the arch.
sights.q: Porta Furba, Via Tuscolana, Roma

sights.name: M.U.Ro: Quadraro murals
sights.blurb: The open-air Museo Urban di Roma: Diavù's Quadraro People, Lucamaleonte's seven wasps and Omino71's mural.
sights.when: Street, any time. The M.U.Ro project's online map lists every work.
sights.q: Via dei Quintili 163, Roma

sights.name: Santa Maria del Buon Consiglio
sights.blurb: The Quadraro parish church (1916), with a 1994 plaque to Don Gioacchino Rey, 'parroco delle trincee'.
sights.q: Via Tuscolana 613, Roma

sights.name: Parco XVII Aprile 1944
sights.blurb: The memorial park for the Quadraro round-up of 17 April 1944 (Operazione Balena), when the Germans deported at least 683 men.
sights.when: Park open 24 h (Google).
sights.q: Parco 17 Aprile 1944, Via Asconio Pediano, Roma

sights.name: Mausoleo di Monte del Grano
sights.blurb: Rome's third-largest burial mound, about 50 m across, tied to the 'Alexander Severus' sarcophagus found in 1582.
sights.when: Reopened 2026; free visits on set days. Check dates.
sights.q: Mausoleo di Monte del Grano, Piazza dei Tribuni, Roma

sights.name: Torre del Fiscale
sights.blurb: A 30 m tower of 1277 where the Claudia and Marcia aqueducts cross twice, set in a park of ruins and wartime shelters.
sights.when: Park 7:30–19:30 daily (Google); the register gives 10:00 to sunset.
sights.q: Torre Fiscale Park, Via dell'Acquedotto Felice 120, Roma

sights.name: Parco degli Acquedotti
sights.blurb: A 240 ha park crossed by seven of Rome's eleven aqueducts, the opening shot of La dolce vita.
sights.when: Open 24 h; avoid after dark (reviewers).
sights.q: Parco degli Acquedotti, Via Lemonia, Roma

sights.name: San Policarpo
sights.blurb: A brutalist church (Nicolosi, 1964–67) whose six beams form a star under a lantern.
sights.q: Piazza Aruleno Celio Sabino 50, Roma

sights.name: Basilica di San Giovanni Bosco
sights.blurb: A 1952–59 basilica by Rapisardi with a dome about 40 m high, the third in Rome.
sights.q: Viale dei Salesiani 9, Roma

sights.name: Cinecittà
sights.blurb: The studio city opened on 28 April 1937, now with a museum and the set of the series Rome.
sights.when: Cinecittà si Mostra: closed Tue (register) – Google also shows Mon closed; book an English tour.
sights.q: Cinecittà, Via Tuscolana 1055, Roma

sights.name: Villa dei Quintili
sights.blurb: A huge Roman suburban villa on the Appia, with a museum, views and a VR experience.
sights.when: Tue–Sun 9:00–16:30 (Google); ticket about €8, valid at other Appia park sites.
sights.q: Villa dei Quintili, Via Appia Nuova 1092, Roma

sights.name: Ippodromo delle Capannelle
sights.blurb: A racecourse of 1926 with the Claudia aqueduct seen from the stands.
sights.when: Racing resumed 4 Sep 2026 with free entry; calendar to 29 Dec; Hippotours via 060608.
sights.q: Ippodromo delle Capannelle, Via Appia Nuova 1245, Roma

sights.name: Villa dei Sette Bassi
sights.blurb: A 2nd-century villa, called 'Roma Vecchia', recently excavated and shown on weekend guided tours.
sights.when: Sat–Sun guided tours at 11:00 and 15:00 (Google; a visitor on 8 Nov 2026). Booking reported; confirm.
sights.q: Villa dei Sette Bassi, Via Tuscolana 1700, Roma

sights.name: Parco della Legalità
sights.blurb: A small park on the site of a demolished Casamonica villa (2018), kept up by volunteers.
sights.when: Daily 9:00–19:00 (Google).
sights.q: Parco della Legalità, Via Roccabernarda 15, Roma

sights.name: INA-Casa Tuscolano: Mamma Roma's estate
sights.blurb: The INA-Casa housing blocks of Tuscolano I–II, the estate of Pasolini's Mamma Roma (1962).
sights.when: Street; people live here. Map pin approximate.
sights.q: Via Lucio Sestio, Tuscolano, Roma

sights.name: Garbatella
sights.blurb: Rome's 1920 garden suburb for port and factory workers: courtyards, arches and stairways in a deliberately picturesque style.
sights.when: Street; the courtyards are semi-public, so walk in quietly.
sights.q: Garbatella, Roma

sights.name: Piazza Benedetto Brin: the first stone
sights.blurb: The square where Garbatella began, with its founding plaque in an arch and the first four lots in barocchetto style.
sights.when: Street; courtyards semi-public.
sights.q: Piazza Benedetto Brin, Roma

sights.name: Alberghi suburbani: the 'hotels' for the evicted
sights.blurb: Sabbatini's 1927–29 dormitory blocks with 997 rooms, built to house families moved out of the centre, with a bottle-shaped plan and a clock stopped at 11:25.
sights.when: Street; people live here.
sights.q: Albergo Rosso, Garbatella, Roma

sights.name: Lotto 8 and Trotta's cottages
sights.blurb: Marconi's lot 8 and Trotta's 1925–27 cottages, built for people moved out of shanties.
sights.when: Street. Map pin approximate.
sights.q: Via Giuseppe Massaia, Garbatella, Roma

sights.name: San Francesco Saverio alla Garbatella
sights.blurb: The suburb's 1931–33 parish church by Calza Bini, with a famous Madonna that locals say saved Garbatella from the 1943 bombs.
sights.when: Daily 7:30–20:00 (Google; weekends to 21:30).
sights.q: Parrocchia San Francesco Saverio alla Garbatella, Via Daniele Comboni 4, Roma

sights.name: Scuola Cesare Battisti and the film squares
sights.blurb: The school whose pillars Moretti used in Caro diario, beside the Garbatella of I Cesaroni and Totò e Marcellino.
sights.when: Street; school grounds closed.
sights.q: Scuola Cesare Battisti, Piazza Damiano Sauli, Roma

sights.name: Dar Moschino
sights.blurb: A 1970s trattoria on Piazza Brin, with horses on the walls and fixed days for tripe and gnocchi.
sights.when: Closed Sunday; book. Tripe on Tuesday, gnocchi on Thursday.
sights.q: Dar Moschino, Piazza Benedetto Brin 5, Roma

sights.name: Biblioteca Moby Dick and Teatro Palladium
sights.blurb: A library inside Sabbatini's 1926–30 public baths, an Ostia-style apartment block reinvented for Garbatella.
sights.when: Library hours; some sources disagree, check before going.
sights.q: Biblioteca Moby Dick, Via Edoardo Borsi 7, Roma

sights.name: The bridge under Piazza Biffi
sights.blurb: A Roman bridge found 7 m down in 2004 over a branch of the Almone, now visible under a plexiglass roof in the square.
sights.when: Street.
sights.q: Piazza Eugenio Biffi, Roma

sights.name: Pyramid of Cestius
sights.blurb: A 36 m white marble pyramid of the 1st century BC built into the Aurelian walls.
sights.when: Exterior always visible. Interior only on guided openings (Sept 2026 dates announced; regular schedule unknown).
sights.q: Piramide di Caio Cestio, Roma

sights.name: Palazzo delle Poste Ostiense
sights.blurb: Libera and De Renzi's 1933–35 post office: diamond end windows, a glass-block oval skylight over the hall and a long portico.
sights.when: Post office hours; go in as a customer to see the hall.
sights.q: Ufficio Postale Roma Ostiense, Via Marmorata 2, Roma

sights.name: Roma Ostiense station
sights.blurb: The station that was rebuilt in a few weeks for Hitler's visit of 3 May 1938; the permanent building opened on 28 Oct 1940.
sights.when: Open (station).
sights.q: Stazione Roma Ostiense, Piazzale dei Partigiani, Roma

sights.name: Ex Mercati Generali
sights.blurb: Saffi's wholesale-market halls on Via Ostiense: a fenced site where the fish pavilion roof collapsed in Feb 2026 and a marsh grew over the buried Almone.
sights.when: Fenced building site; look from Via Ostiense. A student-residence plan (Hines) is in the pipeline.
sights.q: Ex Mercati Generali, Via Ostiense 154, Roma

sights.name: Roma Tre on Via Ostiense
sights.blurb: A university made out of factories: the Bordoni glassworks, the Alfa Romeo works with Isotta's 1961 round wing, and the old Tommaseo school.
sights.when: Campus Mon–Fri 8–20, Sat 8–15 (Google). Courtyards visible from the gate.
sights.q: Università Roma Tre, Via Ostiense 133, Roma

sights.name: Tombs of the San Paolo rock
sights.blurb: A row of Roman tombs on the cliff beside Via Ostiense, once a frescoed chamber, now a site that opens only on special days.
sights.when: Opened by a GEP visit on 26 Sep 2026 (060608); regular opening unknown.
sights.q: Tombe della rupe di San Paolo, Via Ostiense 251, Roma

sights.name: Vasca Navale: the ship-model tank
sights.blurb: The 1929 national ship-model basin, now part of Roma Tre's engineering campus with an optics works and a balloon works.
sights.when: Campus Mon–Fri 7–20, Sat to 13 (Google); the tank is inside.
sights.q: Roma Tre Ingegneria, Via della Vasca Navale 79, Roma

sights.name: INA-Casa Valco San Paolo
sights.blurb: A 1950s INA-Casa estate in Municipio VIII, the working-class neighbour of the university campus.
sights.when: Street; people live here.
sights.q: Valco San Paolo, Roma

sights.name: Catacomb of Commodilla
sights.blurb: A 4th-century catacomb under Via delle Sette Chiese with some of the earliest writing in Italian.
sights.when: By appointment with the PCAS (06 446 5610); reviewers found it closed and unmarked, one got a tour.
sights.q: Catacombe di Commodilla, Via delle Sette Chiese 42, Roma

sights.name: Santa Maria Regina degli Apostoli
sights.blurb: A 1947–54 Baroque church in reinforced concrete, with Alberione's tomb in the crypt.
sights.when: Church hours; Google lists none.
sights.q: Basilica di Santa Maria Regina degli Apostoli alla Montagnola, Via Antonino Pio 75, Roma

sights.name: Montagnola memorial: 10 September 1943
sights.blurb: A monument built round an ancient column to the soldiers and civilians who died here on 10 Sep 1943, with a priest who raised a white sheet.
sights.when: Open park; free.
sights.q: Parco Monumentale dei Caduti della Montagnola, Roma

sights.name: Forte Ardeatino
sights.blurb: An 1879–82 fort of Rome's entrenched camp, blown up by the Germans in 1944, in a 5.5 ha park.
sights.when: Park open; fort fenced.
sights.q: Forte Ardeatina, Via di Grotta Perfetta, Roma

sights.name: Parco di Tor Marancia
sights.blurb: A rustic park along the open Marrana di Grotta Perfetta, saved from building in 2002.
sights.when: Open daily 9:00–20:30 (Google).
sights.q: Parco di Viale Londra, Tor Marancia, Roma

sights.name: Tor Marancia 'Shanghai' murals
sights.blurb: Lotto 1 of Tor Marancia, with 22–23 large murals painted in 2015 on 1947–48 housing blocks nicknamed 'Shanghai'.
sights.when: Courtyard open; people live here.
sights.q: Via di Tor Marancia 63, Roma

sights.name: Santa Francesca Romana all'Ardeatino
sights.blurb: A parish church whose date is disputed, 1938 or 1967.
sights.when: Parish hours.
sights.q: Chiesa Santa Francesca Romana all'Ardeatino, Roma

sights.name: Torri Ligini
sights.blurb: Two 1961 towers on Viale America, known as the 'Beirut of EUR' until they were reclad and reopened on 12 Oct 2026.
sights.when: Street.
sights.q: Torri dell'EUR (Torri Ligini), Viale America 331, Roma

sights.name: Palazzo degli Uffici (EUR)
sights.blurb: Minnucci's 1937–39 office palace with a fountain of 18 two-tone basins, Severini mosaics, the 1960 Olympic model of EUR and a bunker.
sights.when: Exterior free. Inside there is an exhibition 'EUR 90' (Google reviewer); shelter by rare opening.
sights.q: Palazzo degli Uffici, Via Ciro il Grande 16, Roma

sights.name: Archivio Centrale dello Stato
sights.blurb: The state archive in the former E42 Palazzo delle Forze Armate, with an exhibition room and an original of the Constitution.
sights.when: Tue–Thu 10–12 and 15:30–17, free; guided visits by email.
sights.q: Archivio Centrale dello Stato, Piazzale degli Archivi 27, Roma

sights.name: Gismondi's model of Rome (Museo della Civiltà Romana)
sights.blurb: The giant plaster model of imperial Rome by Gismondi, in a museum that is mostly closed and was used as a cemetery in Spectre.
sights.when: Museum largely closed; model-hall reopening announced for Jul 2026 but unconfirmed. Check before going.
sights.q: Museo della Civiltà Romana, Piazza Giovanni Agnelli 10, Roma

sights.name: Il Fungo, the EUR water tower
sights.blurb: A 1957–59 water tank on eight split pillars that feeds the EUR lake cascades, with a restaurant on top.
sights.when: Street; bistro below Mon–Sat 8–20 (Google). Restaurant above reopens at times.
sights.q: Il Fungo EUR, Piazza Pakistan 1, Roma

sights.name: Abbazia delle Tre Fontane
sights.blurb: Three churches on the traditional site of St Paul's beheading, with a Trappist brewery and eucalyptus planted against malaria.
sights.when: Daily 6:30–20:45 (Google); shop Mon–Sat.
sights.q: Abbazia delle Tre Fontane, Via di Acque Salvie 1, Roma

sights.name: Centro Idrico Vigna Murata tower
sights.blurb: An 85–95 m steel water tower with a flying-saucer top that feeds about 400,000 Romans, planned as a science park of water.
sights.when: Closed; view from the park below. FAI opened it on 24 Oct 2026; it opens about once a year.
sights.q: Centro Idrico Vigna Murata, Via del Casale Solaro, Roma

sights.name: Giuliano-Dalmata: the exiles' quarter
sights.blurb: The village built from 1947 for Italians who left Istria and Dalmatia, with a Karst boulder monument and the Fiume museum.
sights.when: Monument open; the Fiume archive-museum Mon–Wed and Fri 15–18:45, Thu 10–12, closed Aug.
sights.q: Monumento ai caduti Giuliani e Dalmati, Roma

sights.name: San Marco Evangelista in Agro Laurentino
sights.blurb: Canino and Rizzi's 1969–71 circular church with two huge columns holding up a flat roof.
sights.when: Mon–Fri 7:30–19:30, Sat–Sun 8–20 (Google).
sights.q: Parrocchia San Marco Evangelista in Agro Laurentino, Piazza Giuliani e Dalmati 20, Roma

sights.name: Acqua Acetosa Laurentina reserve
sights.blurb: A nature reserve around an 8th-century BC fortified village (Tellenae?) and a disused sparkling-water plant.
sights.when: Open 24 h (Google); the settlement itself is closed.
sights.q: Riserva Naturale Laurentino-Acqua Acetosa, Roma

sights.name: Museo Storico della Motorizzazione Militare
sights.blurb: About 300 military vehicles in six pavilions on the Cecchignola army campus.
sights.when: Sat 9–12, free, booking only (06 5023 7374); bring ID. Reviewers were turned away.
sights.q: Museo Storico della Motorizzazione Militare, Viale dell'Esercito 170, Roma

sights.name: Quartiere INCIS Decima
sights.blurb: A 1957–65 neighbourhood by Moretti, Libera and others: a Roman-camp plan with blocks on pilotis and a round central square.
sights.when: Street; park open 24 h.
sights.q: Decima, Via Romualdo Chiesa, Roma

sights.name: Santa Maria Mater Ecclesiae al Torrino
sights.blurb: Pacini's 1986–88 church with a coffered ceiling and four box skylights; its first stone came from old St Peter's.
sights.when: Parish hours.
sights.q: Chiesa Santa Maria Mater Ecclesiae, Via Sciangai 10, Roma

sights.name: Spinaceto
sights.blurb: A 1965-plan estate built along a single spine road, with Chiarini's long 'omnibus' blocks.
sights.when: Street.
sights.q: Viale dei Caduti per la Resistenza, Spinaceto, Roma

sights.name: San Giovanni Evangelista a Spinaceto
sights.blurb: Lafuente and Rebecchini's 1975–79 church of intersecting concrete cylinders, with glass-block lunettes where roof meets walls.
sights.when: Parish hours; parking on site.
sights.q: Parrocchia San Giovanni Evangelista, Via Raffaele Aversa 44, Roma

sights.name: Cimitero Laurentino: Garden of Angels
sights.blurb: A huge modern cemetery with Testa's round copper-roofed chapel in the Giardino degli Angeli (2012).
sights.when: Daily 7:30–17:00 (Google); internal buses on some days.
sights.q: Cimitero Laurentino, Via Laurentina km 13.5, Roma

sights.name: Arco dei Quattro Venti and the Villa Corsini gate
sights.blurb: The arch at the edge of Villa Pamphilj, built on the ruins of the Villa Corsini that the French used against the Roman Republic in 1849.

sights.q: Arco dei Quattro Venti, Piazzale Ragazzi del 1849, Roma

sights.name: Villa del Vascello
sights.blurb: Plautilla Bricci's ship-shaped villa of 1663–68, held by Medici's legion in 1849 and now the seat of the Grande Oriente d'Italia.
sights.when: Private; open only on rare FAI days.
sights.q: Villa il Vascello, Via di San Pancrazio 8, Roma

sights.name: Basilica di San Pancrazio
sights.blurb: A basilica on the grave of the young martyr Pancras, with a catacomb below by booking.
sights.when: Mon–Sat 6:30–12 and 16–19, Sun 6:30–13 and 16–19 (Google); catacomb by booking.
sights.q: Basilica di San Pancrazio, Piazza San Pancrazio 5D, Roma

sights.name: Villa Doria Pamphilj
sights.blurb: A 184 ha park on the Gianicolo with a secret garden, a lake with bald cypress and the Trajan-Paola aqueduct as its north wall.
sights.when: Daily 7:00–20:00 (Google). Some fountains and the theatre are closed for works.
sights.q: Villa Doria Pamphilj, Via di San Pancrazio, Roma

sights.name: Pamphilj columbaria
sights.blurb: Roman columbarium tombs at the edge of the park, with an Augustan white mosaic and painted niches.
sights.when: Not walk-in; ask the Soprintendenza.
sights.q: Colombari di Villa Doria Pamphilj, Via Aurelia Antica 111, Roma

sights.name: Forte Aurelia Antica
sights.blurb: An 1877–81 fort of Rome's ring, restored by the Guardia di Finanza and reopened as a cultural centre on 22 Apr 2026.
sights.when: Daily 12:00–20:00 (Google; check days). Free.
sights.q: Forte Aurelia Antica, Via Aurelia Antica 433, Roma

sights.name: Villa Sciarra
sights.blurb: A hill park with statues from Brignano, a restored aviary, a twelve-months exedra and a 1932 plaque where Mussolini's name was erased.
sights.when: Park hours; PNRR works in lots, expect fences.
sights.q: Villa Sciarra, Roma

sights.name: Monteverde Vecchio villini
sights.blurb: Streets of turreted villini and stairways laid out in 1909 for a new middle-class quarter, from Piazza Rosolino Pilo to Largo Ravizza.
sights.when: Street.
sights.q: Piazza Rosolino Pilo, Roma

sights.name: Pasolini's Monteverde addresses
sights.blurb: Two flats where Pasolini lived: Via Fonteiana 86 (1954–59) and Via Carini 45 (1959–63), with a plaque, plus the bar of Ecce bombo.
sights.when: Street.
sights.q: Via Giacinto Carini 45, Roma

sights.name: Bixio Caffè (ex Caffè Faustini)
sights.blurb: A 1935 neighbourhood bar reopened in November 2025 under Frida Giannini.
sights.q: Bixio Caffè Bistrot, Via Alessandro Poerio 21, Roma

sights.name: Vitali: the Monteverde bar
sights.blurb: A family bar and osteria on Via Lorenzo Valla that began as a tobacco shop and trades as 'dal 1914'.
sights.when: Mon–Wed 7–21, Thu–Sat 7–22:30, Sun 10–15 (Google). Gnocchi on Thursday.
sights.q: Vitali dal 1914, Via Lorenzo Valla 38, Roma

sights.name: Catacomb of Ponziano
sights.blurb: A catacomb 'at the capped bear' with a submerged baptistery fed by a spring and a wartime shelter.
sights.when: By appointment with the PCAS; 2026 access unknown.
sights.q: Catacomba di San Ponziano, Via Alessandro Poerio 59, Roma

sights.name: Site of the Monteverde Jewish catacomb
sights.blurb: The zone where one of Rome's Jewish catacombs lay, destroyed by quarrying; nothing is visible.
sights.when: Nothing visible. Map pin approximate.
sights.q: Via Vincenzo Monti, Roma

sights.name: Grattacieli di Donna Olimpia
sights.blurb: The 1930–32 'skyscrapers' of Donna Olimpia: nine-storey blocks with 534 flats, the setting of Pasolini's Ragazzi di vita.
sights.when: Street; courtyards are residential.
sights.q: Via di Donna Olimpia 30, Roma

sights.name: Scuole Giorgio Franceschi
sights.blurb: The school whose left wing collapsed on 17 March 1951, as in Pasolini's novel; a second Pasolini plaque is here.
sights.when: Street; school grounds closed.
sights.q: Scuola Giorgio Franceschi, Via di Donna Olimpia 45, Roma

sights.name: Mercato San Giovanni di Dio
sights.blurb: Monteverde Nuovo's big tin-roof market, about to be moved to temporary boxes and rebuilt.
sights.when: Mon–Wed 6:30–13:30, Thu–Sat 6–14, closed Sun (Google). Temporary-market works start about 2 Dec 2026; the old market works until about January 2027.
sights.q: Mercato San Giovanni di Dio, Piazza San Giovanni di Dio, Roma

sights.name: Ospedale San Camillo
sights.blurb: A hospital city opened in 1929 as the 'del Littorio', with Tuscan-Renaissance pavilions and a church of the same year.
sights.when: Grounds open; it is a working hospital.
sights.q: Ospedale San Camillo-Forlanini, Circonvallazione Gianicolense 87, Roma

sights.name: Forte Bravetta and the Parco dei Martiri
sights.blurb: A fort used as an army firing range, now a park memorial to people shot here under fascism and in 1944.
sights.when: Park 7:00–20:30 (Google); the parade ground by booking via 060608.
sights.q: Parco dei Martiri di Forte Bravetta, Roma

sights.name: Ponte Marconi
sights.blurb: Rome's longest bridge (235.7 m), begun in 1937 and opened on 26 Feb 1955, seen best from the cycle path.
sights.when: Open.
sights.q: Ponte Guglielmo Marconi, Roma

sights.name: Drugstore Museum and the Portuense necropolis
sights.blurb: A small museum of tombs and finds from the Portuense necropolis, built on the old Purfina land, and the Pozzo Pantaleo nearby.
sights.when: By booking: ss-abap-rm.drugstore@cultura.gov.it or 060608; hours unknown.
sights.q: Drugstore Museum, Via Portuense 317, Roma

sights.name: Sacra Famiglia al Portuense
sights.blurb: A circular 1978 church by Paniconi and Pediconi with a coloured-steel bell tower and a crucifix by Ennio Tesei.
sights.when: Daily 6:30–19:30 (Google).
sights.q: Chiesa della Sacra Famiglia al Portuense, Via Filippo Tajani 10, Roma

sights.name: Nervi's ferrocement warehouse
sights.blurb: A small undulating shed of 1944–45, the first building in ferrocement and the only survivor of Nervi's prefabricated works, hidden in a car park.
sights.when: Exterior from the street; Municipio XI walks include it. Check access.
sights.q: Padiglione di ferrocemento di Pier Luigi Nervi, Via della Magliana 238, Roma

sights.name: Magliana Nuova
sights.blurb: A 1960s estate built 6.5 m below the Tiber embankment, with a history of housing struggles.
sights.when: Street. Map pin approximate.
sights.q: Magliana Nuova, Roma

sights.name: Magliana pumping stations
sights.blurb: Sluice gates and pumps that close when the Tiber rises and lift storm water over the embankment.
sights.when: Exterior; name and capacity unknown. Pin is the riverside park.
sights.q: Parco del Tevere Magliana, Roma

sights.name: San Gregorio Magno alla Magliana Nuova
sights.blurb: Aloysi and Vichi's 1975–77 church of exposed prefabricated panels, raised above its square.
sights.when: Mass hours.
sights.q: San Gregorio Magno alla Magliana Nuova, Piazza Certaldo 85, Roma

sights.name: Ex Oleificio, Borgata Petrelli
sights.blurb: A 20,000 m² olive-oil mill that burned in 2019.
sights.when: Do not enter; current state unknown. Map pin approximate.
sights.q: Via dell'Imbrecciato, Roma

sights.name: Catacomb of Generosa
sights.blurb: A catacomb of the Arval grove, with a fresco of the Crowning of the Martyrs and a ruined basilica above ground.
sights.when: By arrangement: Comitato 349 7930661 and PCAS 06 4465610; autumn Giornata delle Catacombe.
sights.q: Catacombe di Generosa, Via della Magliana, Roma

sights.name: Castello della Magliana
sights.blurb: A c.1480 papal hunting lodge where Leo X heard of the capture of Milan in 1521, held by the Order of Malta since 1959.
sights.when: Occasional Saturday visits 15:30–17:30; book on 349 7930661.
sights.q: Castello della Magliana, Via L. E. Morselli 13, Roma

sights.name: Trullo: poets' walls and murals
sights.blurb: A working-class borgata whose walls carry poems in marker and murals by the Pittori Anonimi del Trullo.
sights.when: Street; open 24 h (Google).
sights.q: Arte di Strada in Via del Trullo, Roma

sights.name: Valle dei Casali reserve
sights.blurb: A reserve around the Fosso di Affogalasino with more than 90 farmhouses, wild parakeets and a botanic garden.
sights.when: Casa del Parco 9–17 (register); reserve open.
sights.q: Casa del Parco Valle dei Casali, Via del Casaletto 400, Roma

sights.name: Palazzo del Governatorato, Ostia
sights.blurb: Fasolo's 1920s town hall for the new seaside town: a corner tower with trophy reliefs and sgraffito by Calzolari.
sights.when: Exterior free; it holds municipal offices (Municipio X). A reviewer says the courtyard can be entered since the restoration.
sights.q: Palazzo del Governatorato, Piazza della Stazione Vecchia 26, Lido di Ostia

sights.name: Santa Maria Regina Pacis, Ostia
sights.blurb: Giulio Magni's church of 1919–late 1920s on the highest dune, on axis with the sea and the town hall.
sights.q: Parrocchia Santa Maria Regina Pacis, Piazza Regina Pacis 13, Lido di Ostia

sights.name: Lido Centro station and the 1921 stele
sights.blurb: A 1951 station for the Roma–Lido line, with a stele saved from the bombed first station in its atrium.
sights.when: Trains about every 12–20 minutes from Piramide (Google reviews, 2025–26).
sights.q: Stazione Lido Centro, Piazzale della Stazione del Lido, Lido di Ostia

sights.name: Ostia fire station (1936)
sights.blurb: A rationalist fire station of 1936 that still works as one.
sights.when: Fire station (reported closed for weeks in Jul 2026); look from the street.
sights.q: Distaccamento Vigili del Fuoco Ostia Lido, Via Angelo Celli 4, Lido di Ostia

sights.name: Palmerini's ICP housing, Ostia
sights.blurb: Camillo Palmerini's public housing of 1926–29 on Corso Duca di Genova: Ostia's small Garbatella.
sights.when: Street. People live here.
sights.q: Case popolari di Corso Duca di Genova, Camillo Palmerini, Lido di Ostia

sights.name: Collegio IV Novembre (ex GIL)
sights.blurb: A 1932–37 school-barracks for boys with a 75 m tower that German engineers blew up in 1943.

p: You walk into an imperial hall at the foot of the Palatine and find it painted from floor to ceiling, layer over layer: this is the oldest Christian monument in the Roman Forum. The building was Roman first, a vestibule to the palace ramps of Domitian's time, and in the 6th century it became a church. For about three hundred years painters kept adding to it, so one wall can carry three or four campaigns of saints and Madonnas on top of each other.

The church survived because it was buried. An earthquake in 847 brought the Palatine slopes down on it, the clergy moved to Santa Maria Nova (today Santa Francesca Romana), and a later church was even built on top of the ruins in 1617. It was removed when excavators found the old church in 1900. After that the site was closed for most of the twentieth century; it reopened in 2016 after a long conservation programme.

The thing to find is the "palimpsest wall" next to the apse, where you can count the layers like strata in a rock face. Byzantine-trained painters worked here in the 7th and 8th centuries, when Rome was still governed from Constantinople, and the church is one of the best places anywhere to see what Greek-style painting looked like in the West before the year 800.

Practical: it is a "SUPER site" of the Parco del Colosseo, so the base Forum ticket does not get you in; book the Full Experience ticket. Ministry hours were 9:30–18:00 daily in 2026, but SUPER sites close on free first Sundays.
s-maria-antiqua.s: Ministero della Cultura (Parco archeologico del Colosseo); fororomano.org; Wikipedia

p: Look at the side walls before you go in: Ionic and Tuscan columns of real Roman temples stick out of the masonry. San Nicola was built in the middle of the Forum Holitorium, the old vegetable market by the Tiber, on top of three temples of the 3rd–2nd century BC (usually named for Janus, Spes and Juno Sospita). The church used the middle temple as its core and simply walled in the columns of the other two.

The name "in Carcere" (in prison) is a medieval mistake. The vaulted rooms in the podium, really shops or storerooms, were taken in the 14th century for the Tullianum prison. Giacomo della Porta finished the façade in 1599, so the outside is a Counter-Reformation front pressed against Republican stonework.

Downstairs is the real treat: a small ticket takes you into the podiums, where you walk in narrow passages between the foundations of the three temples. It is one of the clearest places in Rome to see how a medieval church literally ate the buildings it replaced. Inside, look for the 10th-century inscription on the first column of the right aisle.
Practical: daily except Wednesday, 10:00–17:00 (rome-roma.net, checked May 2026). Guided underground visits also run through local associations.

San Clemente is the famous one, and it earns it: you go down through three Romes in twenty minutes. At street level is a 12th-century basilica with a gold apse mosaic of the Cross as a tree of life. Under it is the 4th-century church it replaced, and under that a 1st-century Roman building with a sanctuary of Mithras, the soldiers' god, still with its stone benches and altar. At the bottom you hear water: an ancient channel still runs through the foundations.

The Irish Dominicans who run the church began digging in 1857 and found the lower basilica almost intact, filled with rubble by the builders of 1100. Its frescoes are among the earliest medieval paintings in Rome.

The clue to find is the Sisinnius fresco in the lower church: a pagan prefect orders his servants to drag off a column, and the painted speech bubbles include rough early Italian ("fili de le pute, traite" – roughly "pull, you sons of whores"). It is one of the first written traces of the Italian language, and it is a curse.
Practical: timed tickets, best bought online; photos are not allowed below. A short walk from the Colosseum, and a good first stop before Santi Quattro Coronati.
s-clemente.s: Basilica di San Clemente; Google Places (hours, 2026); visitor reports

p: Step in and you are inside a ring of columns under a timber roof, more like a tent than a church. Santo Stefano is the oldest and best-preserved centrally planned church in Rome, built in the late 5th century; coins of Libius Severus (461–465) were found in its foundations, and dendrochronology dates the roof timber to about 455. Its round, cross-in-circle plan copies the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem.

The walls are the reason most people remember it. In 1582 Niccolò Pomarancio and Matteo da Siena painted 34 scenes of martyrdom around the ambulatory for the Jesuit college that trained missionaries: boiling, flaying, crushing, each panel lettered A, B, C and keyed to captions in Latin and Italian. It is a field guide to what the students might face. Dickens was among the visitors it disturbed.

The church sits on top of the Castra Peregrinorum, the barracks of soldiers on detached duty (often described as the emperors' intelligence service), and a Mithraeum lies below it. Look also for the marble chair said to be Gregory the Great's, cut from an ancient seat.
Practical: closed Monday; hours vary by source, so check before going. The Mithraeum is closed.
s-stefano-rotondo.s: Cathopedia; Churches of Rome Wiki; idealista (Aug 2026); lechiesediroma.info

p: Under the basilica of Santi Giovanni e Paolo, entered from the sloping Clivo di Scauro, is a whole block of Roman houses from the 2nd to the 4th century: twenty-odd rooms on several levels, many still painted. It is the best place in Rome to see the step between a Roman home and a church, because here a Christian confessio, a little shrine with martyrdom scenes, was painted right into a stairwell of the house.

Tradition says this was the home of two officials, John and Paul, martyred under Julian the Apostate in the 360s, and that the basilica was built over their graves. The excavations, begun by a Passionist priest in 1887, found a house that had been rebuilt and repainted for centuries, including pagan scenes next to Christian ones.

The clue is the confessio on the stair landing: a small niche with figures praying and a scene of arrest. Visitors complain the English captions are poor, so read up before you go, and download any guide first: there is no mobile signal underground.

marcellino-pietro.t: Catacombs of Saints Marcellinus and Peter + Mausoleum of Helena
p: Out on the Via Casilina, beside the traffic of Tor Pignattara, stands the broken drum of a huge imperial tomb: the mausoleum Constantine built, probably first for himself, then for his mother Helena. Behind it lies one of the most richly painted catacombs in Rome, with about 18,000 m² of galleries and something like 15,000 burials in the 3rd century alone.

The catacomb is named for two martyrs of the Diocletian persecution, a priest and an exorcist. Constantine built a circus-shaped basilica over it and the mausoleum against it, so this is one of the first places where an emperor attached his own dynasty to a Christian cemetery. The frescoes, restored in the 2000s with laser cleaning, include banquets, Bible scenes and a rare Christ between Peter and Paul.

The clue is in the name of the district: Tor Pignattara means "tower of the pots". The mausoleum's vault was lightened with clay amphorae (pignatte) built into the concrete, a classic Roman trick. Look for them in the broken dome.
Practical: the catacomb is guided only and must be booked; tours run in the morning and afternoon. Visitors who turn up without booking are sometimes squeezed in.
marcellino-pietro.s: Pontificia Commissione di Archeologia Sacra (catacombeditalia.va); santimarcellinoepietro.it; Ministero della Cultura

p: The Tiber island has been about healing for 2,300 years. In 291 BC Rome brought the cult of Asclepius here during a plague, and the island still holds a hospital (Fatebenefratelli). San Bartolomeo was built over the temple site in 998 by Emperor Otto III, and its Romanesque bell tower dates from the 12th century.

Find three things. On the steps up to the altar is a marble well-head cut from an ancient column drum, its rim worn by bucket chains; it stands over the old sacred spring. On the left wall of the chapel of the Virgin is a 14 cm cannonball, fired by the French from the Via Aurelia in June 1849 while they besieged the Roman Republic; it broke through the front wall and stopped on the altar, and a Latin inscription records that the friars were spared. And behind a grille is a 10th–11th-century Arab bronze basin.
Since 2000 the church has also been the memorial of the "new martyrs" of the 20th and 21st centuries, with objects left by people killed under Nazism, Communism and in mission countries.
s-bartolomeo-isola.s: romasegreta.it; Churches of Rome Wiki; Cathopedia; cosafarearoma.org

p: In an unpromising corner of Magliana, by the river, stands a small medieval church on a three-level stack: a late-13th-century church on top, a crypt from about the 7th century in the middle, and a 2nd–3rd-century Roman tomb chamber at the bottom with traces of painting. It began as a pagan funerary monument along a road and has been reused ever since.
The name is a corruption. The crypt held relics of two Egyptian saints, Cyrus and John; "Abbas Cyrus" became "Abbaciro", then "Pacera", then "Passera". There is no Saint Passera.

Across the road is Santo Volto di Gesù (2006), so this is the best pair in Rome for the whole church story in one stop: a Roman tomb turned into a church, and a 21st-century church by Sartogo and Grenon facing it.
Practical: the church is usually closed; the parish of Santo Volto opens it for Sunday Mass, and local associations run occasional guided visits to the lower levels.

aracoeli-column.t: Santa Maria in Aracoeli: the drilled column
p: Santa Maria in Aracoeli stands on the highest point of the Capitol, at the top of a steep marble stair built in 1348 in thanks for the end of the Black Death. Inside, the nave is carried by ancient columns of different heights and stones, taken from ruined buildings. It was the city's civic church for centuries, where Rome's government met and celebrated.

The clue: count to the third column on the left. It has a hole bored clean through it, about 74 cm long and 3 cm wide, at head height. The traditional story makes it an astronomical device for sighting the sun. In 2014 the astronomer Costantino Sigismondi measured it (axis at azimuth 116°, altitude 17.3°) and concluded that it "was probably not used for meridian observations", though since the column has been moved, its original use is open.

Look also for the Cosmatesque floors and the chapel of the Santo Bambino, a carved wooden Christ Child that Romans took to the sick; the original was stolen in 1994 and a copy is shown. Legend puts here the spot where the Sibyl showed Augustus a vision of the Virgin and Child: "the altar of heaven".

Walk into the courtyard of the old Sapienza university and look up at the end of it: the dome steps up in rings and ends in a spiral lantern that winds like a corkscrew into a crown of iron. Inside, the walls swing in and out so the whole room seems to move. Francesco Borromini built it in 1642–60 as the chapel of Rome's university, founded in 1303.

The plan is pure geometry: two overlapping triangles make a six-pointed star, and Borromini cut and rounded its points into alternating concave and convex walls. There is no separate dome on a drum; the wall simply rises into the vault, so your eye follows the lines from the floor to the lantern without a break. The church has been read as a bee (the Barberini family emblem), a star of Solomon and a symbol of Wisdom; Borromini left no explanation.
The clue: stand in the centre and follow one line of the floor pattern up the wall and into the dome. Outside, the spiral was struck by lightning four times in 32 years, Arte.it notes.
Practical: closed for years, it reopened on 27 October 2026 after a PNRR-funded restoration, free on weekday mornings. The building is the State Archive, so the courtyard gate is the way in.
s-ivo.s: Finestre sull'Arte (27 Oct 2026); SiViaggia; Arte.it; Google Places

p: Sant'Ignazio is the Jesuits' second great church in Rome, and the joke is in the roof. The dome was planned but never built, so in 1685 the painter and mathematician Andrea Pozzo painted a dome on a flat canvas about 17 m across. Stand on the marked disc in the nave and you see a drum, windows and a lantern; walk past the disc and the illusion bends and breaks. The present canvas may be a 19th-century replacement (sources conflict).

The nave vault is the bigger trick: Pozzo painted St Ignatius carried into heaven with the architecture of the church continuing upwards, so the ceiling seems twice as high as it is. It is applied projective geometry, and Pozzo wrote a textbook on perspective that architects used for a century.
The clue: find the two yellow marble discs in the nave floor, one for the vault and one for the dome, and stand on each. Look for the angel holding a concave mirror with the name of Jesus.
Science bonus: the church was built for the Collegio Romano next door, the Jesuit university where Angelo Secchi later ran his observatory on the piers meant for the dome (see Collegio Romano).

Bodies: Robert Bellarmine, the cardinal who judged Galileo's first case in 1616, lies in red cardinal's robes behind glass under the altar of the chapel of San Gioacchino (third on the right). Aloysius Gonzaga and John Berchmans are buried here too.
s-ignazio.s: romasegreta.it; it.wikipedia; Google Places; santignazio.gesuiti.it; Daily Mail (Elizabeth Harper photographs)

p: On elegant Via Giulia a façade carries winged skulls and the motto "Hodie mihi, cras tibi": today me, tomorrow you. This was the church of the Confraternity of Prayer and Death, founded in the 16th century to pull bodies out of the Tiber and collect the dead found in the countryside, people no one would bury. Between 1552 and 1896 they buried more than 8,000.

Ferdinando Fuga rebuilt the church on an oval plan in 1733–37. The cemetery behind it, which ran down to the river, was destroyed in the 1880s when the embankments of the Lungotevere were built; what is left is the crypt under the church, with altars, chandeliers and wall decorations made of bones.

The clue: read the skulls. Many have a date, the place where the body was found and the cause of death written on the forehead, so the room is also a 19th-century register of Roman accidents and drownings.

Practical: Turismo Roma (2026) says the church opens only by appointment through the Associazione Amici del Tevere, which also opens the Sacconi Rossi crypt on the Tiber Island on 2 November. A restoration of the decoration was under way in 2026. The façade, with its winged skeletons, is worth the stop anyway.
orazione-morte.s: Turismo Roma; Fanpage; Soprintendenza Speciale di Roma (PNRR project, 2026); it.wikipedia; America Magazine; map pin approximate

p: Near St Peter's is a hospital that has been working since the 12th century, on the site of an 8th-century hostel for English pilgrims (the Schola Saxonum, hence "in Sassia"). Pope Sixtus IV rebuilt it in 1473–78 around the Corsia Sistina, a single ward 120 m long, frescoed with the story of the hospital's founding and crowned by an octagonal chapel where Mass was said in sight of every bed.

The clue is on the street side: a marble wheel set in the wall, the ruota degli esposti. Parents could put a baby into the wheel, turn it and ring a bell; the child was taken in anonymously. Next to it is an alms slot. Under the portico, on the fourth pillar from the end, a plaque marks the height of the great flood of 1598.

The National Museum of the History of Medicine next door has anatomical models, surgical instruments and an apothecary with a grinder for quinine bark, which for a chemist may be the best stop on the whole map.
Practical: the Corsia and church are shown on booked visits; email well ahead.
s-spirito-sassia.s: monnoroma.it; Turismo Roma; Wikipedia (Museo Storico Nazionale dell'Arte Sanitaria)

p: In 527 Pope Felix IV turned a hall of Vespasian's Forum of Peace into a church, with the round "Temple of Romulus" on the Forum side as its vestibule. The apse mosaic, Christ on red clouds against a deep blue sky, is one of the oldest and most influential in Rome. The clue: at the back of the church a glass window looks straight into the round temple, and on the Forum side the temple still has its original Roman bronze doors.

Look at the apse mosaic properly: Peter and Paul lead the two doctor saints, Cosmas and Damian, towards Christ; on the far left Felix IV holds a model of the church (his figure was remade in the 17th century), and on the right is St Theodore. Below, twelve lambs walk out of Bethlehem and Jerusalem towards the Lamb of God, and a phoenix sits in a palm tree, the old symbol of resurrection. The church floor was raised about 7 m in 1632 because the Forum ground had risen; the original level is still under you.

Two Forum links make this stop worth more than its size. The outer wall of the hall, on Via in Miranda, is the wall that once carried the Forma Urbis, the Severan marble plan of the city; the clamp holes are still there (see the Forma Urbis museum stop). And the round "Temple of Romulus" is named by tradition after Maxentius's young son, who died in 309; scholars also suggest a temple of the Penates or of Jupiter Stator, so the name is not certain. Practical: the church is free, entrance from Via dei Fori Imperiali; a large 18th-century Neapolitan crib is shown in a side room for a small fee; the temple's bronze doors are seen from inside the Forum, with a Forum ticket.
s-cosma-damiano.s: Google Places; fororomano.org; Turismo Roma; Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide)

p: San Crisogono was one of Rome's first parish churches. The church you see was rebuilt in 1123 and remodelled in 1626, with huge porphyry columns said to come from an ancient building; in 1907 the 4th-century church was found intact below it. The clue: go down through the sacristy and walk the old nave, with sarcophagi and early-medieval frescoes, while the trams run overhead.

Also here: in a side chapel, in a glass coffin, Blessed Anna Maria Taigi (1769–1837), a Trastevere housewife and mystic, her remains covered by a wax face made from her death mask. She is often listed as incorrupt; she is mostly wax over bone.
s-crisogono.s: monnoroma.it; museionline.info; visitor report (Mar 2026); Atlas Obscura; Order of the Good Death

p: Legend says this was Cecilia's house and that she survived three days in her own steam bath before being beheaded. Under the church are real Roman houses with a set of round basins, sometimes identified as a tannery or dye works, a nice chemistry question to settle on site. Upstairs, Stefano Maderno's marble Cecilia (1600) lies on her side with the wound visible, carved, it is said, as her body was found when the tomb was opened in 1599.

Cecilia is one of the best-known Roman martyrs, patron of musicians, but the details of her life come from a late legend and cannot be checked. What is real is the stack: a 9th-century church built by Paschal I, who moved her relics here from the Catacomb of Callixtus, on top of Roman houses of the Republic and the Empire.

The excavations are small and damp, entered from the left aisle for a few euros; they are shut during Mass. Look up in the apse for Paschal I's mosaic, with the square blue halo that marks a living pope. Pietro Cavallini's Last Judgement fresco is in the nuns' choir upstairs, open only on some mornings: ask at the convent door.
s-cecilia-scavi.s: Basilica di Santa Cecilia; cosafarearoma.it; Google Places

p: The Tullianum was Rome's only real prison, where enemies like Vercingetorix and the Catiline conspirators were held and strangled. Christian tradition puts Peter and Paul here and tells of a spring that rose so Peter could baptise his guards (legend). The clue: the hole in the floor of the upper room, the only way into the lower cell in antiquity. Visitors find the €10 ticket steep for a fifteen-minute visit.

Go down and the two levels explain themselves. The upper room is a trapezoid of tufa blocks; the lower cell, round and about 2 m high, was reached only through the hole in its ceiling, and may first have been a cistern or a well-house (the name may come from *tullius*, an old word for a spring, rather than from King Servius Tullius). Sallust described it in the 1st century BC as a pit twelve feet underground, dark and foul. Condemned men were lowered in and strangled; Jugurtha starved here in 104 BC, the Catilinarian conspirators were killed here in 63 BC on Cicero's order, and Vercingetorix was strangled after Caesar's triumph in 46 BC.

The Christian layer came later: the name "Mamertine" is medieval, the chapel of San Pietro in Carcere was made in the cell, and above it the carpenters' guild built San Giuseppe dei Falegnami from 1597. The column where Peter was chained and the spring are tradition, not record. Excavations in 2009–2016 reorganised the visit, which opened as a small museum run by the Opera Romana Pellegrinaggi. Practical: entrance on Clivo Argentario, by the Forum's north-west corner; the Gemonian stairs, where executed bodies were thrown out for display, ran just beside it.
tullianum.s: Google Places; omniavaticanrome.org; Sallust, Bellum Catilinae 55; Wikipedia (Mamertine Prison)

p: Domitilla is one of the largest catacombs in Rome. You enter through the semi-underground basilica of Saints Nereus and Achilleus, built in the 4th century by cutting down into the cemetery, so the columns rise straight from the catacomb floor. That is the clue: a church you go down into.

The catacomb is named after Flavia Domitilla, of the Flavian imperial family, on whose land it began (tradition). It runs for several kilometres on several levels. The guided tour shows painted tombs, among them a 4th-century fresco of Veneranda with St Petronilla, and the basilica's carved column with the martyrdom of Achilleus.

Guided tours only, about 30 minutes, daily except Tuesday, 9:00–12:00 and 14:00–17:00; the catacomb is kept by the Divine Word fathers. The Fosse Ardeatine memorial is next door, and San Sebastiano a short walk east.
domitilla.s: Google Places; Catacombe di Domitilla; globetrottingkid.com

s-sebastiano.t: San Sebastiano and the Memoria Apostolorum
p: Under San Sebastiano is the "triclia", a room where 3rd-century Christians met for funeral meals in honour of Peter and Paul, whose relics may have been kept here for a time. The walls are covered with hundreds of scratched invocations ("Petre et Paule, petite pro…"), among the oldest pilgrim graffiti anywhere. The clue is those scratches; see them on the catacomb tour.

The word catacomb comes from here: the place was called *ad catacumbas* ("by the hollows"), and the name spread to all the others. Under the church the tour also shows three pagan family tombs with painted façades, buried when the ground was raised for the triclia.

Upstairs, the basilica (one of Rome's seven pilgrim churches) keeps a stone said to bear Christ's footprints from the Quo Vadis story, and a marble bust of the Saviour attributed to Bernini, rediscovered in the convent in 2001. Church daily 8:30–18:00; catacomb on its own guided tours, check days.
s-sebastiano.s: Google Places; Catacombe di San Sebastiano; Churches of Rome Wiki (not checked on site)

p: Built about 350 for Constantia, daughter of Constantine, this is a round domed hall ringed by twelve pairs of granite columns. The ambulatory vault keeps its original mosaics: birds, vines and cupids treading grapes, pagan in look and Christian in meaning. It shows how the first Christian monuments borrowed Roman decoration. The porphyry sarcophagus is a copy; the original is in the Vatican Museums.

Constantina was no saint: she died in 354, and later Rome confused her with a holy Constance, so the building took her name. Because of the grape-harvest mosaics it was long thought to be a temple of Bacchus, and in the 17th century the Dutch and Flemish painters of the Bentvueghels held drunken initiation nights here, scratching their names on the walls. The mosaics of the dome were lost in the 17th century and are known only from drawings; two apses keep later mosaics of Christ giving the law.

Practical: Via Nomentana 349, entered through the complex of Sant'Agnese fuori le mura, whose catacomb and 7th-century apse mosaic are the other half of the visit (pair them). Free; a coin box lights the mosaics.
s-costanza.s: Google Places; visitor reports; Wikipedia (Santa Costanza)

p: From outside, Santi Quattro Coronati looks like a castle, and that was the point: the Lateran palace was next door and the complex sheltered popes in troubled times. Augustinian nuns still live here. The clue: in the entrance court, ring at the wheel (rota) through which the enclosed nuns pass things; they let you into the Cappella di San Silvestro, painted in 1246 with Constantine's conversion, a piece of papal propaganda showing the emperor leading the pope's horse.

The four crowned martyrs are said to have been stonemasons who refused to carve a pagan statue, which made them the patrons of builders. The first church was large; after the Normans burned this quarter in 1084, Paschal II rebuilt it smaller inside the old walls, which is why the nave is short and the courtyard is so big.

The 13th-century cloister, with its little fountain, is one of the calmest places in Rome; keep your voice down, as the nuns ask. Leave a small offering at the wheel for the chapel. The church shuts at midday, so come in the morning or late afternoon, and combine it with San Clemente down the hill.

Pope Paschal I built Santa Prassede in 817 and added the tiny chapel of San Zeno as a tomb for his mother, Theodora: the only room in Rome fully covered in Byzantine-style gold mosaic. The clue: find Theodora with a square halo, the medieval sign that the person was still alive when the portrait was made. The chapel also holds a column fragment venerated as the column of the Flagellation (authenticity unknown).

In the main church, the apse mosaic shows Peter and Paul presenting Praxedes and her sister Pudentiana to Christ, with Paschal himself holding the model, again with a square halo; on the triumphal arch the elect wait at the gates of the Heavenly Jerusalem. In San Zeno, the vault has Christ in a medallion held up by four angels, and Theodora's portrait is labelled *Theodora episcopa*: the "bishop" title has been read as an honour for the pope's mother, and occasionally, more boldly, as evidence of women's office (contested).

The story behind the church is a legend of the early Church: Praxedes was said to have hidden the bodies of martyrs and gathered their blood, and a round porphyry slab in the nave floor marks the well where she put them (tradition). Paschal moved thousands of martyrs' remains here from the catacombs, as an inscription in the church lists. Practical: the usual entrance is a side door on Via di Santa Prassede, two minutes from Santa Maria Maggiore; it closes at midday and San Zeno needs coins for the lights.
s-prassede.s: Google Places; visitor reports; Wikipedia (Santa Prassede); Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City

p: The Baths of Diocletian had round towers at the corners of their enclosure; in 1598 Caterina Sforza Cesarini had one of them turned into this church. The coffered dome, lit only from an opening at the top, makes it a miniature Pantheon, and the acoustics are remarkable. It pairs with Santa Maria degli Angeli, the same baths turned church by Michelangelo, five minutes away.

Look up: the dome is about 22 m across, with octagonal coffers shrinking towards the oculus, and in the niches round the drum stand eight large stucco saints by Camillo Mariani (c. 1600). The bath tower's Roman brick is still the outer wall; the round plan is not a design choice but the shape of the building that was there. The church was given to French Cistercians (Feuillants), hence St Bernard.

Practical: Piazza San Bernardo, opposite the Moses fountain of the Acqua Felice and a minute from Santa Maria della Vittoria with Bernini's St Teresa; open mornings and late afternoons, closed at midday. Together with Santa Maria degli Angeli and the Aula Ottagona this lets you trace the outline of Diocletian's baths, the largest in Rome, across three buildings.
s-bernardo-terme.s: Google Places; visitor reports; Wikipedia (San Bernardo alle Terme)

vincenzo-anastasio.t: Santi Vincenzo e Anastasio a Trevi
p: While the crowds face the fountain, turn round. This was the parish of the Quirinal palace, and from Sixtus V (died 1590) to Leo XIII (died 1903) the praecordia, the heart and viscera removed for embalming, of 22 popes were brought here in urns. The clue: two marble plaques in the sanctuary list all 22 names. The façade (Martino Longhi the Younger, 1646–50, for Cardinal Mazarin) has so many columns that Romans called it "il Canneto", the reed bed.

Why here: from the late 16th century the popes lived much of the time in the Quirinal palace up the hill, and this was its parish church. When a pope died in the palace, his body was embalmed and the removed organs were brought down in an urn; the custom ended with Leo XIII, and Pius X stopped it. The plaques in the apse are the only visible trace; the urns are not on show.

The façade was paid for by Cardinal Mazarin, the Italian-born minister of France, and Martino Longhi the Younger crowded it with eighteen columns, set at three depths so the front seems to step forward. Practical: open most of the day; you are inside in ten steps from the Trevi crowd, and it is quiet.
vincenzo-anastasio.s: Walks in Rome; Wikipedia (list of extant papal tombs; Santi Vincenzo e Anastasio a Trevi); Google Places

p: Under Santa Maria della Concezione on Via Veneto, the Capuchin friars arranged the bones of their dead brothers into arches, chandeliers and rosettes. A sign tells you: "What you are now, we once were; what we are now, you will be." It is the city's best-known ossuary and the obvious comparison for the smaller, stranger crypt of Santa Maria dell'Orazione e Morte. Hawthorne set a chapter of *The Marble Faun* here.

The bones are those of about 3,700 friars, moved here when the order left its old convent near the Trevi in 1631, and added to until the 1870s, when burial inside the city was banned. There are six small chapels in a row, each named for what is on the walls (pelvises, skulls, leg and thigh bones); a few friars are dressed in their habits, and on the ceiling of the last room the skeleton of a child of the Barberini family holds a scythe and scales. Tradition says the soil was brought from Jerusalem.

The church above was built in 1626–31 for Cardinal Antonio Barberini, brother of Urban VIII; his floor slab before the altar reads only "Here lies dust, ash and nothing". Practical: the ticket includes a small museum of the Capuchins, which shows a *St Francis in Meditation* attributed to Caravaggio (attribution debated); no photos in the crypt; cover shoulders and knees.
capuchin-crypt.s: Google Places; Hawthorne, The Marble Faun (ch. XXI); cappucciniviaveneto.it; Wikipedia (Capuchin Crypt)

p: In the courtyard of San Pietro in Montorio, Bramante built in about 1502 a tiny circular martyrium with Doric columns and a dome, on the traditional spot of Peter's crucifixion. It is the first building of the High Renaissance and the model for the dome of St Peter's. Go down to the crypt, where a beam of light falls on the spot. Sorrentino shot a scene of *La grande bellezza* in the cloister.

Its plan is a perfect circle inside a small square cloister that Bramante also designed but never built; the courtyard you stand in is a compromise. Everything is in proportion to the column module, which is why such a small building reads as a monument in drawings and treatises for the next four centuries.

The church of San Pietro in Montorio belongs to the Spanish state, and the Tempietto is reached through the courtyard of the Real Academia de España. The site is free and quiet. Walk down to the crypt, and on the way out look at the cannonball of 1849 on the church's left flank and the Fontanone dell'Acqua Paola up the hill.
tempietto.s: Real Academia de España en Roma; Google Places; visitor reports

p: Before 1870 the popes did not allow Protestant churches inside the walls. As soon as Rome became Italy's capital, the American Episcopalians built this striped Gothic church on Via Nazionale (G. E. Street, 1873–80). The clue: in Edward Burne-Jones's apse mosaics, look for the saints with famous faces: Lincoln, Garibaldi and Grant are said to be among them.

The mosaics took a generation: Burne-Jones designed them in England from 1883, they were set by Venetian craftsmen, and his assistant Thomas Rooke finished the last panel after his death in 1898. The apse shows Christ enthroned in the Heavenly Jerusalem; the lower band, the Church on earth, is where the famous faces are said to be (J. P. Morgan, a benefactor, is often named as one; the identifications are tradition, not record). The striped stone and brick outside are Street's English Gothic, unique on Via Nazionale.

Practical: corner of Via Nazionale and Via Napoli; open on weekdays, with English services on Sunday and regular concerts. It pairs with the Tempio Valdese in Prati and the Non-Catholic Cemetery as the map's places of Rome's Protestant minorities after 1870.
st-pauls-walls.s: stpaulsrome.it; Turismo Roma; Google Places; Wikipedia (St Paul's Within the Walls)

p: From the street the dome shines like metal, because it is: San Gioacchino's octagonal dome was clad in aluminium in 1897, when aluminium was still a new, expensive metal. Inside, its blue surface is pierced with six-pointed stars of coloured glass that glow when the sun is on them. The local site romamia claims it is the oldest aluminium building element in Rome still in use.

The church was built in 1891–98 (finished 1911) by Raffaele Ingami for the priestly jubilee of Leo XIII, whose name was Gioacchino Pecci; Catholic nations each paid for a chapel, so there are fourteen "national" chapels, and the Tsar gave two columns of the portal. It stands in Prati, the new quarter built after 1870 by the Italian state right next to the Vatican, and it is the papacy's answer in stone.
Look up at the iron frieze under the roof: cypresses, stars and lilies from Leo XIII's coat of arms. During the German occupation, refugees hid inside the dome.

The Waldensians are Italy's oldest Protestant church, persecuted for centuries and allowed to build in Rome only after 1870.
