p: Found in 1501 and set up by Cardinal Carafa, the statue became the city's notice board for "pasquinades". The best-known, against the Barberini pope who stripped bronze from the Pantheon: "What the barbarians did not do, the Barberini did." Notes are still taped to it.

What survives is a battered Hellenistic group, a copy of a 3rd-century BC original, usually identified as Menelaus holding the body of Patroclus; the face and arms are gone. It was found in 1501 during roadworks by Palazzo Orsini (now Palazzo Braschi) and named, by different stories, after a sharp-tongued tailor, barber or schoolmaster of the street. It is the chief of Rome's "talking statues", with Marforio, Madama Lucrezia, Abate Luigi, Babuino and Il Facchino; anonymous verses pinned on one were answered on another.

Popes hated it: Adrian VI is said to have wanted it thrown into the Tiber, and guards were posted on it at times. Practical: Piazza di Pasquino, at the back of Palazzo Braschi a minute from Piazza Navona; notes now usually go on a board beside the statue rather than on the stone.
pasquino.s: Google Places reviews; Turismo Roma; Wikipedia (Pasquino; Talking statues of Rome)

landsknecht.t: Villa Farnesina: the Landsknecht graffito of 1528
p: The villa of the banker Agostino Chigi is famous for Raphael's frescoes. In the Sala delle Prospettive, among the painted columns, a German soldier of the imperial army that sacked Rome in 1527 scratched a line in Gothic script dated 1528, mocking Clement VII (who had in fact shut himself in Castel Sant'Angelo). It was found during restoration. Similar scratches, one praising Luther, are on Raphael's frescoes in the Vatican.

The Sack of Rome began on 6 May 1527, when the unpaid army of Charles V broke in; many of the German mercenaries were Lutherans, and they treated the papal city as Babylon. The graffito is part of that story: written by a soldier billeted in a banker's villa, scratched into a fresco by Peruzzi, the architect of the house.

The Farnesina now belongs to the Accademia dei Lincei. Upstairs, ask for the Sala delle Prospettive and look along the painted colonnade at standing height; the scratched lines are faint, so bring the photo from a guide. Downstairs are Raphael's Galatea and the Loggia of Cupid and Psyche.

Pier Paolo Pasolini was a regular at Pommidoro, a family trattoria in working-class San Lorenzo, and Maria Callas came here too. On the evening of 1 November 1975 he dined here with the actor Ninetto Davoli and paid by cheque; hours later he was murdered on the beach at Ostia. The family never cashed the cheque, and it hangs framed inside.

The place closed after the 2020 lockdown, and the owner Aldo Bravi died in 2021; his grandson reopened it in 2023. Reviews praise the carbonara and the tripe. After dinner Pasolini picked up Pino Pelosi at Termini and took him to Al Biondo Tevere on the Ostiense (see that stop).

The late stop on 1–2 November 1975, a few hours before the killing at Ostia; a chair said to be Pasolini's is kept by the entrance. Visconti shot *Bellissima* (1951) here with Anna Magnani. The terrace over the Tiber is the reason locals come.

The night of 1–2 November 1975: Pasolini had dinner at Pommidoro in San Lorenzo, picked up Pino Pelosi near Termini, stopped here so Pelosi could eat, then drove to the Idroscalo at Ostia, where he was killed. The trattoria keeps the memory without making a shrine of it.
Practical: closed Monday; phone ahead (06 5741172). Sit on the terrace over the river in the evening. The Basilica of San Paolo and the Gazometro are each about a kilometre away.

Pasolini made Pigneto his set for *Accattone*, and Necci was the crew's bar. Myth flag: the owner says the bar seen in the film was a set built in a wine shop at no. 50, with furniture borrowed from Necci. Pigneto is still the neighbourhood of the films: Via Montecuccoli, where *Roma città aperta* was shot, is ten minutes away.

The film's own street is Via Fanfulla da Lodi, round the corner. No. 50 was the set bar (now a house); the railing and gate at the corner of Via del Pigneto are still recognisable, while the film's nasone was moved to Via Ludovico da Terni. Murals on the street quote Pasolini, among them *Io so i nomi* ("I know the names") and *Piccola Maria*.

Necci itself is a working bar-restaurant open from breakfast to late, the neighbourhood's living room rather than a museum. Pair it with Vini e Olii at Via del Pigneto 18 and the Pigneto street market at Via L'Aquila on a weekday morning.
necci.s: Turismo Roma (Pasolini itinerary); Google Places; KonMap Rome research notes (Nov 2026)

p: Open since 1922, Rosati was the postwar meeting place of writers and painters; Fellini's café, Canova, is across the square. With Caffè Greco closed since October 2025 and Aragno turned into an Apple Store, it is the best surviving literary café in Rome, if you can take the prices and a 19% service charge.

The interior keeps its 1920s look: wood, mirrors and the Art Nouveau lettering. In the postwar years the left-wing writers gathered here, among them Moravia, Elsa Morante, Pasolini, Calvino and Flaiano, while the cafés across Piazza del Popolo drew a different crowd; Canova is where Fellini liked to work. Today you pay for that history and the view of the obelisk and the twin churches.
Practical: standing at the bar is far cheaper than a table outside; the terrace is the place to watch the piazza in the evening. Combine with Santa Maria del Popolo and the walk up to the Pincio.
rosati.s: Google Places reviews; local press; Turismo Roma

p: Founded by the Augustinians and open to all from 1604, the Angelica keeps some 200,000 items in a hall redesigned by Luigi Vanvitelli in the 18th century. No single famous reader is documented, only centuries of scholars. It is also the "Vatican archive" of the *Angels & Demons* film, since the Vatican refused to allow filming.

The founder was Angelo Rocca, an Augustinian bishop and papal librarian, who gave his books on condition they be open to anyone: that is why the Angelica is counted among the first public libraries in Europe, with the Bodleian (1602) and Milan's Ambrosiana (1609). In 1762 it bought Cardinal Passionei's huge library, and its shelves are strong on theology, the Reformation quarrels and early science, including herbals and alchemical texts.

What to look for from the door: Vanvitelli's "Vaso" (1765), a tall hall wrapped in wooden shelving with a gallery running round it, lit from above. Practical: Mon–Fri mornings; visitors may look from the entrance, and guided visits of the hall run on some afternoons by booking. The building is the Augustinian convent next to Sant'Agostino, which has Caravaggio's *Madonna of Loreto* with the pilgrims' dirty feet.
angelica.s: Google Places; thatfilmspot.com; bibliotecaangelica.cultura.gov.it; Treccani (Angelo Rocca)

p: Wood panelling, blown-glass bookcases and showcases on a sliding rail: the shop looks as it did two centuries ago, and sells rare books, prints and antiques. In *John Wick: Chapter 2* Keanu Reeves comes here for the plans of the catacombs. Buy something small and the owner will tell you the story.

Practical: Largo Febo 14–16, just behind Piazza Navona and opposite the ivy-covered Hotel Raphael. The founding date is given variously as 1835, "the 19th century" and 1909, so treat the age as uncertain; Rome's tourist office lists it among the city's historic shops, run by three generations of booksellers, with visitors said to include Greta Garbo and Pope John XXIII. Look for the showcase on rails and the back room with a hidden door. Prints of Rome are the affordable things to buy.
cascianelli.s: movie-locations.com; Google Places; Turismo Roma; Il Foglio (Aug 2025)

p: Rossellini shot *Roma città aperta* in 1944–45 with the war barely over, on real streets. Pina, played by Anna Magnani, runs from this doorway after the truck taking her fiancé and is shot down in the street: one of the most famous scenes in cinema. The bombed building she points at, opposite at no. 36, is real.
The scene was based on the death of Teresa Gullace, shot on Viale Giulio Cesare on 3 March 1944 (see that stop). Pigneto and Necci are a few minutes' walk away.
montecuccoli.s: davinotti.com; it.wikipedia; Ecomuseo Casilino; Il Messaggero

crispi-theft.t: Via Francesco Crispi: Ladri di biciclette
p: In Vittorio De Sica's *Ladri di biciclette* (1948) Antonio Ricci, an unemployed man who has just got a job pasting up posters, has his bicycle stolen on his first morning while he is up a ladder pasting a poster of Rita Hayworth. Without the bike he loses the job; the rest of the film is father and son searching Rome for it. The theft was shot here, on Via Francesco Crispi.

davinotti.com pins the theft to the columns of no. 18 (now the Gagosian gallery) and the stairs of the old modern-art gallery in the reverse shot. Other scenes: the labour office queue at Via del Gran Paradiso and Via Scarpanto in Val Melaina (with a plaque), and Porta Portese, where a young Sergio Leone appears as a seminarian in the rain.

Neorealism in one street: De Sica cast a factory worker, Lamberto Maggiorani, as Ricci and filmed in real streets with real crowds. Practical: Via Crispi runs downhill from Via Sistina towards Via del Tritone; the Gagosian is at no. 16–18, and the Capuchin Crypt and Piazza Barberini are five minutes away.

Fellini shot the fountain scene on winter nights in 1959. Most of the Via Veneto nightlife was rebuilt at Cinecittà (Teatro 5), and the St Peter's dome staircase too; only Ekberg's dawn return at the Excelsior was shot on the real street. Turn round to Santi Vincenzo e Anastasio, the church of the 22 popes' hearts.

The fountain itself is Nicola Salvi's, built from 1732 and finished in 1762 after his death; it is the mostra, the show end, of the Acqua Vergine, an aqueduct opened by Agrippa in 19 BC that still feeds it. The water arrives almost level, which is why the fountain sits low in a small square instead of on a hill. The big travertine vase on the right, the 'asso di coppe', is said to have been put there to block the view of a barber who mocked Salvi's work; that is a story, not record.

The basin area is now ticketed for non-residents; the square stays free, and late at night it is almost empty. Throwing a coin is the old promise to return; the city collects over a million euros a year from the basin and gives it to Caritas. For the water itself, go to the Vicus Caprarius two streets away, where the aqueduct's Roman castellum is 9 m under the street.

The marble mask, probably an ancient drain cover, is said to bite the hands of liars (legend). In *Roman Holiday* (1953) Peck pretends it has; Hepburn's scream was real, the story goes, because she had not been told. The church behind it, Santa Maria in Cosmedin, has an 8th-century crypt cut into Roman remains.

The mask itself is a marble disc about 1.75 m across, a bearded face with holes for eyes, nose and mouth, usually read as a river god or Oceanus. It may have been a drain cover from the nearby Temple of Hercules, or a fountain mask; it has stood in the church portico since 1632. The "mouth of truth" story is medieval: the *Mirabilia* tradition said it bit the hand of anyone who swore falsely, and a later tale has an unfaithful wife cheat the test by arranging a staged embrace just before she swore.

Inside, Santa Maria in Cosmedin is one of the best small medieval churches in Rome: a 12th-century Cosmatesque floor, the marble choir enclosure, a tall Romanesque bell tower, and a crypt cut into the walls of an ancient building. The name comes from the Greek community that held it from the 8th century (*kosmidion*, "ornament"). Across the road are the round Temple of Hercules Victor and the Temple of Portunus, the old cattle-market harbour; the Cloaca Maxima outlet is a few minutes away. Practical: the queue moves fast; a small donation for the photo.
bocca.s: thetrainline.com; almostginger.com; Wikipedia (Bocca della Verità; Santa Maria in Cosmedin)

p: The stairs pass under the old Borgia palace; local tradition calls the lane the Vicus Sceleratus, where Tullia drove her chariot over her father's body (legend). Michelangelo's Moses is at the top. *John Wick: Chapter 2* staged its stair fight here.

The stairs run from Via Cavour up to San Pietro in Vincoli, through a dark vaulted passage under a tower and a loggia that tradition gives to the Borgia: Vannozza Cattanei, Pope Alexander VI's mistress and mother of Cesare and Lucrezia, is said to have lived here (tradition, not proven). The street over the top is Via di San Francesco di Paola. Livy's Vicus Sceleratus, the "wicked street" where Tullia drove over her father King Servius Tullius, was on the Esquiline; putting it exactly here is local lore.

Practical: always open, steep and often dirty; at the top, San Pietro in Vincoli has Michelangelo's Moses for the tomb of Julius II and the chains said to be Peter's. The church closes for a midday break.
borgia-steps.s: movie-locations.com; Google Places reviews; Livy 1.48; Wikipedia (San Pietro in Vincoli)

mi7-funari.t: Via dei Funari: the yellow Fiat of Mission: Impossible
p: In *Mission: Impossible – Dead Reckoning Part One* (2023) Ethan Hunt and Grace, handcuffed together, swap a stolen car for a tiny yellow vintage Fiat 500 and drift it one-handed over Rome's cobbles. Via dei Funari, on the edge of the Ghetto, is listed as part of that chase (where they pick up the Fiat); the exact frames were not checked here.

The chase then runs past the Fori Imperiali and down the Spanish Steps; the steps' close-ups were shot on a UK replica and the car was an electric conversion. The "police station" with a real Colosseum view is the former school in Via delle Carine.

The street is worth a slow walk even without the film. Its name means "rope-makers"; at the end, in Piazza Mattei, is the Turtle Fountain (Giacomo della Porta's design, Taddeo Landini's bronze boys, 1580s; the turtles were added in the 17th century, often credited to Bernini, unproven). Palazzo Mattei di Giove, along the street, has a courtyard lined with ancient reliefs and busts, visible when the gate is open. Santa Caterina dei Funari's façade (1560s) closes the view the other way.
mi7-funari.s: movie-locations.com; Hagerty; autoevolution.com; Wikipedia (Fontana delle Tartarughe)

continental.t: Rear of the Vittoriano: the Continental (John Wick 2)
p: In *John Wick: Chapter 2* (2017) Rome's branch of the assassins' hotel, "Il Continentale", is a grand stone entrance: the side of the Vittoriano that houses the Museo Centrale del Risorgimento, towards Via di San Pietro in Carcere.
Interiors are the Grand Hotel Plaza on Via del Corso; Rome's modern-art gallery plays a New York museum, with the Empire State Building added digitally; the party is at the Baths of Caracalla.

Stand here and the film is the least of it. This side of the monument looks straight down on the Forum of Caesar and the Mamertine Prison, and the Risorgimento museum inside (entrance on this side) tells the story the Vittoriano was built to celebrate. The glass lift to the Terrazza delle Quadrighe starts from the Aracoeli side, a few minutes round the building. Practical: exterior always visible; museum and lift on the Vittoriano ticket.

gnam-wick.t: Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Moderna: Rome playing New York
p: In *John Wick: Chapter 2* (2017) the steps and façade of the Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Moderna play a New York museum, where John meets Santino on the steps, and the long mirror-room fight takes place in a show inside.
The skyline behind it was added in post-production. The gallery is worth the visit for itself: a Belle Époque palace of 1911 with Italian art from the 19th and 20th centuries.

Cesare Bazzani designed the palace for the 1911 exhibition celebrating fifty years of Italian unity, in Valle Giulia beside Villa Borghese. The collection runs from Canova to Burri, Fontana and Pascali, with foreign works such as Klimt's *Three Ages of Woman*, Van Gogh and Monet. Practical: Viale delle Belle Arti 131, closed Monday; since 2016 it calls itself simply "La Galleria Nazionale"; the café on the terrace is a good break.
gnam-wick.s: movie-locations.com; atlasofwonders.com; lagallerianazionale.com; pin: Google Places (Nov 2026)

spectre-civilta.t: Museum of Roman Civilisation: Spectre's funeral
p: For *Spectre* (2015) the production wanted the Verano; the confraternity that runs it refused, so fake tombs were set between the columns here. The colonnade is pure EUR, built for the cancelled 1942 fair.

In the film this is the funeral of Marco Sciarra, where Bond meets his widow (Monica Bellucci). The two long blocks joined by the colonnade were built for E42 to house the museum of Roman civilisation, completed after the war.

The museum, with Gismondi's huge model of ancient Rome, has been closed for years; a reopening of the model hall was announced for July 2026 and is not confirmed. The colonnade is free to walk any time.

ripley-coins.t: San Luigi dei Francesi: Ripley's coin lights
p: The Contarelli chapel holds Caravaggio's St Matthew cycle; the coin-operated lights are real, and *Ripley* (2024) uses them for a scene. Sant'Ivo and the Pantheon are a few steps away.

The three paintings, done in 1599–1602, were Caravaggio's first public commission: on the left *The Calling of St Matthew*, where a shaft of light follows Christ's pointing hand into a tax office (scholars still argue which man is Matthew); in the middle *St Matthew and the Angel*, a second version after the first was rejected (that one burned in Berlin in 1945); on the right *The Martyrdom*, with Caravaggio's own face among the onlookers at the back. Netflix's *Ripley* (2024, Steven Zaillian, in black and white) makes Ripley a man who stalks Caravaggio's paintings across Rome and Naples; this chapel is one of his stops.

Practical: San Luigi is the French national church, free, closed for a long midday break; the lights in the Contarelli chapel take €1 coins and run for a minute or two, so be ready. In the second chapel on the right are Domenichino's frescoes of St Cecilia.

ad-popolo.t: Santa Maria del Popolo: Angels & Demons
p: The novel's Path of Illumination runs from here to St Peter's Square (the West Ponente relief at the obelisk), Santa Maria della Vittoria (Bernini's Ecstasy of St Teresa), the Four Rivers fountain in Piazza Navona and Castel Sant'Angelo. The Rome diocese refused the film crew, so the church interiors were rebuilt in Hollywood and St Peter's Square was a replica at a racetrack in Inglewood, California. The exteriors are real. The church itself has two Caravaggios in the Cerasi chapel.

In the book, the first altar of science is the Chigi Chapel: Raphael's design for the banker Agostino Chigi, with Bernini's *Habakkuk and the Angel* and *Daniel and the Lion* added for Pope Alexander VII Chigi in the 1650s, and the floor mosaic of a winged skeleton holding the family arms. Brown's "demon's hole" is the opening in that floor. The chapel is real and as strange as the novel makes it, but the Illuminati path is fiction: Bernini's works were made for the Chigi, not for a secret society. Practical: free, Piazza del Popolo; closed at midday and during Mass; bring coins for the lights.
ad-popolo.s: movie-locations.com; CBS News / AP (2008); Wikipedia (Chigi Chapel)

p: The legend: a pet monkey carried a baby to the top of the tower, the father vowed a lamp to the Virgin if the child came down safe, and the lamp has burned ever since (legend). Hawthorne made it the home of his heroine Hilda in *The Marble Faun* (1860). Assassin's Creed Brotherhood also models the nearby Sant'Antonio dei Portoghesi.

Look up at the top of the tower on the corner of Via dei Portoghesi and Via dei Pianellari: a small shrine to the Virgin with a lamp, still kept lit. The tower is a medieval one built into a later palace (Palazzo Scapucci), one of the few in the centre to keep its battlements. Hawthorne lived in Rome in 1858–59 and wrote *The Marble Faun* from what he saw; his Hilda, an American copyist, lives at the top and tends the lamp herself, which is why visitors from the 19th century came to see it.
Practical: street only, two minutes from Sant'Agostino and the Angelica; there is nothing to enter.
hilda-tower.s: Turismo Roma; Hawthorne, The Marble Faun (ch. VI)

p: Goethe came to Rome under a false name and stayed with Tischbein, who painted him lounging in the Campagna. The museum keeps drawings and letters. Myth flag: the story that he was a regular at Caffè Greco does not come from his book.

Goethe arrived on 29 October 1786 as "Filippo Miller", a painter, and stayed until April 1788 apart from a long trip to Naples and Sicily. These rooms on Via del Corso are where he lodged with Tischbein and a circle of German artists; Rome turned him from the storm-and-stress writer of *Werther* to the classical poet of the *Roman Elegies*. His *Italian Journey*, written up decades later (1816–17 and 1829), is still the best-known travel book about Italy.

Practical: Via del Corso 18, near Piazza del Popolo; a small museum run by a German cultural association, with drawings, letters and first editions, and changing shows; closed Monday, check hours. Tischbein's famous portrait of Goethe in the Campagna is in Frankfurt; the museum shows reproductions.
Carlo Emilio Gadda's "palazzo degli ori" is probably invented, but the city put a plaque at no. 219. The novel's other places, Marino and Pavona in the Castelli, are real; Tor di Gheppio is not.

Gadda's novel *Quer pasticciaccio brutto de via Merulana* (1957) is set in 1927: a jewel theft and a murder in the same middle-class block, investigated by Commissario Ingravallo, who never solves them. It is written in a mixture of Roman dialect and dense literary Italian, and Pietro Germi filmed it in 1959 as *Un maledetto imbroglio*.
There is nothing else to see; the plaque is the stop. Via Merulana runs from Santa Maria Maggiore to the Lateran, so take it on the way,.
merulana-219.s: museq.it; Il Messaggero; pin: Google Places (Nov 2026)

p: Painted in 2014 and restored in 2023 with photocatalytic paints, the mammoth nods to the tusks found at Casal de' Pazzi nearby. The slogan reads "Qui ci manca tutto, non ci serve niente": we lack everything, we need nothing.

The mural is on the Rebibbia metro station, the end of line B. Zerocalcare grew up in Rebibbia and made it the home of his comics and of the Netflix series *Strappare lungo i bordi* (2021); the mammoth became the quarter's emblem, a joke about a place known mainly for its prison.

The real animal is down the road: the Casal de' Pazzi museum (Viale Egidio Galbani 6) shows an Aniene riverbed about 200,000 years old with tusks of a straight-tusked elephant, not a mammoth. Entry is free with booking on 060608. Casa Pasolini, the flat in Via Tagliere where *Ragazzi di vita* was written, is about a kilometre away.
mammoth.s: ATAC; Quotidiano.net; Sovrintendenza Capitolina (Casal de' Pazzi)

de-pedis.t: Via del Pellegrino: the end of the Magliana gang's boss
p: The gang ran drugs and gambling in 1970s–80s Rome and was tied to every dark story of the period. De Pedis was then buried, scandalously, in the basilica of Sant'Apollinare until 2012; the link with the disappearance of Emanuela Orlandi is speculation. The gang's base was a bar on Via Chiabrera in Marconi.

Enrico "Renatino" De Pedis was shot dead here on 2 February 1990 by former associates; he was the gang's link to money and to people in high places, and the model for "Dandi" in Giancarlo De Cataldo's novel *Romanzo criminale* (2002) and its film and series. His burial in Sant'Apollinare was allowed by the Vicariate; after years of press campaigns the tomb was opened in 2012, the body was moved and cremated, and the bones found with it were tested: no trace of Emanuela Orlandi was found.

Practical: nothing marks the spot, and the pin is approximate; Via del Pellegrino runs from Campo de' Fiori towards the Chiesa Nuova. Sant'Apollinare is by Piazza Navona if you want to see the church itself. A dark-history stop: think of it as the place where the period's story ended, not as a sight.
de-pedis.s: Wikipedia; Wanted in Rome; turismo.it; ANSA (May 2012); pin: Google Places (Nov 2026)

p: Mussolini began digging into Monte Soratte in 1937. From September 1943 to June 1944 it was the headquarters of Field Marshal Kesselring, and Allied bombers hit it in May 1944. From 1967 NATO and the Italian government rebuilt part of it as an anti-atomic shelter for the President and the state's leaders. Just over 4 km of tunnels were dug of a planned 14 km, including a 1.3 km atomic core; the "over 40 km" in some sites has no source.
Since November 2024 an electric narrow-gauge train runs through 2.5 km of galleries that had been closed. Command rooms, dormitories and a power plant survive.

Benedict lived here as a hermit around 500 before founding his order. The monastery clings to the rock in layers of chapels painted from the 13th century on. The clue: Francis of Assisi shown without halo or stigmata, so painted before his canonisation in 1228, probably on a visit in his lifetime.

Monks from Calabria founded it in 1004 and it has kept the Greek rite for a thousand years, inside a Renaissance fortress wall. The clue: in Domenichino's chapel of the founders (1608–10), the young man holding the horse is said to be the painter himself, with Guido Reni and Guercino among the bystanders (tradition).

Sabaudia was founded in 1933–34 on land drained from the Pontine marshes, a showpiece of rationalist planning. Ferruccio Ferrazzi's 15 m mosaic in a parabolic niche shows the Annunciation over a landscape of reclamation; look for the tiny Mussolini at the threshing machine. Today the farms of the plain are worked largely by Punjabi Sikhs, whose gurdwara is in the same town.

Opened on 6 May 1960, it is the burial ground of the German dead of Anzio and the battles for Rome. In *Il sorpasso* (1962) Gassman and Trintignant pass it on their drive. The Commonwealth cemeteries at Anzio are 20 km further on.

Around twenty seats side by side over a channel of running water, with a gutter in front for the sponge on a stick: the latrine by the Forum Baths is the best-preserved public toilet of the Roman world, and the closest match on this map to an ancient urinal still in use.

s-maria-vittoria.t: Santa Maria della Vittoria: Saint Victoria's body
p: Most people come for Bernini's Ecstasy of Saint Teresa in the Cornaro chapel, and it is worth it: a saint fainting on a marble cloud, an angel with a gold arrow, and the Cornaro family watching from theatre boxes on either side. Then look for the glass case. Inside lies Saint Victoria, an early martyr from the catacombs, dressed and given a wax face and hands built over her real skeleton. Up close you can see the bones where the wax has worn: teeth, parts of the hand. It is one of the few full bodies in Rome you can walk right up to.

Victoria's story is the standard one for Roman virgin martyrs: a pagan suitor refused, a death sentence. Bodies like hers were taken out of the catacombs in the 17th and 18th centuries, named, dressed and sent to churches all over Catholic Europe; the wax mask is how a bone became a person you could pray to. Treat her identity as tradition, not record.

The church was begun in 1608 for the Discalced Carmelites and renamed after the Catholic victory at the White Mountain in 1620. Dan Brown made it a stop in Angels & Demons, so expect a few people with the book.
Practical: Google lists 7–12 and 16–18 (Sunday from 9). Free; come between Masses and keep quiet near the case.
s-maria-vittoria.s: Atlas Obscura; Churches of Rome Wiki; Wikipedia; Google Places

s-francesca-romana.t: Santa Francesca Romana: the saint's skeleton and Peter's knees
p: Go up the steps from the nave and down either side of the sanctuary into the crypt: there, in a glass coffin, lies Frances of Rome as a skeleton, still in the habit of her order and holding her prayer book. She is the saint of the city's widows, the poor, and, since the 20th century, car drivers. The church stands on top of the Forum, so you can step out of the crypt into two thousand years of ruins.

Frances Buzzi (1384–1440), a Trastevere noblewoman, founded the Oblates of Mary in 1425 to nurse the sick and feed the poor. She claimed she could see her guardian angel; Ercole Ferrata's oval relief of 1648 in the crypt shows her with him. The church, built over a corner of Hadrian's Temple of Venus and Rome, was first Santa Maria Nova, the 'new' St Mary that replaced the buried Santa Maria Antiqua after 847; it took her name after she was made a saint in 1608.

The second thing to find: in the south transept, behind a small iron grate, two dark basalt stones said to carry the prints of Peter's knees. The legend says the magician Simon Magus flew over the Forum to prove his powers, Peter knelt and prayed, and Simon fell to his death. It is pure legend, but an old one.
Practical: Google lists daily 10–17. Free. Pair it with Santa Maria Antiqua below the Palatine for the old church this one replaced.
s-francesca-romana.s: Atlas Obscura; Churches of Rome Wiki; Wikipedia; Through Eternity; Google Places

valentine-skull.t: Santa Maria in Cosmedin: Saint Valentine's skull
p: Everyone queues outside for the Mouth of Truth; inside, on the left wall, in a gilded case with a crown of dried flowers, is a skull with the name Valentine painted across the forehead. Entry to the church is free and the door is next to the queue.

Whose skull it is cannot be settled. There were at least two early martyrs called Valentine, a Roman priest and a bishop of Terni, both said to have died around 269, and the stories may have merged. The bones reportedly came out of a Roman excavation in the early 1800s; more than ten places in Europe claim relics of 'the' Valentine. Nothing in the early sources links him to lovers: that came much later, through Chaucer's poems.
The church itself is one of Rome's best medieval ones, built on an ancient grain-distribution hall and given to the Greek community; since 1964 it has been the church of the Melkite Greek Catholics.
valentine-skull.s: The Local Italy (Feb 2024); National Geographic; Through Eternity; Catholic Telegraph; Google Places

st-peters-bodies.t: St Peter's: popes in glass and Bernini's skeletons
p: St Peter's has three popes whose bodies you can see. Pius X lies in a crystal coffin under the altar of the Presentation, face and hands covered in silver. John XXIII, moved up from the grottoes in 2001 and found well preserved, lies under the altar of St Jerome with a wax-covered face. Innocent XI lies under the Transfiguration altar (older guides put him in the St Sebastian chapel, where John Paul II now is). And in the apse and the left transept, Bernini made Death a character on two papal tombs.

Urban VIII's tomb (1627–47), right of the Chair of Peter: a gilded skeleton leans out of the sarcophagus and writes the pope's name in the book of the dead. Alexander VII's tomb (1671–78), Bernini's last, over a doorway: a bronze skeleton heaves up a huge drape of red-and-white marble and holds up an hourglass to the kneeling pope. The door underneath is a real door, which is the joke: Death comes out of it.

Why glass coffins at all: incorruptibility was long read as a sign of holiness, and showing the body made the saint present. In practice most 'incorrupt' bodies have been treated: John XXIII's had been injected with formalin at his death, and wax and silver masks cover what time did.
Practical: daily from 7 (Google: to 19:10). Free, long security line; go early. The Scavi tour below is a separate booking.
st-peters-bodies.s: stpetersbasilica.info; Christianity Today (Jun 2001); ANSA (Oct 2022); Through Eternity; Google Places

p: Under the floor of St Peter's is a Roman street of family tombs, buried when Constantine levelled the hillside in the 320s to build his basilica on top. The guided tour walks you down it and ends at a corner where, through a gap, you see the box of bones that Pius XII's and Paul VI's excavators identified as Peter's. A graffito found there is read as 'Peter is here'.

The identification is disputed: the bones were found in a wall niche and moved around during the dig, and archaeologists disagree. What is not disputed is the necropolis itself, one of the best-kept Roman cemeteries you can enter.

Practical: about 250 people a day. Book by email with the Ufficio Scavi of the Fabbrica di San Pietro, giving a range of dates; they assign the slot. About €20 in 2026; closed Sundays; an older source says over-15s only. Cheap 'tombs of the popes' tours are usually the grottoes, not this. Map pin approximate (the office is by the Arch of the Bells, left of the basilica).
scavi.s: artvisitguide.com (verified Nov 2026); The Catholic Traveler; The Tour Guy (Apr 2026); map pin approximate; pin: Google Places (Nov 2026)

chiesa-nuova.t: Chiesa Nuova: Philip Neri under a silver mask
p: Philip Neri, the cheerful priest Romans called 'Pippo bbono', lies in the chapel left of the high altar, in an urn with a silver mask over his face. He wanted his church plain and whitewashed; his followers covered it in gold and Rubens altarpieces after he died in 1595. From a door in the transept you can reach his private rooms, including the Red Room and his chapel.

Neri founded the Oratorians, ran pilgrim hostels, and made Counter-Reformation Rome laugh; he was made a saint in 1622. Hours for his rooms are separate and shorter than the church's: check at the sacristy.
chiesa-nuova.s: Turismo Roma; La Nuova Bussola Quotidiana; Google Places

p: Borromini's church on Piazza Navona stands where, tradition says, the young Agnes was exposed and martyred in the arcades of Domitian's stadium around 305. Her skull is here, in its own Chapel of the Sacred Head, given to the church by Pius X in 1900; the rest of her lies in Sant'Agnese fuori le Mura, where her body was found in 1605.

Go down to the crypt, the only surviving part of the old church, for the stadium's ancient vaults and Algardi's relief of the miracle of her hair (it grew to cover her). Practical: closed Mondays; one visitor found the crypt closed at weekends.
agnese-skull.s: La Nuova Bussola Quotidiana (2021); santagneseinagone.org; Sapienza (IRIS); Google Places

p: The Jesuits' mother church holds two founders. In the right transept, above Pietro da Cortona's altar, hangs a reliquary with the right forearm and hand of Francis Xavier, the missionary who died off the coast of China in 1552 and whose body is in Goa; the arm was cut off and sent to Rome in 1614. The Jesuits say it baptised hundreds of thousands. In the left transept, Ignatius lies in a gilded bronze urn under Pozzo's lapis-and-silver altar.
Look up too: Baciccio's ceiling, where painted figures spill over the frame and cast shadows on the vault. Pozzo's trick corridor is in Ignatius' rooms next door, with its own hours.
gesu-xavier.s: New Liturgical Movement (Dec 2025); Through Eternity; Aleteia; CBC; Google Places

sm-maggiore-pius.t: Santa Maria Maggiore: Pius V in a crystal coffin
p: In the Sistine Chapel of Santa Maria Maggiore (Sixtus V's, not Michelangelo's) the far left wall is the shrine of Pius V by Domenico Fontana, 1588; below it the Dominican pope who organised the fleet of Lepanto lies exposed in a crystal coffin. Sixtus V faces him across the chapel.

The basilica is also where Pope Francis chose to be buried in 2025, in a plain tomb that draws queues. And under the high altar, in the confessio, are the wooden slats venerated as the manger of Bethlehem: Rome has a relic for almost everything.
sm-maggiore-pius.s: Churches of Rome Wiki; Italia.it; EWTN; Metropolitan Museum; Google Places

s-croce-relics.t: Santa Croce in Gerusalemme: the Passion relics
p: This basilica began as a room in the palace of Helena, Constantine's mother, who, the tradition says, brought back earth from Calvary and the relics of the Passion. They are now in a cold 1930 chapel reached by stairs from the left transept: fragments of the Cross, a nail, thorns from the crown, a finger said to be Saint Thomas's (the finger he put in the wound), and a worn walnut board with a three-language inscription: the Title of the Cross.

The Title is the interesting one. It was found in 1492 walled up behind a brick marked TITULUS CRUCIS. Some scholars defend it as Pilate's original; a 2002 radiocarbon test by physicists at Roma Tre dated the wood to about 996–1146. The finger is said to have come to Rome through Bridget of Sweden; most of Thomas's relics are in Ortona.
Practical: the church is open daily (Google: 7:30–19); a visitor warns the relics chapel can close earlier. Free. Combine with the Lateran, ten minutes' walk.
s-croce-relics.s: Wikipedia; Vatican News (Feb 2023); Through Eternity; Aleteia; Google Places

sylvester-cenotaph.t: Lateran: the sweating tomb of Sylvester II
p: Behind one of the nave pillars of Rome's cathedral is the memorial of Sylvester II, pope from 999 to 1003. He was Gerbert of Aurillac, the most learned man of his age, who taught the abacus and Arabic numerals in the West; enemies whispered that he owed it to a pact with the devil. The legend that grew around his tomb says the slab sweats, and some versions add that his bones rattle, before a pope dies. The devil story is rumour, the scholar was real.

Gerbert had studied in Catalonia, close to Arab learning, and taught in Reims; he was tutor to Emperor Otto III, who made him pope. Medieval chroniclers turned the learning into magic: a talking bronze head, a deal with the devil, a death foretold in Jerusalem that came true in the Roman church called Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.

What you see is a memorial, not the tomb as it stood in the Middle Ages; Borromini rebuilt the nave in the 1640s. The Lateran is free; it is the pope's cathedral, older than St Peter's. Look also for Giotto's fragment of Boniface VIII proclaiming the Jubilee of 1300, on a pillar of the right aisle.

Inside the door of Santa Sabina, Rome's best-preserved 5th-century basilica, a round black stone sits on a twisted column. The legend says the devil threw it at Saint Dominic while he prayed and missed; scholars think it is a Roman counterweight from a set of scales. While here, look at the cypress-wood doors in the porch, among the oldest Christian carvings anywhere, with one of the earliest Crucifixion scenes.
Nearby on the Aventine, Sant'Alessio keeps the wooden stairs under which, legend says, Saint Alexius lived unrecognised for 17 years in his own family's house.

teresa-foot.t: Santa Maria della Scala: Teresa of Ávila's foot
p: In the chapel left of the sanctuary of this Carmelite church is the right foot of Teresa of Ávila, cut from her body and sent from Spain in 1617; it has been in this chapel since 1905. A scientific examination begun in 2024 described the mummification of her foot, arm and face as natural.

Practical: Google lists 10–13 and 16–19. In summer 2026 the foot travelled to Spain for veneration, so check it is back before making a trip. Upstairs is the 17th-century Spezieria, the pharmacy of the papal court.
teresa-foot.s: Catalogo generale dei Beni Culturali (ICCD); Postulazione OCD (2024); Ávilared (Jul 2026); Google Places

ludovica-albertoni.t: San Francesco a Ripa: Bernini's dying Ludovica
p: At the end of the left transept, in a chapel lit by a window you cannot see, a woman lies on a heap of marble cushions, head thrown back, hands pressed to her breast. This is Bernini's Blessed Ludovica Albertoni, finished in 1674 when he was in his seventies: his last great sculpture, and a deathbed as theatre. Her remains are in the altar beneath her.

Ludovica (1473–1533) was a Roman noblewoman who, widowed, joined the Franciscan Third Order here and spent her fortune on the poor of Trastevere; she died of fever. A descendant, Cardinal Paluzzi Albertoni, nephew by adoption of Pope Clement X, had her beatified in 1671 and commissioned Bernini, who reportedly did it for free. Whether she is dying or in ecstasy is the old argument, and Bernini meant it to be both.
Compare her with his Teresa in Santa Maria della Vittoria, 25 years earlier: same hidden light, same fainting saint, but here no audience and no angel. The chapel's restoration has finished.
Practical: Google lists daily 7–12:30 and 16–19:30; free. Ask a friar about Saint Francis's cell behind the sacristy. Giorgio de Chirico's tomb is also in this church.
ludovica-albertoni.s: Wikipedia; Turismo Roma; Finestre sull'Arte; Through Eternity; Google Places

s-andrea-quirinale.t: Sant'Andrea al Quirinale: Kostka on his deathbed
p: Stanislaus Kostka, a Polish noble who walked to Rome to become a Jesuit against his family's will, died in the novitiate here in August 1568, aged 17. Upstairs, in his reconstructed rooms, Pierre Legros carved him in 1702–03 lying on his deathbed: white marble face and hands, a black-marble Jesuit gown, a yellow-marble blanket. It is one of the strangest and most moving sculptures in Rome.
Downstairs is Bernini's oval church, which he called his most perfect work. Practical: closed Mondays; the rooms are reached from the sacristy, usually for a small offering.
s-andrea-quirinale.s: Wikipedia; Smarthistory; La Tribune de l'Art; Regione Lazio; Google Places

s-maria-popolo.t: Santa Maria del Popolo: Gisleni's skeleton
p: Inside the door on the left, behind an iron grate, a skeleton wrapped in a yellow-marble shroud folds its arms over its chest. It is the tomb that the architect Giovanni Battista Gisleni designed for himself before he died in 1672. Above and below are medallions of a chrysalis and a butterfly: the skeleton is not Death but the dead man himself, waiting to come out new.

Gisleni worked for decades at the Polish royal court as architect and stage designer, and the tomb is a piece of stage design. In the Chigi chapel, designed by Raphael for the banker Agostino Chigi, look down: an inlaid stone floor, probably by Bernini, shows a winged skeleton holding up the Chigi arms over the family crypt.
The church is a museum of tombs from the 15th to the 19th century, plus two Caravaggios in the Cerasi chapel and the Angels & Demons stop. Medieval legend put Nero's grave here.
Practical: short and broken hours (Google: weekdays about 8:30–12 with a Mass break, 16–18; Sunday afternoon only); a visitor found it closed in June 2026.
s-maria-popolo.s: Through Eternity; Wikipedia; Churches of Rome Wiki; Biuletyn Historii Sztuki (2024); Google Places

gesu-maria.t: Gesù e Maria: Death with an hourglass
p: Right of the entrance of this Baroque church on Via del Corso, Domenico Guidi's monument to Monsignor Camillo del Corno (1680s): a skeleton in flowing robes, grinning, holding an hourglass and the dead man's portrait, while two little angels put out candles. Across the entrance, his uncle Giulio's monument by Ercole Ferrata has winged Time tearing the black cloth with the epitaph.
Hours are not published (Turismo Roma says to phone). Unverified: whether it is open outside Mass times.
gesu-maria.s: Through Eternity; Catalogo generale dei Beni Culturali (ICCD); Turismo Roma

p: Domenico Guidi's tomb of Cardinal Lorenzo Imperiali (about 1674) turns death into slapstick: a skeleton gapes as Fame lifts the coffin lid and an eagle flies off to heaven, out of reach. The same church has Saint Monica's tomb (Augustine's mother), Caravaggio's barefoot Madonna di Loreto in the first chapel left, and a Raphael prophet on a pillar.
Practical: Google lists daily 8–12:30 and 16–19:30; free.

s-lorenzo-damaso.t: San Lorenzo in Damaso: Bernini's flying skeleton
p: This church has no façade: it is built inside the Renaissance Cancelleria palace. In the entrance hall, the memorial to Alessandro Valtrini (1639), designed by Bernini and made by his workshop: a winged skeleton with ragged feathers flies up holding the dead man's portrait in front of a black marble curtain. Three churches gave Valtrini a monument; this is the one worth finding.
Also here: the memorial to Pellegrino Rossi, Pius IX's minister, stabbed on the palace stairs on 15 November 1848.
s-lorenzo-damaso.s: Wikipedia; Turismo Roma; Catalogo generale dei Beni Culturali (ICCD); Google Places

monterone.t: Santa Maria in Monterone: Death holds an empty tomb
p: A small, quiet church between Largo Argentina and the Pantheon. It keeps the monument to Cardinal Stefano Durazzo (1667), by a follower of Bernini: a winged skeleton hovers with his portrait medallion. The tomb is empty: his remains went back to Genoa.
Only one source describes it; where in the church it stands was not checked. Closed Sundays (Google).

s-pietro-vincoli.t: San Pietro in Vincoli: the reaper and the chains
p: People come for Michelangelo's Moses and Peter's chains; stay for Death. In the nave, the tomb of Cardinal Cinzio Aldobrandini (about 1705, by Carlo Bizzaccheri with Pierre Legros) is a grimacing winged skeleton with a scythe and an hourglass, spine showing, looming over a sarcophagus. The cardinal himself is nowhere: only his family arms. A few metres away, the tomb of Mariano Pietro Vecchiarelli has two identical skeletons carrying his portrait.

The chains are under the high altar, in a gilded case. The legend says the empress Eudocia sent one set from Jerusalem to Pope Leo the Great, and when it touched the Roman set, from Peter's prison, they fused into one. The church is 5th century; Michelangelo's Moses is all that was finished of the giant tomb of Julius II.
Practical: Google lists Mon–Sat 7:30–12:20 and 15–17:50, Sunday from 9; free. Building works were going on inside in 2026.
s-pietro-vincoli.s: Through Eternity; Queen's University (2023); european-traveler.com; Wikipedia; Google Places

p: In the basement of Palazzo Massimo, next to the coins and jewellery, lies the only known embalmed Roman: a girl of about eight from the second half of the 2nd century AD, found in 1964 at Grottarossa on Via Cassia inside a marble sarcophagus carved with hunting scenes. Her family had her embalmed Egyptian-style, and buried her with jewels and a jointed doll, which are shown beside her.
The museum upstairs is one of Rome's best (the Boxer at Rest, Livia's garden room). Practical: Tue–Sun 9–19, closed Mon; Museo Nazionale Romano ticket.
grottarossa-mummy.s: Turismo Roma; Ministero della Cultura; ancientrome.ru; artsupp

p: Rome's crime museum was founded in 1931 in the Carceri Nuove on Via Giulia and moved in 1975 to the Palazzo del Gonfalone, built in 1827 under Leo XII as a reformatory for boys. It holds instruments of punishment, weapons from famous crimes and the red cloak of Mastro Titta, the papal executioner. It has been closed for maintenance for years; in August 2026 a contract was reportedly awarded to design the works, so reopening is years away.
Worth a look from outside on the way between Santa Maria dell'Orazione e Morte and Mastro Titta's house: the whole papal machinery of death sat in this part of Rome.
museo-criminologico.s: Turismo Roma; zero.eu; visitor reports on Google (2026)

p: Everyone has seen the outside; the reason to book the Full Experience is to see the machine. Under the arena floor runs the hypogeum, a grid of corridors, cages and shafts where animals and scenery were lifted into the light through trapdoors. One lift has been rebuilt as a working replica, so you can see how a crew of men on capstans pushed a cage up into the sand. The attic level, reached by a panoramic lift, gives the opposite view: the whole bowl from the top, the way the cheapest seats saw it.

Vespasian began the building in about AD 70 on the drained lake of Nero's Golden House, and Titus opened it in 80; Domitian added the underground. It held around 50,000 people, seated strictly by class, and some seat inscriptions reserving places still survive. After the games ended in the 6th century it became housing, workshops, a fortress and, above all, a quarry: the holes that pock the travertine are where iron clamps were dug out, and its stone went into Palazzo Venezia, the Cancelleria, Palazzo Barberini and St Peter's.

Practical: the standard 24-hour ticket (€18) covers the first two levels plus the Forum and Palatine. The Full Experience (€24) adds the arena floor, the underground or the attic, valid over two consecutive days. Tickets are released 30 days ahead and the underground sells out; some resellers still show older prices.

Walking down from the Capitol or in from Largo della Salara Vecchia, you are in the valley where Rome was governed for a thousand years: the Senate house, the temples, the speakers' platform, the Sacred Way. Most of it is broken columns, so the trick is to go into the few buildings that still have a roof. The Curia Iulia, the Senate house rebuilt under Diocletian, keeps its marble floor in red and green stone; the round Temple of Romulus still turns on its original Roman bronze doors.

The valley was a marsh until the Cloaca Maxima drained it in the 6th century BC. The Republic's political life happened here; emperors kept adding temples and arches until the space was crowded with monuments. In the Middle Ages it silted up and became the Campo Vaccino, the cow field, and its marble was burned for lime. Excavation from the 19th century onwards took it back down to the ancient level.

Practical: the ordinary 24-hour ticket covers the Forum; the Forum Pass SUPER (€18) adds the SUPER sites, including the Curia, the Temple of Romulus, Santa Maria Antiqua and the pepper warehouses (Horrea Piperataria), and has no time slot. On free first Sundays the SUPER sites stay closed. The Park's Friday evening tour includes a SUPER pass for the next day.
foro-romano.s: Parco archeologico del Colosseo, SUPER sites list (2026)

palatino-augusto.t: Palatine: Houses of Augustus and Livia
p: The Palatine is where Rome says it was founded and where the emperors lived; the word palace comes from its name. Most of it is the vast brick shell of Domitian's palace, but the reason to come is small: the House of Augustus, where the first emperor lived modestly by later standards, with rooms painted in the Second Style. In the "room of masks" the walls are painted as a stage set, with theatre masks and false architecture that seems to open the room outwards.

Next door is the House of Livia, his wife, with frescoed garlands and fake windows. Nearby, the Aula Isiaca has Egyptian-style paintings from the time of Caligula, now shown beneath the Renaissance Loggia Mattei that was built over it. These rooms survived because later emperors filled them in to build on top, which is also why they were rediscovered only in the 20th century.

Practical: both houses are SUPER sites, so you need the Forum Pass SUPER or a Full Experience ticket. The House of Augustus is closed on Mondays and the House of Livia on Tuesdays. The Domus Tiberiana rooms and the lower floor of the Palatine Museum are also open.

Michelangelo's square on the Capitol is the front door; the museum is in the two palaces facing each other across it, and the best part is underneath. A tunnel lined with Roman inscriptions, the Galleria Lapidaria, runs under the piazza and climbs into the Tabularium, the Republic's record office, whose arches frame the Forum from above. It is the best balcony in ancient Rome, and few visitors find it.

The collection began in 1471, when Pope Sixtus IV gave a group of ancient bronzes to the people of Rome, which makes it the oldest public museum in the world. The original bronze equestrian Marcus Aurelius is inside, under a glass roof; the one in the piazza is a copy. It survived the Middle Ages because people believed the rider was Constantine, the first Christian emperor. Other bronzes include the She-Wolf and the Boy with a Thorn.

Look also at the fountain of the Dea Roma below the Senator's Palace and the Egyptian lions at the foot of the stair: both belong to the Acqua Felice of 1587, the aqueduct Sixtus V brought to the hills. 2026 ticket price was not checked.
capitolini.s: Capitoline Museums; Sovrintendenza Capitolina. 2026 price not verified

p: It looks like a park, and that is the point: the long hollow between the Palatine and the Aventine is the shape of the track itself, about 600 m long. Stand at one end and you can read the turning post and the stands from the slope of the grass. At the curved south-east end, excavations show the brick seating and the shops that lined the outside, with the medieval Torre della Moletta standing on top.

Chariot racing here went back to the kings; under the empire the circus held perhaps 150,000 people, far more than the Colosseum. Two Egyptian obelisks once stood on the central barrier; both now stand elsewhere, in Piazza del Popolo and outside the Lateran. Today the field hosts concerts and the city's big celebrations.
circo-massimo.s: Sovrintendenza Capitolina. Access details not re-checked in 2026

p: Look at the curved wall from Via del Teatro di Marcello: two orders of Roman arches, Doric below and Ionic above, and on top of them a palace with windows, shutters and plants. People really live up there. This is Rome's clearest example of stacked time, a building that never stopped being used, only changed owners.

Augustus finished the theatre in 13–11 BC and named it after his nephew and heir Marcellus, who had died young. In the Middle Ages the Savelli family turned it into a fortress; Baldassarre Peruzzi built their palace into the top in the 16th century, and the Orsini later took it over. The 1920s–30s isolation works cleared the houses around it.
Walk on past the three columns of the Temple of Apollo Sosianus to the Portico d'Ottavia and the Ghetto; the theatre is the hinge between the ancient city and the Jewish quarter.

The marble altar Augustus's Senate voted in 13 BC is now sealed in a glass box by Richard Meier, the first modern building in the historic centre and still argued about. Inside, the processional frieze shows the emperor's family walking to a sacrifice, children tugging at their parents' clothes. The lower panels are covered in acanthus scrolls; look closely and you find lizards, snakes, birds and insects hidden in the leaves.

The altar was excavated in pieces from under Palazzo Fiano and rebuilt here in 1938 for the bimillenary of Augustus's birth, with the Res Gestae, Augustus's own account of his deeds, carved on the outside wall facing his mausoleum. Read it from the street.

Nearly 90 m across, this was the largest circular tomb in the ancient world, built by Augustus for himself and his family as early as 28 BC. Today you see it from the new Piazza Augusto Imperatore, opened on 6 June 2025, where travertine steps lead down to the ancient ground level and show how far Rome has risen around it.

Its later lives are the story: a medieval Colonna fortress, a garden, an arena for bullfights and animal shows (iron rings from that time were visible on the 2021 visits), and from 1908 to 1936 the Augusteo concert hall. Mussolini stripped it back to the ruin and framed it with the 1930s blocks around the square, whose inscriptions still celebrate him.

Practical: it closed again on 6 June 2022 for a museum fit-out designed by Rem Koolhaas's office and funded by Bulgari. The city forecasts the end of works for the end of 2026, but nothing has been announced. Beware an Arte.it article titled "reopens after 14 years" that appears dated November 2026: it is the 2021 article.

This is the most complete piece of ancient Rome you can walk through as a building rather than a ruin: a curved brick complex of shops, halls and offices stepping up the Quirinal slope. Inside you walk on the Via Biberatica, an ancient street still paved with basalt, between shopfronts with their door frames and windows intact.

Apollodorus of Damascus built it in the early 2nd century AD to hold up the hillside cut away for Trajan's Forum, and to house the services of the forum. The upper terraces look down on the forum and on Trajan's Column, its spiral of reliefs telling the Dacian wars. The museum also explains the imperial fora that Mussolini's Via dell'Impero buried in the 1930s.

Below street level, right next to Trajan's Column, is one of the two library halls that flanked it: one for Latin scrolls, one for Greek. You go down into a large hall at the ancient floor level, see the marble friezes recovered from it, and then a video projection rebuilds the room around you with its shelves and columns.

Trajan's forum, inaugurated in AD 112 and designed by Apollodorus of Damascus, was the largest of the imperial fora, and its libraries sat on either side of the column so readers could study its reliefs from the upper floors. The hall opened to the public on 16 November 2026 as part of the Jubilee-era Caput Mundi programme; it is new enough that regular hours were not yet published.
biblioteca-traiano.s: Manual check, Nov 2026 (PNRR Caput Mundi opening); visitor reviews. Hours unverified

p: You walk into a hillside and find a palace: high corridors, painted vaults and, at the centre, the Octagonal Room, lit through an oculus in its concrete dome, built decades before the Pantheon. In another room the vault mosaic shows Ulysses handing wine to the Cyclops Polyphemus, one of the first vault mosaics known. It is about 10 °C inside all year, so bring a layer; you get a hard hat.

Nero built the Golden House after the fire of AD 64 across the centre of the city, with a lake where the Colosseum now stands. After his death his successors buried it: Trajan filled the rooms with earth and built his baths on top, which is why the paintings survived. In the 1480s artists lowered themselves into the "grottoes" to copy them, and the style they copied became known as grotesque.

Practical: open only Friday to Sunday, by booking, with a guided tour and a virtual-reality section (€26), or unguided at 12:00 and 17:00 (€18). Despite what some pages say, it is not free on first Sundays. On the third Thursday of the month the Park runs Highlights visits for 23 people.
domus-aurea.s: Parco archeologico del Colosseo (colosseo.it, 2026); manual check Nov 2026

p: In the substructures of Trajan's baths on Colle Oppio, a new museum shows the Città Dipinta, a 1st-century fresco of a walled city seen from above, with streets, buildings and a harbour. Nobody knows whether it is a real place or an ideal one. Next to it is a large wall mosaic found in the same excavations. You enter through a double door that keeps the temperature steady for the paintings.

These rooms belonged to buildings that stood here before Trajan, and survived because his engineers buried them under the platform of his baths, as they did Nero's Domus Aurea next door. The museum opened on a trial basis on 12 September 2026, running to 31 March 2027; it is visited by booking only. The lead water pipes (fistulae) of the baths are shown at the entrance.
terme-traiano.s: Manual check Nov 2026; visitor reports (Sep–Oct 2026). Pin from Google

p: Above ground the brick halls are so high that the scale is hard to read; the frigidarium alone could hold a church. Underneath is the part that explains how it worked: service galleries up to about 6 m high, wide enough for carts, where slaves moved wood to the furnaces that heated the floors, plus a water-driven mill and the largest mithraeum in Rome, the cave-like shrine of a cult popular with soldiers.

Caracalla opened the baths in 212–216 AD; they could take some 1,600 bathers at a time and worked until the Goths cut the aqueducts in 537. In 1960 the frigidarium hosted the Olympic gymnastics, and the summer opera is still staged here.

Practical: the day ticket is about €8, with combined tickets including the Tomb of Cecilia Metella and the Villa dei Quintili. The underground and mithraeum opened only on the "Notturno Imperiale" evenings, the last on 15 October 2026; watch the Soprintendenza site for 2027.
caracalla.s: Soprintendenza Speciale di Roma; press on Notturno Imperiale 2026

porta-s-sebastiano.t: Porta San Sebastiano and Museum of the Walls
p: The Via Appia leaves Rome through this twin-towered gate, and inside it a small museum lets you climb up and walk along the top of the Aurelian Walls for a stretch, with the Appia running away south below. On the gate's jamb, look for the Archangel Michael carved in 1327 with an inscription about a battle fought here.

Aurelian built the walls in the 270s against barbarian raids; Honorius raised them around 400. Just inside the gate the so-called Arch of Drusus has nothing to do with Drusus: it carried a branch of the aqueduct that fed the Baths of Caracalla. In the 1940s the gate was the home of the Fascist party secretary Ettore Muti.

Out from Porta San Sebastiano the Appia narrows between walls, tombs and cypresses, and after a few kilometres the original basalt paving appears, rutted by cart wheels. This is the road Appius Claudius began in 312 BC to Capua and later Brindisi, lined for miles with tombs because Roman law kept burials outside the city.

On the way: the little church of Domine Quo Vadis, where by legend Peter met Christ while fleeing Rome, with a copy of the stone said to bear his footprints; the catacombs of San Callisto and San Sebastiano; and the round Tomb of Cecilia Metella, with the Caetani family's medieval castle grafted onto it. Sunday is the day to walk or cycle it.
appia-antica.s: Parco archeologico dell'Appia Antica. Traffic rules unverified

p: Bernini's colonnade (1656–67) is meant as the arms of the Church reaching out, but the square has two tricks to find on the ground. Between the obelisk and each fountain is a disc marked "Centro del colonnato": stand on it and the four rows of columns line up behind each other into one. And the obelisk works as a giant sundial: a meridian line runs north from it in the paving, with marble discs showing the signs of the zodiac where the noon shadow falls during the year.

The obelisk itself is Egyptian, brought by Caligula for his circus on this hill, the circus where Peter was martyred by tradition. It stood beside the old basilica until 1586, when Sixtus V had Domenico Fontana move it here with 900 men and 140 horses, a feat watched in silence on pain of death. Around its base is a wind rose of the compass points.
Practical: the square is free. The queue for the basilica is for the security check, not for tickets.
piazza-s-pietro.s: Fabbrica di San Pietro; K1 discovery run. Meridian attribution (Gilii, 1817) not checked

p: Inside the central door, set in the floor, is a disc of red porphyry, the rota porphyretica from the old basilica, where by tradition Charlemagne knelt to be crowned emperor on Christmas Day 800. Walk up the nave and look down again: brass markers show how long other great cathedrals would be if laid inside this one. The scale is the message, and the markers make it measurable.

The basilica you see was begun in 1506 under Julius II to replace the 4th-century church of Constantine, and took 120 years and most of the great architects of the age: Bramante, Raphael, Michelangelo, who designed the dome, Maderno and Bernini. Below the floor are the Grottoes with papal tombs, and below them the Scavi, the Roman necropolis with the grave identified as Peter's.

The dome climb is worth it for the passage between the inner and outer shells, where the stair leans with the curve, and for the roof terrace where you meet the giant statues from behind. Book online (€17 stairs, €22 with the lift); old €8–10 prices are outdated. Shoulders and knees covered.

Most people run the corridor to the Sistine Chapel; slow down in the Gallery of Maps. Its walls carry 40 frescoed maps of the regions of Italy painted in the 1580s from surveys by Ignazio Danti, a Dominican cartographer and astronomer, with cities, roads and battles drawn in. It is a 16th-century atlas you walk through, and the ceiling above it is as dense.

Other things to find: the Cortile della Pigna with its giant Roman bronze pinecone that once spouted water near the Pantheon; the Salone Sistino of the library, frescoed for Sixtus V; and Bramante's original spiral ramp of around 1505, not the 1932 double helix by Momo that everyone photographs at the exit. Michelangelo's Last Judgment finished its maintenance in March 2026.

Practical: €20 at the desk or €25 online, only on the official site. Free on the last Sunday of the month (next: 29 Nov 2026), which means huge queues. Closed on Catholic holidays including 8, 25 and 26 December.
musei-vaticani.s: museivaticani.va (tariffs and hours, 2026); manual check Nov 2026

p: Go in and the first thing is Roman: a brick ramp that spirals up inside the drum of Hadrian's mausoleum, built in AD 123–139 to hold the ashes of the emperors. Everything above is papal. The tomb became a fortress because it was the strongest building on the river; popes used it as a refuge, a treasury and a prison.

On the way up, find the stufetta of Clement VII, a tiny painted bathroom with hot-water plumbing, and the papal apartments. At the top is the bronze angel, sheathing his sword: by legend the Archangel Michael appeared here in 590 to end a plague, giving the castle its name. The terrace view runs straight down Via della Conciliazione to St Peter's, and is where Tosca jumps in Puccini's opera.

Practical: €18 from 1 July 2026, with a name on the ticket. The first Monday of each month to the end of 2026 has a cheap evening opening (14:00–20:00, €5, at the desk). The Passetto to the Vatican is a separate booking.
castel-s-angelo.s: Ministero della Cultura, Castel Sant'Angelo page (2026)

p: Running over the rooftops of Borgo is a wall with a corridor along its top: the Passetto, about 800 m from the Vatican palace to Castel Sant'Angelo. On the visit you walk along it, on top and inside, looking down into the streets of Borgo on one side and back to St Peter's on the other.

It was built into the Leonine Wall of around 852, put up after Saracens sacked St Peter's in 846. Its famous moment came on 6 May 1527, when the troops of Charles V broke into Rome: Pope Clement VII ran along the corridor to the castle while most of the Swiss Guard died covering his escape. The visit includes the Bastione di San Marco.
Practical: only guided or timed visits, Friday to Sunday, booked online (€24–30 including the castle). Groups are small because the corridor is narrow.

St Peter's is not Rome's cathedral; this is. Constantine gave the Lateran palace to the bishop of Rome soon after 312, and his basilica here is the mother church of the Catholic world. Borromini remodelled the nave in the 1640s, wrapping the old columns in giant piers with niches for the apostles.

The things to find: on a pillar of the right aisle, a fresco fragment attributed to Giotto's circle showing Boniface VIII proclaiming the first Jubilee in 1300; the cloister by the Vassalletto workshop, with twisted columns inlaid with glittering Cosmati mosaic; and outside, the octagonal baptistery of the 4th–5th century, the model for baptisteries across Europe. In the square stands the tallest obelisk in Rome, brought from Karnak by Constantius II and re-erected by Sixtus V in 1588.
Across the road is the Scala Santa. The €14 combo covers the cloister, baptistery, Scala Santa chapel and treasury.
laterano.s: Basilica di San Giovanni in Laterano; K1 discovery run

p: Pilgrims climb these 28 steps on their knees, praying on each one, because tradition says they are the stairs of Pilate's palace in Jerusalem that Christ climbed before his trial, brought to Rome by Constantine's mother Helena. You can watch, or join, or take the side stairs on foot. What you kneel on is not the marble: since 1723–24 the steps have been cased in walnut to protect them, with small windows over the spots said to be stained with blood.

Domenico Fontana built the present building for Sixtus V in 1589 to house the stairs and the Sancta Sanctorum, the private chapel of the medieval popes, which was kept when the old Lateran palace was demolished. In 2019 the steps were shown without their wooden casing for the first time in about 300 years, from 11 April to 9 June.
Practical: the stairs are free. The Sancta Sanctorum, with its 13th-century frescoes and the Acheropita icon "not made by human hands", costs €3.50 in cash and is closed on Sundays.

Of the four papal basilicas this is the one that kept its early-Christian body: the nave mosaics are from the 430s, the oldest Marian cycle in Rome. Since April 2025 it also holds the tomb of Pope Francis, between the Pauline and Sforza chapels: a slab of Ligurian stone from his grandparents' region, inscribed only FRANCISCUS, with a copy of his iron pectoral cross. Most visitors come for that now.

Two more things are easy to miss. In the floor beside the high altar is a simple slab marking the tomb of the Bernini family, Gian Lorenzo included; the greatest sculptor of Baroque Rome lies under a line of text. And under the basilica, on a guided visit, is a Roman building with heating cavities and a fresco of an agricultural calendar showing the work of the months.

Practical: the basilica is free. The Loggia route (€12) takes you up to Filippo Rusuti's late 13th-century façade mosaics and Bernini's spiral stair. The Esquilino obelisk behind the apse is one end of Sixtus V's star of straight streets.
s-maria-maggiore.s: Basilica di Santa Maria Maggiore; Romasegreta; manual check Nov 2026 (underground booking)

p: The huge nave, with its forest of granite columns, looks ancient but is mostly 19th-century: the old basilica burned on the night of 15–16 July 1823, and it was rebuilt to the old plan. Run your eye along the top of the walls: a band of mosaic medallions shows every pope from Peter onwards, with blank spaces left for the future.

Below the altar a window shows the marble sarcophagus held to be Paul's, with a chain relic beside it. The cloister by the Vassalletto workshop survived the fire, with twisted and inlaid columns, and so did the 12th-century Easter candlestick, carved with scenes of the Passion.
The plain beyond the basilica was where Paolo Orlando planned, in the 1900s, the docks of a canal port joining Rome to the sea; it was never built, but it is why industrial Ostiense grew here.
s-paolo-fuori.s: Basilica di San Paolo; OS2 discovery run (Orlando's canal)

p: Stand under the oculus and look up: a 43 m concrete dome with a 9 m hole at the top, and nothing holding it but its own shape. The concrete is graded, heavy aggregate near the base and light volcanic pumice near the crown, so the dome gets lighter as it rises; it is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. Then look down: the floor is slightly domed too, with small drain holes under the oculus to take the rain.

Agrippa's name is on the porch, but the building is Hadrian's, of around 125 AD. It survived because in 609 it became a church, Santa Maria ad Martyres, and it has been in use ever since. Raphael asked to be buried here and lies in a niche on the left; the first two kings of Italy are here too. On sunny days the disc of light from the oculus moves across the coffers through the day like the hand of a clock.

Practical: since 1 July 2026 entry costs €7, under an agreement between the Ministry and the Diocese of Rome. Book a timed slot; the ticket office closes at 18:00. A portico column shows how high the 1598 Tiber flood reached, about a third of the way up.
pantheon.s: MiC–Diocese of Rome agreement (Apr 2026); K1 discovery run

p: The piazza is long, narrow and rounded at the north end because it is a stadium: Domitian built a track for athletics here in AD 86, and the houses were built on its stands, so the square kept its outline. Walk to the curved north end and you can see the houses following the line of the old seating.

In the middle is Bernini's Fountain of the Four Rivers (1651), with the Danube, Ganges, Nile and Río de la Plata around an obelisk. The guides' story that the Plata figure raises his arm in fear of Borromini's church opposite is a myth: the fountain was finished before the façade of Sant'Agnese in Agone was begun. Another myth says the fountains run on the Acqua Paola; they are fed by the Acqua Vergine, the same water as the Trevi.
Under the square's north end you can visit what survives of the stadium itself.
navona.s: K1, K2 discovery runs; manual check Nov 2026 (water supply)

p: From Via di Tor Sanguigna you go down about 4.5 m to the ground level of Domitian's stadium and walk among the travertine arcades and brick vaults that held up its stands. It is the clearest way to understand Piazza Navona above: the square is the track, the buildings are the seats.

The stadium held athletic contests on the Greek model, which Domitian promoted. It was used into late antiquity; Saint Agnes was martyred, by tradition, in one of its arches, where Sant'Agnese in Agone now stands.
stadio-domiziano.s: K1 discovery run. Price not verified

p: At the foot of the steps is the Barcaccia, a half-sunk stone boat by Pietro Bernini, Gian Lorenzo's father (1627–29). It sits below street level for a practical reason: the Acqua Vergine arrives here with very little pressure, so the fountain could not throw water upward and was set low instead. The story that it recalls a boat stranded by a Tiber flood is a legend.

The steps themselves, by Francesco De Sanctis (1723–25), were paid for by the French to link the Spanish embassy's square with their church of Trinità dei Monti above. Since 2019 sitting on them has been banned, with fines. Keats died in the house on the right at the bottom, now the Keats–Shelley museum.

In the corridors of the convent behind the church are two 17th-century anamorphoses: murals painted so distorted that from most places they look like landscapes or nothing at all, and only from one point resolve into a figure, a saint at prayer. They are scientific work as much as art, made by Minim friars who were mathematicians: Emmanuel Maignan and Jean-François Nicéron, who wrote a treatise on optical perspective.

Maignan also made a catoptric sundial: a small mirror on the window sill throws a spot of sunlight onto the ceiling, which is painted with lines showing the hours and dates. Visiting means booking a guided tour with the community that runs the convent.
trinita-anamorfosi.s: K1 discovery run; manual check Nov 2026 (booking contact)

p: The palace on Rome's highest hill was built from 1583 for the popes as a summer residence out of the malarial valley; after 1870 it became the royal palace, and since 1946 the residence of the President of the Republic. The visit takes you through the Cortile d'Onore and the state rooms of the piano nobile, where routes also include contemporary works.

Outside, the square holds the Dioscuri, two Roman giants with their horses, with an obelisk and a fountain: the end of the Acqua Felice line. The changing of the guard takes place in front of the palace.
quirinale.s: visite.quirinale.it (2026); manual check Nov 2026 (closed days conflict)

p: Look at the Rape of Proserpina: Pluto's fingers press into the back of her thigh, and the marble seems to give like flesh. Bernini was in his early twenties. In the next rooms, Apollo and Daphne catches the moment she turns into a laurel, and his David bites his lip as he aims. The six Caravaggios are upstairs and down, including the sick young Bacchus and the David with the head of Goliath that is his own face.

Cardinal Scipione Borghese, nephew of Paul V, built the villa as a showcase in the 1610s and commissioned much of it; the state bought it in 1902. The picture gallery upstairs is the floor most people rush.
Practical: you must book a two-hour slot. The Depositi, a store of more than 260 paintings hung frame to frame, can also be visited by booking. The per-slot visitor numbers may have changed in 2026.
borghese.s: Galleria Borghese (tickets, Nov 2026); manual check Nov 2026

p: On the top floor is a room that was taken whole from Livia's villa at Prima Porta: all four walls painted as a garden, with pines, oaks, quince, pomegranate and some 69 kinds of birds, under a blue sky. It was a semi-underground summer dining room, and it is studied by botanists as a record of Roman plants. Sit on the bench and you are inside it.

Downstairs is the Boxer at Rest, a bronze of an exhausted fighter, cut and bruised, with inlaid copper for the blood on his face and cauliflower ears. The basement holds the coin collection. The original frescoes from the Ipogeo degli Ottavi are also here.
palazzo-massimo.s: K1 discovery run; Museo Nazionale Romano. Hours unverified

p: Behind the façade on Via del Corso is a private palace with its art still hung as the family hung it, frame to frame. In a small room of its own is Velázquez's portrait of Pope Innocent X (1650), the Pamphilj pope, so sharp that the sitter is said to have called it "troppo vero", too true. Bernini's marble bust of the same man stands beside it, so you can compare two great portraits of one face.
The Galleria degli Specchi, a gilded hall of mirrors, is the showpiece of the palace. The collection also has early Caravaggios, including the Rest on the Flight into Egypt.

Before the paintings, take the stairs: on the left Bernini's square staircase, on the right Borromini's oval helical one, the two rivals of Baroque Rome working on the same palace for the same pope, Urban VIII. The palace was built in the 1620s–30s, partly with travertine taken from the Colosseum, which the Barberini used as a quarry ("what the barbarians did not do, the Barberini did").

In the great hall, Pietro da Cortona's ceiling, the Triumph of Divine Providence, pours over the edges of its frame. The collection includes Raphael's Fornarina and Caravaggio's Judith Beheading Holofernes. A mithraeum in the gardens opens only on rare visits.
barberini.s: K1, K2 discovery runs. Hours unverified

p: Romans call it the typewriter or the wedding cake, but the glass lift up the back takes you to the terrace of the two bronze chariots, and the view is the reason to go: the Forum and Colosseum on one side, the domes of the centre on the other, the Capitol right below.

The monument to Victor Emmanuel II, first king of united Italy, was built from 1885 to 1935, and it cut away part of the Capitoline hill and a medieval quarter to make room; it also holds the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. Its white Botticino marble is foreign to Rome's travertine and brick, which is much of why it stands out so harshly.
vittoriano.s: K2 discovery run; manual check Nov 2026 (VIVE ticket)

p: The university campus Marcello Piacentini planned in 1932–35 is a complete set of Italian interwar architecture, each faculty by a different architect. In the Aula Magna of the rectorate is Mario Sironi's mural "Italy between the Arts and the Sciences" (1935, over 90 m²). After the war it was papered over, then almost entirely overpainted in 1950 by Carlo Siviero, who erased a horseman (probably Mussolini) and the fascist date. A restoration from July 2015 with the national conservation institute removed the overpaint; the regime's imagery was brought back on purpose, for the record.

Walk round the campus: Gio Ponti's Mathematics building has a horseshoe plan with three marble ramps in the court; Giuseppe Pagano's Physics building, in brick-coloured clinker tiles with no regime symbols, is where Fermi's group moved from Via Panisperna; Michelucci's Earth Sciences and Capponi's Botany follow. In the main court stands Arturo Martini's Minerva.
Inside the campus are the Primo Levi chemistry museum and the Museo Sergi, which holds the Saccopastore Neanderthal skulls.
