sapienza.s: Sapienza (uniroma1.it, restoration and tour pages); K1 discovery run; ON run

p: Step in and look up: the oval dome is covered in a honeycomb of crosses, octagons and hexagons that get smaller towards the lantern, so the dome seems much higher than it is. The whole church, built by Francesco Borromini for Spanish Trinitarian friars from 1634, is said to fit inside one of the piers holding up St Peter's dome.

The plan is a set of curves pushed and pulled against each other, and the wavy façade (finished only after Borromini's death in 1667) bends around the street corner at the Quattro Fontane crossroads. The tiny cloister next door, with its two storeys of columns and convex corners, is as inventive. Stand outside at the crossroads to see obelisks at the end of three streets.

Count the columns of the nave: they are ancient granite, taken from Roman buildings, and their capitals do not match, some Ionic, some Corinthian, a few still carrying pagan gods. The church was rebuilt in the 1140s with whatever good stone could be found. In the apse, the 12th-century mosaic shows Christ with his arm around his mother on a single throne; below it Pietro Cavallini's panels of the Life of the Virgin (late 13th century) are among the first steps towards the painting of Giotto.
The portico is lined with fragments of inscriptions and early Christian carvings found in the area. The square in front, with its fountain, is the evening living room of Trastevere.

sacre-stimmate-crypt.t: Bone crypt of the Sacre Stimmate
p: Below the church of the Sacred Stigmata of St Francis, on the corner of Largo Argentina, is a newly restored crypt where the bones of the dead were set into the walls in patterns, with frescoes painted to look like coloured marble around them. It is a smaller cousin of the Capuchin crypt and of Santa Maria dell'Orazione e Morte, and almost nobody knows it.

The church was rebuilt in the early 18th century (finished 1721, façade by Giovanni Battista Contini) for the confraternity of the Stigmata on the site of an older church. Its parish kept the right to bury in the floor, which is why the crypt filled. The church also holds a relic said to contain a drop of St Francis's blood.
Practical: after restoration the crypt opened free on three Thursday afternoons, 26 November, 3 and 10 December 2026. Later openings are not yet announced.
sacre-stimmate-crypt.s: Manual check Nov 2026 (opening dates). Map pin from Google

p: A few steps from the Trevi Fountain, a stair goes down 8–9 m under the street into a Roman neighbourhood: an apartment block and a castellum, a distribution tank of the Aqua Virgo built under Hadrian. Water from the same aqueduct still seeps through the stone and pools in the tank. It is the best place to see that the Trevi is not just a fountain but the visible end of a working Roman water line.

The site was found in 1999 during works to turn the old Cinema Trevi into a new one, and it opened as the "Città dell'Acqua" in 2004. A small display shows the coins and objects found, including some thrown as offerings.
vicus-caprarius.s: K2, X1 discovery runs; manual check Nov 2026 (hours)

p: The great white fountain on the Gianicolo, built for Pope Paul V in 1610–12 with marble from the Forum, is the mostra of the Acqua Paola, the aqueduct he restored from Lake Bracciano. Water pours from the five arches into a basin added in 1690, and from the terrace in front you get one of the best views across the city.

The water did work, too: from 1901 until the 1930s its fall drove a small hydroelectric plant, Rome's first. Behind the fountain, in a garden opened only on booking and some summer evenings, is the "primo castello di divisione", the first tank where the water was split into channels for the city below. Paola water feeds Ponte Sisto's fountain and the fountains of St Peter's Square.
fontanone-paola.s: K2, X1 discovery runs; manual check Nov 2026 (openings)

p: Sixtus V brought the Acqua Felice into Rome in 1587, the first aqueduct built since the Romans, to supply the dry hills where he wanted the city to grow; this is its show-end, by Domenico Fontana. Moses strikes water from the rock in the middle niche, and he is notoriously out of proportion: Romans mocked him from the day he was unveiled.

The aqueduct, named after the pope's birth name Felice Peretti, runs in from the south-east over the arches of the ancient Aqua Marcia, through Porta Furba and the Arco di Sisto V. Its water also feeds the Quirinal's fountains, the Triton at Piazza Barberini and the Dea Roma on the Capitol.

Porta Maggiore is an aqueduct bridge: the Aqua Claudia and Anio Novus, finished under Claudius in AD 52, crossed the Via Praenestina and Via Labicana here on two great travertine arches. The inscriptions on the attic record Claudius and later repairs. Aurelian later made it a gate in his walls.

In front of it is the tomb of Eurysaces, a freedman baker of about 30 BC, whose tomb is shaped with rows of round openings like the mouths of bread ovens or grain measures, and a frieze showing every stage of breadmaking. Today trams, trains and traffic all knot through the same point: it is still a junction of flows.

The hill rises about 35 m above Testaccio and is made entirely of broken pottery: amphorae that brought olive oil from Spain and North Africa to the warehouses by the river. Oil soaked into the clay and made the jars impossible to reuse, so they were smashed and stacked here in neat terraces, with lime to cover the smell, from the 1st to the 3rd century. Estimates run to about 53 million jars.

The sherds still carry stamps and painted labels naming producers, weights and dates, which makes the hill an archive of the Roman economy. Later Romans used it for carnival games, and its cool interior was dug into for wine cellars, now restaurants and clubs around its base.
Practical: climbs are guided, on the Sovrintendenza calendar, for up to 30 people, booked on 060608.
monte-testaccio.s: X1, X2 discovery runs; manual check Nov 2026 (booking)

p: Between the blocks of Via Florio and Via Rubattino stand long walls of small tufa blocks set in a net pattern: part of a building about 487 m long, usually identified as the Porticus Aemilia, a warehouse of the river port of 193 BC. Some scholars think it was a ship shed instead. Either way it is one of the first big concrete buildings in Rome.

This was the Emporium, where goods unloaded on the Tiber were stored and sorted. The broken oil jars from it went onto Monte Testaccio. Fragments of the Horrea Galbana, the grain warehouses, survive nearby.

Around AD 203–211 the whole city was carved in marble at a scale of about 1:240 and fixed to a wall in the Temple of Peace: every building, staircase and column. It broke into more than a thousand pieces. In this museum on the Celio the surviving fragments are set into the floor over Giambattista Nolli's great map of 1748, so you look down and see an ancient building sitting on the street that replaced it.

It is essentially one room, and visitors split between finding it the best map in the world and not worth the ticket; for anyone who likes maps it is the former. Outside, the Celio park has a display of ancient tombstones and a café.
forma-urbis.s: X1 discovery run; manual check Nov 2026 (hours). Pin from Google

p: The collection of Sapienza's pathology institute is not for everyone: some 900 preserved hearts with congenital defects, many from before surgery could correct them, plus other organs showing diseases as they were before modern treatment. It is a medical museum in the old sense, built for teaching, and a student usually shows visitors round.

Visitors who turn up without writing first find it shut; book by email and enter from the Policlinico gate next to the metro, then follow the signs. The comparative anatomy museum, with whale skeletons, is a few minutes away on Via Borelli.
anatomia-patologica.s: X1 discovery run; manual check Nov 2026 (booking)

p: On the ground floor of the Cannizzaro building, named after the chemist who sorted out atomic weights in 1858, is a museum of the Rome school of chemistry: his glassware and instruments, and the equipment Gian Alberto Blanc used for early radioactivity research. It was founded in 1986, opened in 1992 and named after Primo Levi, the chemist and writer.

It feels more like a store than a showroom, but the professors who open it are enthusiasts, and some cases can be seen from the atrium when it is shut. Pair it with the Museo Sergi and the campus walk.
primo-levi.s: X1 discovery run; manual check Nov 2026 (hours)

arte-sanitaria.t: Museum of the History of Medicine (Arte Sanitaria)
p: Inside the old Santo Spirito hospital is a museum of how medicine was practised: Ercole Lelli's 18th-century anatomical waxes, a reconstructed 17th-century pharmacy with its jars, surgical instruments, and the table on which the body of Goffredo Mameli, poet of the national anthem, was dissected after he died of his wounds in 1849. A wooden model shows the hospital as it was.
Santo Spirito, founded by Innocent III around 1200, is one of the oldest hospitals in Europe, and its Corsia Sistina ward is next door. Visits are limited to Tuesday mornings in booked groups.
arte-sanitaria.s: X1 discovery run; manual check Nov 2026 (booking)

p: Rome's municipal slaughterhouse, designed by Gioacchino Ersoch and opened in 1888–91, killed and butchered the city's cattle until 1975. The iron overhead rails along which carcasses slid from shed to shed are still there, with weighing machines and the cattle pens, so you can read the process in the buildings. It is why Testaccio's cooking is all quinto quarto, the offal the workers were paid in: oxtail, tripe, sweetbreads.

Today the sheds hold Roma Tre's architecture school, the Pelanda arts centre, the Città dell'Altra Economia and a market; some pavilions are still derelict. Over the gate is a sculpture of a winged figure wrestling a bull.

From Via Magna Grecia you see the reason to come: a concrete spiral ramp, actually two interlaced ones, one up and one down, climbing the corner of the building to a car park on the roof above the market hall. The structure is by Riccardo Morandi, the engineer of the Fiumicino hangars and the Genoa bridge, with the building by Vittorio Di Fausto, around 1957.
The market has been closed for rebuilding, with traders selling from temporary stalls outside; the new market is promised for late 2026 or 2027. The ramp is what the conservation fight is about.
metronio.s: X1 discovery run; manual check Nov 2026 (works)

nazareno-arches.t: Acqua Vergine arches, Via del Nazareno
p: Look through the gate at Via del Nazareno 14 and three travertine arches of the Aqua Virgo appear, sunk below today's street, with a long inscription recording that Claudius rebuilt them after Caligula's works had damaged them. This is the same water that comes out of the Trevi a few hundred metres on.

Agrippa built the aqueduct in 19 BC; it runs almost entirely underground and has never stopped working, the only Roman aqueduct in continuous use. In Via del Bufalo nearby more arches show at street level, and fifteen more are in the basement of the Rinascente store on Via del Tritone.
nazareno-arches.s: K2 discovery run; pin: Google Places (Nov 2026)

p: Stand at the corner by San Carlino and turn: down one street is the obelisk of Santa Maria Maggiore, down another the obelisk of Trinità dei Monti, down a third the obelisk of the Quirinal, and at the end of the fourth, Michelangelo's Porta Pia. Each corner has a fountain, of a river god or a goddess, fed by the Acqua Felice.

This is Sixtus V's plan in one spot: in five years (1585–90) he cut straight streets between the pilgrimage churches and marked their ends with obelisks so pilgrims could see where to walk. The crossing of the Strada Pia and the Strada Felice is its knot. Traffic is constant, so look from the pavement.

ponte-sisto-view.t: Ponte Sisto and the Paola fountain
p: The pedestrian bridge from Via Giulia to Trastevere was built for Sixtus IV for the 1475 Jubilee, the first new bridge in Rome since antiquity; the round hole in the middle, the "occhialone", lets floodwater through. Inside it runs a pipe of the Acqua Paola, the water from the Gianicolo.

At the Trastevere end, the fountain in Piazza Trilussa is the Fontanone di Ponte Sisto, moved here in 1898 from Via Giulia when the river walls were built. Look up from the bridge and you see it stacked in line beneath the big Fontanone on the hill: two ends of the same water.

aventine-keyhole.t: Aventine keyhole and the Orange Garden
p: In the square Piranesi designed for the Knights of Malta in 1765, people queue to put an eye to the keyhole of a green door. Through it, at the end of an avenue of clipped hedges, the dome of St Peter's sits perfectly framed. You look through Maltese territory, across Italy, to the Vatican: three states in one view.

Whether the alignment was intended is not documented, but it is too good to be accidental. A minute away, the Giardino degli Aranci, a walled orange garden, has a terrace over the river and the whole centre.

This narrow walkway is the last surviving piece of the Alessandrino quarter, a neighbourhood laid out in the 1580s over the ruins of the imperial fora. In 1924–32 the quarter was demolished to build the Via dell'Impero, now Via dei Fori Imperiali, a straight parade road from Piazza Venezia to the Colosseum that cut the fora in half.

From the walkway you look down into the Forum of Trajan and Augustus, at the level the demolition exposed. The view along the 1932 road towards the Colosseum is one of the engineered sightlines of Fascist Rome. Expect fences while the CArMe works run until 2027.
via-alessandrina.s: K2 discovery run; manual check Nov 2026 (works)

gianicolo-cannon.t: Gianicolo terrace and the noon cannon
p: From Piazzale Garibaldi the whole centre lies below you, domes and bell towers named on the guide boards. At midday a soldier fires a blank from the cannon on the slope under the terrace, so that the city's bells could set their time; it is very loud, so watch from the terrace or stand close with fingers in your ears.

The hill is a memorial to 1849, when the Roman Republic defended the walls here against the French; Garibaldi on horseback stands in the square, and busts of his volunteers line the avenue. A short walk down, the lighthouse given by Argentine Italians in 1911 flashes the colours of the flag at night.

Cardinal Girolamo Casanate left his books to the Dominicans of Santa Maria sopra Minerva in 1700, and they built this library for them. The monumental hall by Antonio Maria Borioni is lined with tall wooden shelves and a gallery, and holds a pair of globes made by Silvestro Moroncelli in 1715–16, one of the earth and one of the sky, and an armillary sphere.

It is still a working research library; the hall is shown at events such as the Domenica di carta and by booking. The Dominicans of the Minerva ran the Inquisition's tribunal, and Galileo abjured in the convent next door in 1633.
casanatense.s: K1, X1 discovery runs; manual check Nov 2026 (booking)

p: Next to the Chiesa Nuova, Borromini built the oratory and house of Philip Neri's congregation in 1637–50, and its library, the Salone Borromini, is one of the great rooms of Rome: shelving on two levels behind a gallery, under a high vaulted ceiling, still in use. You can see it free on weekday mornings.

The brick façade on the square bends in and out, concave then convex, meant as the embrace of open arms. Round the corner on Via dei Filippini is Borromini's clock tower. The complex also houses the Casa delle Letterature.

On Via Gregoriana, just above the Spanish Steps, the painter Federico Zuccari gave his house a door and two windows framed as gaping monster mouths in the 1590s: you walk in through the jaws. It is now the Max Planck Institute's art-history library.
Inside, Juan Navarro Baldeweg's library of 2013 was built within the old walls, with a courtyard of light going down through the floors. Tours run for researchers; the façade is free any time.
hertziana.s: K1 discovery run; manual check Nov 2026 (tours)

p: The window stops people: shelves of porcelain heads, glass eyes, arms and legs, and dolls with bandages. This is a family workshop that has repaired dolls, puppets and religious statues for generations. Inside you can see the work in progress.
The founding date is uncertain: some accounts say 1939, others the postwar years. Either way it is one of the last craft shops of its kind in the centre.
doll-hospital.s: X1 discovery run; manual check Nov 2026. Map pin approximate

p: The round fountain in Piazza della Repubblica marks the arrival of the Acqua Pia Antica Marcia, the restored Aqua Marcia, opened by Pius IX in 1870 just before Rome fell to Italy. Mario Rutelli's four bronze nymphs, of lakes, rivers, oceans and underground waters, riding sea creatures, were added in 1901 and caused a scandal for their nudity; the central sea god Glaucus came in 1912.
The square itself follows the exedra of the Baths of Diocletian; the curved arcades sit on the baths' outline, and Santa Maria degli Angeli is built into the bath halls.

From the terrace Giuseppe Valadier built in the early 19th century you look straight down on Piazza del Popolo and the three streets of the Tridente, Via del Corso, Via di Ripetta and Via del Babuino, fanning out from it. It is the best place to see that this part of Rome is planned, not grown: the popes laid it out so that pilgrims coming in from the north gate were channelled into the city.
Behind you is the Pincian obelisk, made in Roman times for Hadrian's favourite Antinous, and the busts of famous Italians that line the park's avenues.

piazza-sempione.t: Piazza Sempione and the garden city
p: Montesacro is a piece of Rome built on the garden-city idea: low blocks and villini set among gardens, not the dense grid of the centre. Piazza Sempione is its stage. Innocenzo Sabbatini's two arcaded blocks of 1923, called semintensivi because they sit between a villino and a tenement, face each other across the square, and the tufa-rusticated Palazzo Pubblico closes it, looking along the axis towards Ponte Tazio over the Aniene.

The plan follows Gustavo Giovannoni's idea of a village with a clear centre. The church of the Santi Angeli Custodi, which Giovannoni designed in 1922–24, closes the same axis between Sabbatini's blocks. Walk the arcades, then notice how quickly the scale drops to garden villas once you leave the square.
Practical: the town hall is a working office, so stay in the arcades and the square.
piazza-sempione.s: Register research on Città Giardino Aniene; Giovannoni and Sabbatini attributions from the architectural literature cited there; Google Places

villini-aniene.t: Villini of the Città Giardino Aniene
p: The first houses of the garden city were small villini in a village style: stair towers, tufa walling, pitched tiled roofs. The Impiegati Statali cooperative had 82 built to Fasolo's designs. Roughly half of them survive; where a villino has been replaced by a block, the original garden gate is often still standing in front of it, which is the quickest way to read what was lost.

Walk the streets between Piazza Sempione and Viale Adriatico and count the gates. Parva Domus, a second cooperative of villini beyond Viale Adriatico, is mentioned in the research but its survival is not confirmed.
villini-aniene.s: Register research (Città Giardino Aniene); Map pin approximate.

p: GIL was the Fascist youth organisation, and Gaetano Minnucci's Montesacro branch of 1934 is one of its clearest rationalist buildings: plain volumes, the long gym hall, a tower. Its surface is the surprise, a skin of Carrara marble only two centimetres thick, which is why the weathering and patching are easy to see up close.

It was named for a local sports figure after the war and has stayed a gym ever since, so nothing here is staged for visitors. A story that the old diving board survives is unconfirmed; treat it as a rumour until you see it.
ex-gil-montesacro.s: Register research (ON, manual pass); Google Places

p: The bridge carried the Via Nomentana over the Aniene in Roman times and still does for walkers. Only one travertine arch is ancient fabric; the rest was rebuilt, and the tower and the little crenellated house on top belong to the Middle Ages and to Pope Nicholas V's fortification.
The tradition that Charlemagne met Leo III here in the year 800 on his way to be crowned is a tradition, not a fixed fact. The bridge is also the natural entry to Monte Sacro just north of it.

Roman tradition puts the first secession of the plebs here in 494 BC: the common people walked out to the hill, and Menenius Agrippa talked them back with his fable of the stomach and the limbs. Whether it was this hill exactly is uncertain, but the name stuck. The brick structure on the slope called the tomb of Menenius Agrippa is an imperial-period tomb with the wrong name.

In August 1805 the young Simón Bolívar climbed the hill and swore, on the spot, to free his country from Spain. A bust (2005) and bilingual glass panels in the park mark it; the bust has been vandalised in 2014 and again in 2024.

Tufello is one of the twelve borgate ufficiali, the official outlying settlements the state built in the Fascist years. Its housing, designed by Sforza for the IACP from 1940 and finished in the 1940s, is 20 'comb' blocks, each made of three joined stair-cores, set out so that each stair serves a few flats and opens into a shared courtyard.

The point of seeing it is the quality of the plan, not any one facade. Walk Piazza degli Euganei and into a courtyard from the street edge, and keep to the public ways: this is a lived-in neighbourhood.

When the old streets in front of St Peter's were cleared to open the Via della Conciliazione, the people living there were moved out to the edge of the city. These blocks of 1932–33 in Val Melaina were one of the places they were sent. The name 'Valle Melaina' is an invented one, chosen for the new quarter.
It belongs with Primavalle and Garbatella in the story of the 1930s evictions: grand clearance in the centre, plain housing at the margin.

tufello-martiri.t: Tufello's four martyrs and the 'Benvenuti' mural
p: On Via Scarpanto a plaque and a row of stumbling stones name four antifascists from the quarter who were killed in the war years, and a mural at the entrance of the borgata says 'Benvenuti al Tufello'. It is a small stop that shows how an official Fascist settlement became a base for resistance.

The four are Riziero Fantini, Filippo Rocchi, Renzo Piasco and Antonio Pistonesi. Tufello was one of the regime's borgate ufficiali, built to rehouse families moved out of the centre, and like Quarticciolo and Quadraro it turned into a base of the Resistance during the German occupation of 1943–44. The mural and the plaque are the quarter telling that story about itself.

Look for the plaque and the brass stumbling stones set in the pavement, and the welcome mural at the entrance of the estate. The comb-shaped blocks of the borgata are on Piazza degli Euganei close by, and the *Ladri di biciclette* plaque is at the corner of Via Gran Paradiso. Gigi Proietti grew up in these streets.

gran-paradiso.t: Ladri di biciclette: Via del Gran Paradiso and Parco Jonio
p: In De Sica's 1948 film Antonio Ricci gets his job, and his bicycle, at a labour office in Val Melaina. A plaque of 2014 on the former office, at the corner of Via del Gran Paradiso and Via Scarpanto, marks the real location.
Nearby, in Parco Jonio, 108 panels painted by students recreate the film as a strip of frames.
gran-paradiso.s: Register research (ON, ON2, manual pass); Map pin approximate.

p: Canino and Rizzi's church of 1975–78 turns its walls into a section through the ground: pillars of travertine alternate with pillars of the darker peperino, like strata. It is a good example of the church-building of the 1970s, when the Rome Vicariate commissioned plain, strong, geometric buildings for the new suburbs.

The Vicariate's programme of new parishes followed the city outwards in the 1960s and 70s; Val Melaina had grown from the 1930s blocks into a dense quarter with no church big enough. Canino and Rizzi also built San Marco Evangelista at Laurentino, with the same taste for heavy, legible structure.
Open only round Mass times, but the stone pillars are visible from outside. It is a few minutes from San Frumenzio and the Tufello stops, so it fits the northern church day without a detour.

Giorgio Guidi's church of 1970–73 has a central plan, an elliptical apse and a curved porch; the older, smaller church that served the parish first stands beside it. The central plan is the Vatican II idea in concrete: the congregation gathers round the altar, not in a line behind it. The date is 1970–73, not the later date some sources give.

Talenti was built quickly in the 1960s for the middle class moving north-east, and Sant'Achille is its parish church. Giorgio Guidi was the architect of Primavalle and its church of Santa Maria della Salute a decade earlier; the change from his axial borgata church to this round hall shows how fast church design moved after the Council.
Open round Mass times. It is on the northern church day with San Frumenzio and the Val Melaina churches; Metro B1 is the nearest line.
sant-achille.s: BeWeB; Google Places; pin: Google Places (Nov 2026)

p: Coppedè is an architectural fantasy in the middle of the Trieste district: a small quarter laid out around Piazza Mincio, where every building is different. Under the arch of the Ambasciatori buildings a wrought-iron chandelier hangs in the passage, a quotation from the 1914 film Cabiria; the Palazzo del Ragno has a giant spider on its front and the word LABOR over the door; the Villini delle Fate decorate their walls with the emblems of Florence, Venice and Rome. In the piazza stands the Fontana delle Rane, with twelve frogs, of 1924.

The quarter is often read as Masonic code. Those readings are folklore. A better use of the visit is to look at the materials: coloured plaster, brick, mosaics and ironwork, and the way they mix medieval, Baroque and Art Nouveau motifs without a rule.

The quarter was a favourite film set for giallo directors: Bava used the Ragno in La ragazza che sapeva troppo, Argento used it in The Bird with the Crystal Plumage and Inferno. The famous story that the Beatles bathed in the frog fountain in 1965 is a legend with no photograph or report; their Rome concerts that year were at the Adriano theatre.
coppede.s: Register research (ON, ON2, manual pass); Google Places

p: This covered market on Piazza Alessandria was designed by Elena Luzzatto, one of the first women to build in Rome, in 1928–29, and it was her first work. The building is decorated with reliefs of vegetables and produce and with the wolf of Rome. Where the fasci stood, the stone was chiselled away in 1946 and the gaps show.
A plaque to the architect has been put by one of the entrances. Luzzatto went on to design Primavalle's market (1950) and the Flaminio cemetery.
mercato-nomentano.s: Register research (ON, manual pass: 1928–29, not 1930s); Google Places

p: Two storeys of Roman brickwork stand in a car park on the edge of the Via Nomentana: a tomb of the mid-2nd century, whose front fell away and left what looked like a high-backed chair, hence the Devil's Chair. The walls are blackened by smoke, a frieze of coloured brick still runs round, and a stair goes down to a buried lower chamber.
It is the sort of monument Rome lets stand in the middle of a roundabout. Look for the change of brick colour in the frieze.

Giuseppe Sergi founded the Roman school of anthropology, and the museum is a lab frozen in time: shelves of skulls, casts, measuring instruments and teaching tables. The prize pieces are the two Saccopastore crania, found in a gravel pit by the Aniene in 1929 and 1935, which in 2015 were re-dated to about 250,000 years ago.
The pit itself, on Via di Saccopastore, has nothing to see; the street name is all that marks it. The museum is on the second floor of the Città Universitaria.
museo-sergi.s: Register research (ON2, manual pass); Google Places

museo-iss.t: Istituto Superiore di Sanità and its museum
p: The Istituto Superiore di Sanità is the state's public health body. Its building is by Amendola (1931–34), with Nicolini's relief of Science of 1950 on the front. The museum inside holds old physics instruments and exhibits on public health. It was renewed in July 2026; book first.

The institute was founded in 1934 with money from the Rockefeller Foundation, which was then fighting malaria across the world; it took part in Italy's anti-malaria campaigns. Several Nobel laureates worked here, among them Daniel Bovet, who won in 1957 for his work on drugs, including antihistamines and muscle relaxants.

The building is in the university quarter. The museum is not walk-in; email to book a guided visit. It suits the science thread of the map with the Primo Levi chemistry museum and the Museo Sergi nearby.
museo-iss.s: Istituto Superiore di Sanità; Google Places

p: The basilica stands over the tomb of the young martyr Agnes, and you go down into it by a long stair whose walls are lined with Christian inscriptions from the catacombs. The apse mosaic dates from Pope Honorius I (625–38) and shows Agnes between two popes against a gold ground.
Constantine's daughter Constantina built the round mausoleum next door, now Santa Costanza. The catacomb below is visited with a guide.

Luigi Moretti's block of flats at Viale Bruno Buozzi 64 breaks every rule of the street. The facade is split and angled, with windows and balconies set in shifting panels, and under it the base is faced in rough stone as if the building grew out of rock. It is one of the best Roman buildings of the postwar years, and the famous actor Totò lived here (Google review).
Look at the join between the rough base and the smooth upper floors, and at the flat roof edge. People say it is neglected; judge the state of the facade yourself.
girasole.s: Register research (ON, manual pass); Google Places

p: In October 1867 a band of Garibaldian volunteers set out to raise a revolt in Rome and fought a battle on this hill. Enrico Cairoli died here; a brick plinth marks the spot where a small almond tree stood. 1999 plaques carry the volunteers' last words, 'siamo caduti da forti' (we fell strong), and a column of Tiber marble stands on an artificial reef.
A plaque at the park also remembers the Italians killed at Nassiriya in 2003. From 1997 to 2000 the park became a small sculpture park.

villa-ada.t: Villa Ada: where Mussolini was arrested
p: On the afternoon of 25 July 1943, the day after the Fascist Grand Council voted against him, Mussolini came to the royal villa to see the king. Victor Emmanuel III told him the war was lost and he was out; on leaving, he was arrested on the north forecourt and put into an ambulance, which took him to the Podgora barracks. The royal villa is now the Egyptian embassy.
In the park itself, look for the metasequoia planted in 1940. The royal bunker is in the same park and has its own stop.

The royal bunker is the Savoy family's own air-raid shelter, dug under the hill of Villa Ada. The rooms are arranged in a ring so that blast would be deflected round them, there is a tunnel for cars, and at the top the shelter shows its concrete 'shield' and a mushroom-shaped exit. It is cool inside, 14–17 °C, and the furnishings are original.
Reopened to the public on 27 February 2026 with guided tours only. Disputed: prices (two lists exist) and when it was built, November 1940 or November 1942.
bunker-villa-ada.s: Register research (ON, manual pass); Google Places

p: The Via Guido Reni sheds were the army's electrical and precision-instrument works of 1906, 23 sheds in all, later used by the city for exhibitions and events. Plans by COIMA would demolish all but two. As of November 2026 nothing has been demolished, so this is the moment to see it as it is.

Walk along Via Guido Reni and look over the fence: long brick sheds with pitched roofs, built when the army made its own electrical and precision equipment. The plan is to turn the area into a new district with a science museum, the Città della Scienza, keeping two sheds.
Pair it with the Auditorium and MAXXI across the road: Zaha Hadid's museum also stands on former barracks, so this is the third time the military quarter has been remade.
guido-reni.s: Register research (ON, manual pass); Google Places

auditorium-villa.t: Auditorium Parco della Musica and its Roman villa
p: When Renzo Piano's three concert halls were being built, workers found a 6th-century BC farm and villa under the site. The plans were changed, the halls moved and the remains are shown in a small free museum with wooden models of the phases and a river-god eave tile. The Santa Cecilia academy's historic collection of about 500 instruments is displayed here too.
A free visit costs nothing: the museum, the cafe and the bookshop are open to the public.
auditorium-villa.s: Register research (ON2, manual pass); Google Places

p: Ponte Milvio carried the Via Flaminia over the Tiber. Only the three central arches are Roman; the rest was rebuilt, and Valadier added the tower at the north end in the 1800s. In AD 312 Constantine won the battle here that changed the Empire.
Lovers' padlocks have been cleared from the bridge, but stray ones still turn up.

Ressa's church of 1960–62 is built from two circular drums set off-centre. The windows are grouped in threes to make crosses, and the roof beams radiate from the middle. It is the best of the modern churches in the Vigna Clara quarter and is worth a stop if you are going on to the Ponte Milvio.

Vigna Clara was laid out in the 1950s by the Società Generale Immobiliare as a smart new quarter on the hills north of Ponte Milvio, and its parish church had to match. Alberto Ressa also built San Pio X alla Balduina; here he plays with circles, the shape of the early Christian martyria.
Open round Mass times. Look up inside at the radiating beams. From here the Vigna Clara station and Ponte Milvio are a 20-minute walk downhill.

The dam, designed by Gaetano Minnucci and opened on 12 May 1951, holds back the Tiber just north of the city. Enel runs the 17 MW plant. When the gates open a siren sounds, and the river below changes level.
On the hill behind stands the Rocca di Castel Giubileo, a medieval castle built on the ancient town of Fidenae; it is sealed and dangerous.

fidenae-cut.t: Fidenae: the cut and the collapsed amphitheatre
p: Tacitus tells the story: in AD 27 a freedman called Atilius built a cheap amphitheatre at Fidenae for a gladiator show, and it collapsed with a huge crowd inside. He gives 50,000 dead or injured, probably a large exaggeration; the Senate banned such shows afterwards. The railway trench exposes the red tuff of the hill, the lapis Fidenas used in Roman building.

Fidenae was a Latin town on the Salaria that fought Rome repeatedly and was destroyed, by Livy's account, in the 5th century BC. Its acropolis is placed on the Villa Spada hill. Suetonius gives 20,000 dead in the collapse; Tacitus says Atilius was exiled and that the Senate barred anyone with less than 400,000 sesterces from staging games.

Nothing marks the amphitheatre; the spot is not known. What you see is the red tuff with black scoria in the railway cut, the stone Vitruvius and Pliny name. Come for the story and the geology, not for a ruin.

Opened on 21 April 1928 as the Littorio airport, with a reach of the Tiber for seaplanes, it was where Tazio Nuvolari raced a Caproni plane in 1931. The Allies bombed it on 19 July 1943, the same day as San Lorenzo.

It was the base of Ala Littoria in the 1930s, and its two-level hangars let planes roll out from inside. In the bombing of 19 July 1943 the airport was hit with the Littorio rail yard; a local historian estimates at least 200 dead across both, not an official count. The Germans blew up the buildings on 26 May 1944. In 1997 U2's PopMart concert was held on the field.

Today it is a working airfield for light aircraft and helicopters. The plaque to six railwaymen killed in 1943, said to be at the tunnel mouth on Via Salaria, was not found. View from Via Salaria or the Tiber cycle path.

Farneto was built for Italia '90 to carry fans to the Stadio Olimpico, and used for eight days, 60,000 fans in a fortnight. It has since become an emergency access to the railway tunnel under Monte Mario.

Italy built a ring of new stations for the 1990 World Cup, and several were abandoned within weeks: Farneto is the most extreme. Vigna Clara, built at the same time, stood closed for decades and only opened in 2022.
Nothing to enter; the platforms and shelters are visible from the road. The Monte Mario reserve and the Foro Italico are close.

The fort of the 1880s stands on the site of Antemnae, a town older than Rome, and under it are archaic tuff walls. The first casemates have collapsed. An association used the fort for events until the end of October 2026; its future after that is not known.

Antemnae, 'before the rivers', stood where the Aniene meets the Tiber. Legend says it was one of the first towns Romulus took, after the rape of the Sabine women; by the end of the Republic it was a villa, and Pliny lists it among the vanished cities. The fort, one of fifteen built to ring Rome after 1870, cut away much of the hill.

Since then the fort has been an army radio depot and a squat. It stands on the highest point of Villa Ada; the park around it is open, but the fort itself only for events. Look for the stretches of archaic tuff-block wall on the slopes. Ask the Municipio II whether access has been renewed before going.

saxa-rubra.t: Saxa Rubra: kiln and Roman road at the RAI
p: Saxa Rubra, 'the red rocks', gets its name from the red tuff here. Beside the entrance of the 1990 RAI broadcasting centre you can see a Roman kiln, the cylindrical drum of a mausoleum and a length of the Via Flaminia's basalt paving, all kept as the studios were built around them.
The Roma–Viterbo railway stops here, which makes it an easy add-on to the Prima Porta walk.
saxa-rubra.s: Register research (ON, manual pass); Map pin approximate.

villa-livia.t: Villa di Livia at Prima Porta
p: This was the villa 'ad Gallinas Albas' (at the White Hens) of Livia, the wife of Augustus. The semi-underground room found here was painted all round with a garden: trees, fruit, birds. The original frescoes were moved to Palazzo Massimo, and on site you see full-size copies and the heated rooms of the bath wing.
The site was restored under the PNRR and reopened for a free weekend in September 2026. Regular days are still unconfirmed.

A Roman four-way arch of the Constantinian period at a crossing of the Via Flaminia, later walled up as a farmhouse and fort. It still has its cross vault, and the rows of clamp holes show where the marble facing was ripped off. Exhibits explain the battle of Ponte Milvio and show weapons from it.

Walk round the outside first: the brick arch is embedded in the walls of a farmhouse, with later windows cut into it. Inside, look up at the Roman cross vault and at the clamp holes that show where the marble cladding was taken off.

The arch is often linked to Constantine's victory at Ponte Milvio in 312, fought a few kilometres south on this road. It opens on a monthly calendar and on event days; check before you go. Train: Roma–Nord, Sacrofano stop.

Romans call it the Palazzaccio, the ugly great palace. It was built from 1889 to 1911 on a concrete raft over the mud of Prati, and the stone is just a facing over an early reinforced-concrete frame. The step down from three storeys to two at the sides is the scar of a third floor that was never built. A 1912 inquiry found costs had grown from 8 to 39 million lire, and the architect Guglielmo Calderini killed himself in 1916. Orson Welles filmed his version of The Trial here.
Prati itself, laid out in 1872–73 as the quartiere Cahen, is built on a plain grid with Republican and Risorgimento street names and no church on Piazza Cavour.

On 9 January 1900 nine young men founded Società Sportiva Lazio sitting on a bench in this square. A founders' plaque of 2000 is on the 1906 tram-station facade, and each 8–9 January fans light flares at midnight.

The founder usually named is Luigi Bigiarelli, a soldier. The club began as a running club, the Società Podistica Lazio, and took its sky blue and white from the Greek flag, in honour of the Olympics. Football came a few years later; Lazio's first real ground was the Rondinella near the Flaminio.
It is a two-minute stop on Piazza della Libertà, by the Tiber in Prati. If you are here on the night of 8–9 January, expect crowds and smoke.

The Hennebique company's system was used here by the builder Porcheddu: a single concrete arch of 100 m with a rise of just 10 m, the world's longest concrete span when opened in 1911. Parapet inscriptions at mid-span give the figures.
Walk to the middle and read the parapet inscriptions; then go down to the riverside path and look at the arch from below: it is very flat for its length, which is what made it remarkable in 1911.
It was built for the 1911 exhibition marking 50 years of Italian unity, held in the grounds of Valle Giulia and Piazza d'Armi on both sides of the river; the bridge joined them.
ponte-risorgimento.s: Register research (ONW2, manual pass); Map pin approximate.

p: The piazza is the middle of the Della Vittoria quarter, built after the First World War. Raffaele De Vico designed the garden and fountain, which is made to look like a Roman nymphaeum, with pools, small cascades and rustic paving. Ermenegildo Luppi made the sculptures, including fantastic animals on the floor of the basin. Fasces reliefs were partly chipped away. The water comes from the Acqua Vergine, the same aqueduct as the Trevi, so it is drinkable.
The quarter's old name 'delle Vittorie' (1938) survives on some signs.

The RAI's headquarters on Viale Mazzini was designed by Berarducci in 1965–66. In front of it stands Francesco Messina's bronze Cavallo morente. Nearby the Teatro delle Vittorie was a RAI studio from 1961 (Canzonissima) and was sold in 2026.

The RAI moved its headquarters here in the 1960s, when television was becoming the country's common language. The building is the place where Italian politics fights over appointments: 'Viale Mazzini' is shorthand for the state broadcaster's management in the press.

Exterior only. The dying horse is a large bronze on the forecourt, easy to see from the pavement. The Della Vittoria quarter round it has the Piazza Mazzini fountain and early 20th-century housing blocks.

The hall opened in 2009 and has 270+ stalls. Counters are colour-coded: green for produce, red for meat, blue for fish. The oldest licences are in the central aisle, with an egg stall that has traded since 1924, and Diavù painted portraits of Anna Magnani on the staircases. There is a study room inside.

Start at the central aisle and work outwards: the oldest licences are there. The colour code helps you read the hall at a glance, and the portraits of Anna Magnani on the stairs are a nod to the market-woman roles she played.
Open Monday to Saturday from 7:00 to 14:00, and to 19:00 on Tuesday and Friday. Come before 11:00, when the stallholders still have time to talk.

A 15th-century casale and post house on the Via Trionfale, an osteria since 1877. Look up in the dining room for the Strozzi arms on the vault and at the octagonal brick piers of the walled-in portico. Locals fill it at lunch.
The building was a stop for travellers and pilgrims on the old road into Rome from the north, a day's stage before St Peter's. The walled-in portico shows where carts once stood in the shade.
Open Monday to Saturday for lunch and dinner and Sunday lunch; the opening days given online disagree, so ring first. Book at weekends.
antico-falcone.s: Register research (ONW, manual pass); Google Places

p: Tradition says a leper hospital stood here from 1187. A wall of the hospital survives with the Santo Spirito double cross on it, and the little church and the Borgo San Lazzaro behind it keep the name. Sunday Mass is the safest time.

Lepers were kept outside the city, and the Via Trionfale was the road pilgrims took to St Peter's from the north, so a hospice here served both. It was later run by the Santo Spirito hospital, whose double cross is the one on the wall. Most of the hospital collapsed in 1937.
The church is small and usually locked; Sunday Mass is the time to see inside. The Borgo San Lazzaro is a handful of old houses below the traffic of Via Trionfale.

The INAF observatory sits in Villa Mellini on the crest of Monte Mario. Its Copernican museum holds the Mercator and Cassini globes, and a 34 m solar tower stands in the grounds. Italy's longitudes were measured from here until 2011 (the Roma 40 datum), a number you convert to Greenwich by adding 12°27'08.4''.
Visits are by booking or at public events; one visitor reported the gates looking closed, so ask first.

Until Italy moved to the European ETRF2000 system in 2011, all Italian maps measured longitude from Monte Mario. The belvedere gives a clear view over the Vatican and the city; one reviewer calls it the best view of Rome with no tourists, in a park that is abandoned and littered.

To convert a Roma 40 longitude to Greenwich, add 12°27'08.4". The origin was the survey tower on top of Monte Mario, later absorbed into the fort and the observatory. The INAF observatory at Villa Mellini next door has a Copernican museum and a 34 m solar tower.
Go at sunset for the view, but keep your bag close: the park is neglected. Combine it with the Zodiaco belvedere a few minutes away.
roma-meridian.s: INAF Osservatorio Astronomico di Roma; Google Places

p: Monte Mario is made of sand and clay left by a sea that covered this area. Geosite 138 on Via del Farneto shows the Monte Mario Formation: Pleistocene sands over Pliocene clays, with cold-water shells such as Arctica islandica, scallops and Nassarius, which is the reason for its fame among geologists. Fossils are protected, so look and photograph only.

The cold-water shells are the surprise: species that now live in the North Atlantic lived here during cold phases of the Pleistocene, when the Mediterranean was colder. The hill's sands record the old sea level and coastline.
The exact outcrops are hard to find; follow the paths of the Monte Mario reserve near Via del Farneto and look at cuttings where pale sand shows under the soil.
monte-mario-fossils.s: Register research (ONW, ONW2); Map pin approximate.

p: The terrace gives a view from the Alban Hills in the south to Monte Soratte in the north. The old restaurant is closed and the area is neglected, but the view is the reason to come.

Monte Mario is the highest hill in Rome, about 139 m. The name comes from the restaurant Lo Zodiaco, which was a classic place for romantic evenings with the city lights below. The Parco della Vittoria round it is a steep wooded park with trails down to the Foro Italico.
Come by bus to Viale del Parco Mellini; the roads up are steep. The prime meridian belvedere is a short walk.
zodiaco.s: Google Places; RomaToday; pin: Google Places (Nov 2026)

p: Designed by Luccichenti, Pifferi and Ressa and opened in June 1963, the hotel was cut up into a zigzag plan with brown brick, to look smaller from the city. It still provoked a campaign by the journalist Antonio Cederna in the 1950s; the exact article is not traced.

The Hilton was built on land of the Vatican's property arm and became a symbol of the speculation that covered Monte Mario's slopes; Cederna wrote against it. It opened as the Cavalieri Hilton, and is now the Rome Cavalieri, part of the Waldorf Astoria group.
Only the lobby and bars are open to non-guests. The best view of the building is from below, from the Foro Italico, where its long zigzag crowns the hill.
The cemetery holds French soldiers of the 1943–44 Italian campaign, It is on the north slope of Monte Mario; the entrance is on a minor lane.

It holds French soldiers of the 1943–44 Italian campaign. Many served in General Juin's French Expeditionary Corps, which included North African troops; in May 1944 the corps broke through the Aurunci mountains south of Rome.
It is a quiet, well-kept place on the north slope of Monte Mario. Open Monday to Friday 8–16 and Saturday 8–13; the entrance is on Vicolo dei Casali di Santo Spirito, a minor lane.

Raphael began the villa in 1518 for Cardinal Giulio de' Medici. The elephant fountain recalls Hanno, the pet elephant of Pope Leo X. It is now a state guest house, so you will see it only from outside.

Raphael died in 1520, and Antonio da Sangallo the Younger and Giulio Romano carried on. The villa was damaged in the Sack of 1527, when the cardinal was Pope Clement VII; it took its name from 'Madama' Margaret of Austria, who lived here later. Giovanni da Udine designed the elephant fountain, after Hanno, the pet elephant of Leo X.

It is used by the Foreign Ministry for state guests and is closed to visitors; the loggia, one of the great rooms of the Renaissance, is seen only on rare special openings. From the road you see little more than walls and trees.

Valle Aurelia once had 17 or 18 brick kilns, which gave Rome much of its brick. The Veschi works stopped in 1960. The oval kiln, umbrella roof and chimney were restored, then enclosed by the Aura shopping centre in 2018 and vandalised again.
The valley's old name, Valle dell'Inferno, comes from the smoke of the kilns, though other explanations exist. The workers' shanty settlement here was bulldozed in July 1981.
fornace-veschi.s: Register research (ONW, ONW2, MB); Google Places

p: The Vatican railway was built after the 1929 Lateran Treaty, and the viaduct of 143 m with eight arches carries it over Via Aurelia; fasces and Savoy arms are cut into it. The Roma San Pietro station dates from 1894. A walkway now runs beside it with a view of Michelangelo's dome.
One reviewer finds the view modest; the story and the old rail line are the point.

A greenway of about 8 km on the former rail line. It passes a disused viaduct and an old single-track tunnel under the minor seminary, and climbs by a zig-zag ramp to Via Nicolò V. Ettore Scola filmed Brutti, sporchi e cattivi among real shacks here, with the dome of St Peter's behind.
Start at the Valle Aurelia end and walk up. The old line was replaced by the new railway in a tunnel, which freed this route for walkers and bikes.
From the top of Monte Ciocci the view across the valley to the dome of St Peter's is the one Scola used: the shacks are gone, the angle is the same.
monte-ciocci.s: Register research (ONW, ONW2, MB); Google Places

p: Guidi's borgata ufficiale of Primavalle, begun in 1936–37 and inaugurated in 1939, was built for families cleared from the old streets before St Peter's. Its blocks are comb-plan buildings with gallery access; only 11 of 27 planned lots were built. A mural by Costanzi maps the original nucleus, and Rossellini filmed part of Europa '51 here.
The 1973 Primavalle fire (the rogo) happened in a block here; the plaque is unclear.
primavalle-borgata.s: Register research (ONW, ONW2, MB); Map pin approximate.

p: Giorgio Guidi consecrated this church in 1960 as the end point of the borgata's main axis. The campanile is 35 m and clad in travertine.

Primavalle was one of the official borgate, built for families evicted from the Spina di Borgo when the Via della Conciliazione was cut. Guidi drew the borgata plan in the 1930s; the church, built in 1957–60 at the end of Via Federico Borromeo, finished it as he intended, so the axis runs from the old blocks to the bell tower.
Open round Mass times. Walk the axis from the comb-shaped blocks to the church to see the plan. Santa Maria Assunta, the first church of the borgata, is a few streets south.

One of the forts built to ring Rome after 1870. Military intelligence moved in in 1925, and it now holds AISE, the external intelligence agency, named after Nicola Calipari. It appeared on the 2025 €5 coin.

The fort is named after the Braschi family, nephews of Pius VI, who owned the land. Nicola Calipari was the intelligence officer killed by US fire in Baghdad on 4 March 2005 while bringing out the freed journalist Giuliana Sgrena; the agency's site now carries his name.
Closed and guarded; do not photograph the gates. The Pineto park nearby gives open views over the valley.

A public-housing quarter of 1978–84 organised as four 15-storey towers round a piazza set on a raised deck, with traffic below. It is one of the clearest examples of the late-1970s idea of a 'town in a block'. The designers are likely Barucci with Passarelli and Vittorini, but that is not confirmed.
Stand on the raised deck in the middle and look up at the four towers: the idea was a self-contained quarter with shops and services on the deck and cars kept underneath.
It is a lived-in estate. Visit by day, keep cameras discreet, and pair it with the Primavalle borgata nearby, the 1930s answer to the same housing problem.
torrevecchia.s: Register research (ONW, ONW2, MB); Map pin approximate.

p: A wooded valley inside the ring road. Cork oaks (the name means 'cork-oak place') grow on the warm slopes, hornbeam and chestnut on the cool ones. More than 630 plants are recorded, 44 of them found nowhere else in Rome, and a small population of spectacled salamanders lives in the streams. Reviews say paths can be overgrown and ticks are common.

Enter from Via Augusto Conti or Via Angiulli and follow the stream down into the valley: within a few minutes the traffic noise drops away. Compare the two slopes: sun-facing with cork oaks, shaded with hornbeams and chestnuts.
The valley survived because it was too steep and wet to build on. Wear proper shoes and long trousers.
Ressa's church of 1957–61 has a crucifix by Morbiducci and an octagonal crypt entered from the square. The altar scene in The Last Man on Earth (1964) was filmed here.

The Last Man on Earth (1964), with Vincent Price, used Rome's modern quarters, including EUR, as an empty American city after a plague; the church was the set for the final altar scene. The Balduina was built up in the 1950s for the professional middle class, and the church is a landmark of its square.
Open round Mass times. The crypt is entered from the piazza. Ressa also built Santa Chiara at Vigna Clara; the two show the same architect working in two quarters a few years apart.

The underground tomb of the Octavii dates from the early 3rd century. Octavia Paolina, who died at six, was painted among flowers in the Elysian Fields; that fresco was moved to Palazzo Massimo. Her father's fluted sarcophagus is still in the tomb, while hers is in Milan, and a 2026 petition asks for its return.
The tomb is below ground beside the railway at Ottavia; you go down to a vaulted chamber where the sarcophagi stood. Ask the guide to show the copy of the girl's fresco and where it was on the wall.
Visits are free by booking (06 47788343) and run when staff are available; a restoration is planned. FL3 train to Ottavia, then a short walk.

Sarti built it in 1866 as a village fountain and communal wash-house fed from a branch of the Acqua Paola, one of the far ends of the water line that begins at the Fontanone on the Gianicolo. It lies below the level of the road.
Pius IX ran a branch of the Acqua Paola out here for the farm labourers on the Campagna estates. Look for the wash basins inside and the semicircular trough facing the road.
A short stop by the roadside; take care with traffic on Via Trionfale. Monte Mario station on the FL3 is the nearest stop.

The mill made pasta and flour for a large part of Rome until the late 1960s, in a quarter that was built beside it and bombed with it. Artists took the empty halls from 1973 and became the 'Scuola di San Lorenzo'.
Go for the courtyard and the gallery, not for any one object. Woodman photographed here in 1977–78, and the yard is the setting people look for.
Only the foundation's gallery is open to visitors; the studios are working spaces and private. Check the current show before you go, because the gallery opens in the afternoon only.

Montessori's first Casa dei Bambini opened here for the children of a block built by the Istituto Romano di Beni Stabili, the Talamo-designed tenements that replaced San Lorenzo's slums from 1904. The idea was to give working parents' children a school inside the block.

The building survived the bombing of 19 July 1943 and still houses young children. Google pins it at no. 58, where the register had a rougher point; the plaque answers the old argument about which door it was.
Nearby, the Talamo blocks themselves (Via degli Equi, Largo degli Osci) are the same project seen from the street.

On 19 July 1943 American bombers hit the San Lorenzo rail yards and the streets around them. The register finds the traces within about 300 m of the cemetery gate: a 1965 plaque by Accrocca, a plaque to deported Jews, lists of the dead, and scars in the quadriportico of the Verano.
At Piazzale del Verano, Pius XII's statue records his visit; the photograph usually used for it is actually from 13 August, not the day of the raid. A Hazon–Barengo plaque is also here.
There is no single marker: this is a walk of small plaques. The pin is approximate; look for the viaduct itself.
bombing-1943.s: Register research (OE, OE2); Map pin approximate

p: Marani has served this corner since 1928. Its covered patio is the useful part: a shaded place to sit after the Pastificio and Via dei Volsci.
Via dei Volsci also held the Autonomia base at no. 32 and Radio Onda Rossa at no. 56 (1977), which are only addresses now.
The monument is about 41 m across, and the recent works brought back the ancient entrance and floor levels and added new lighting.
Reviews disagree on what is open: one mentions ongoing works and an anti-intrusion system, another says the tomb is not open to people. Assume exterior only unless a visit date is announced.
In summer the park hosts an evening bar, readings and music. The Google pin (Via Prenestina 73) is used here; the register's earlier point was several hundred metres too far west.

Accattone was shot in the Pigneto and nearby borgate. The register places the film's bar at no. 50 (now a house), the railing and gate at the Via del Pigneto corner, and a nasone that was moved to Via Ludovico da Terni.
Two murals refer to the film's world: 'Io so i nomi' and 'Piccola Maria'. Of the film's sets, only the street layout is dependable.
The pin is the street, as Google gives it. The old Pigneto is a few streets wide, so read the corner, not the number.

Via della Marranella is the centre of 'Banglatown', and the film *Bangla* (2019) is set in this quarter. The register notes garage mosques at Via Serbelloni 23 and Via della Marranella 68, several of them sealed in 2017–19.
Treat it as a street to walk, eat and shop in. The Pisacane school nearby is part of the story of how the quarter's children are taught.

parco-sangalli.t: Parco Sangalli and the Aqua Alexandrina
p: The Aqua Alexandrina was built in AD 226 under Severus Alexander to feed his baths. Here its arches stand in a residential park, and you can see on the piers where the shacks of the old borghetto were built against them.
Reviews are frank: worn grass, litter, a rough neighbourhood, but 'beautiful Roman structure'. It is worth the stop.
More of the same aqueduct runs east along Viale Togliatti (see the Centocelle walk).

villa-de-sanctis.t: Villa De Sanctis and the quarries below
p: Under the park lie quarry galleries that supplied pozzolana, the volcanic ash Roman concrete is made from. The register lists tours of the Labirinto Casilino; check dates with the operator, since none are confirmed here.
The park itself opened in 1994 on former car-breakers' land, with a small sculpture park (Parco delle Sculture) and the Villa Fiori nearby. Reviews describe a running track of about 1 km and a pool.
Walk on to Tor de' Schiavi, a few minutes east.
villa-de-sanctis.s: Register research (X2, MD, OE2); Google Places

p: The mausoleum stands in the Villa Gordiani park among cisterns and the remains of an octagonal hall. The register describes a barrel vault on one central pillar and a painted medallion in the dome; a 13th-century tower was added.
The name comes from Rossi dello Schiavo, an owner in 1571. The old Borgata Gordiani, the shanty settlement of Pasolini's *Accattone* and *Il gobbo*, has gone.
The park has parrots, a playground and drinking water.
Casilino 23 (from 1964) is one of the postwar estates planned as a unit, not as separate buildings: slabs fan out from four centres. The pin is the market gallery inside it.
The register notes that Scanferla's block, with six external spiral stairs, is near Via Banal / Via Balzani. That is unconfirmed, so treat it as a lead.
Walk the paths between the blocks rather than around the edge.
Wilbur Wright flew here between 15 and 26 April 1909, and the first film shot from an aeroplane was made here. The runway is now a 350 m coloured sports track.
The park also holds traces of the ancient Villa ad Duas Lauros and the Villa della Piscina. The new section opened on 22 September 2026, with about 600 trees planted on cleared car-breakers' land.
A reviewer in July 2025 reports soil clean-up still under way and hopes for completion by 2030, so expect fences.
centocelle-airfield.s: Register research (OE, OE2, MB); Google Places

p: This is the tallest part of the Aqua Alexandrina in the city. Walk along Viale Togliatti, Via dei Pioppi and Via degli Olmi to see the viaduct from below.
The pin is approximate; look for the viaduct itself.
alessandrina-togliatti.s: Register research (OE, OE2); Map pin approximate

p: A neighbourhood restaurant with wine from the barrel and long-established Roman dishes, in a part of town most visitors skip.
Pin from Google Places.
Pietralata began in 1922 as a veterans' settlement and later became an official borgata. Its streets carry mineral names such as Feronia and Peperino.
The hill north of it is the site of AS Roma's planned stadium, approved on 28 September 2026 with works due to start in 2027; the finish date is reported as 2029 or 2031. Today it is an empty field.
pietralata-borgata.s: Register research (OE, OE2, MB); Google Places

tiburtino-iii.t: Santa Maria del Soccorso, Tiburtino III
p: Look for the frieze and the majolica tondo the register describes.
A reviewer notes it was built in the late 1930s and later restored.
The old farm buildings were turned into three renovated blocks with a garden. Reviewers like the quiet and the wooden beams, but one reports a temporary closure after flooding, so check first.

A vaccheria is a cow-house: this was a dairy farm of the Roman Campagna before the Tiburtino estates surrounded it, and the library keeps the long farm buildings with their wooden roof beams. In the garden about 40 seats sit under a holm oak, the best outdoor reading place in this part of Rome.

It is a municipal library (Biblioteche di Roma), at Via Grotta di Gregna 37, free and open to anyone. One recent report mentions a temporary closure after flooding, so check before going out of your way.
The museum preserves part of a riverbed from about 200,000 years ago, with more than 2,000 fossils and 1,500 flints, and a tactile tusk. It is the real animal behind the 'mammoth' mural in Rebibbia.
Reviewers report that staff give private tours, sometimes in English, and that only one room was open on one visit. One had a car broken into in the nearby car park, so take valuables with you.
Walk on to Casa Pasolini, 700 m east.
casal-de-pazzi.s: Register research (OE, OE2, MB); Google Places

p: The 70 m² flat was bought by Pietro Valsecchi and given to the Ministry, after fears it would be sold privately. It keeps some original floors, tiles and wallpaper and a photo archive.
Reviewers say the curators act as guides and some walking tours of the neighbourhood start here.
The Rebibbia prison, filmed in *Cesare deve morire* (2012), is a short walk away but is exterior only.

Alberto Gatti, with Diambra De Sanctis, designed the estate for the IACP along Viale Morandi (nos. 8–156). It is a Viennese Hof stretched into a loop. The 'Morandi a Colori' centre and the Ilaria Alpi footbridge are part of it.
San Cirillo Alessandrino (2012) stands on the high point of the estate.
morandi-complex.s: Register research (OE, MB); Map pin approximate

p: Reviewers describe it as ruined and closed, with a farm selling local produce nearby and fields that run towards Conca d'Oro.
The tower has marble torch rings on its face; around 1900 the farm was a malaria-ridden place, a lead the register has not confirmed.
cervelletta.s: Register research (OE, OE2, MB); Google Places

p: The revolt of 8 September 1974 is remembered by a plaque to Fabrizio Ceruso; the register does not say more, so read the plaque on site. The quarter's murals include the SanBa series by Iacurci.
In Piazza Recanati a Blu mural shows St Basil with the police detail painted over.
The pin is the street.
san-basilio.s: Register research (OE, OE2, MB); Google Places

p: Agrippa opened the Aqua Virgo on 9 June 19 BC to supply his baths in the Campus Martius. It runs about 19 km, almost all underground, and it is the only ancient Roman aqueduct still working. Its water supplies the Trevi, the Spanish Steps fountain and Piazza Navona.
At the source the register lists a 1930s piezometric tower and a medieval spring tower. The flow is about 0.35 m³/s and the whole fall is only some 4–6 m, which is why the line follows the contours.
The Google pin is the Acea plant, about 500 m east of the register's point.
The crag was the site of Collatia. Axel Munthe set up a clinic in the castle in 1881.
Reviewers are lukewarm: the show inside is good but you see little from the castle, and parking is awkward. They advise parking at the station.
lunghezza.s: Register research (OE, OE2, MB); Google Places

p: The bridge is named for its position at the ninth Roman mile of the Prenestina. A reviewer notes the northern section is overgrown. An older bridge was left inside the central arch.
The register mentions a votive sanctuary with 752 feet and 142 hands, but this is unconfirmed. The Google pin is about 2 km south-east of the register's rough point.
Gabii developed between the 9th and 8th centuries BC along the Via Prenestina and controlled the road. The lake beside it was drained in the 19th century.
The register lists a Juno temple and a 'Regia' with infant burials. Plan a visit on a day the Soprintendenza confirms.

torre-gaia-church.t: Santa Maria Causa Nostrae Laetitiae, Torre Gaia
p: It was built for the Breda workers' village and carries the dedication of the Madonna dell'Archetto icon. A reviewer calls it a simple Fascist-era basilica.

Tullio Rossi, who designed many Roman parish churches of the 1930s (Santa Maria del Soccorso at Tiburtino III, Santa Maria Assunta at Primavalle), built it in 1939–41 for the village of the Breda workers. He chose a soft, almost Rococo style rather than the stripped classicism of the time, so the church looks older than it is.
It stands on Piazza Siderea, a short walk from the Torre Gaia stop of Metro C. Open in Mass hours. It fits a far-east day with Tor Bella Monaca's Madre del Redentore and the Jubilee Church.
torre-gaia-church.s: Google Places; KonMap Rome research notes (Nov 2026)

p: Ridolfi and Frankl built it on a garage (1952–54); the concrete band marks the join and the crown is of perforated brick.
Walk to the second Mancioli house, a short step away at Via Vulci 9.

Mario Ridolfi was the leading architect of Rome's postwar "neorealism", the INA-Casa Tiburtino estate among his works. For private builders he made palazzine, the Roman middle-class block of flats, and he turned them into experiments with balconies, brick and roof lines. Palazzina Mancioli II, at Via Vulci 9 (1958–60), is the last of them in Rome.

The first Mancioli house is round the corner at Via Lusitania 29 (1952–54, with Wolfgang Frankl). It was built on top of an existing garage: look for the concrete band where the new block meets the old, and the crown of perforated brick at the top. Both are private: street view only.
mancioli-2.s: it.wikipedia (Mario Ridolfi); KonMap Rome research notes (Nov 2026)

p: Forleo and Boccuni designed a retro church in an era when most new Roman churches were modern. Reviewers call the inside modern and calm.

Look at the façade: it is a travertine copy of Santa Cristina at Bolsena, a Renaissance front on a church built in 1955–66. Forleo and Boccuni went back to the past at the moment Rome's new churches were going concrete and abstract, which makes it an odd and useful stop on a modern-church day.

It stands on Piazza Asti and is the first stop of the south-east church day. The second name is Annibale Maria Di Francia, a Messina priest canonised in 2004. Open for prayer through the day; check Mass hours for the interior.
s-antonio-annibale.s: Google Places; KonMap Rome research notes (Nov 2026)

p: STEFER was the tram operator of the Castelli line. The register notes Fellini's *Intervista*, which used it.
The Alberone market is due to move into the area around 2027. Treat the mall as a way to see the surviving roof.
The tombs, mostly 2nd century AD, are well preserved and you can see them from close by. Part of the original basalt road surface is visible.
Reviewers say you can be almost alone there and that a guide may explain the tombs.
The tomb is that of Annia Regilla, wife of Herodes Atticus, who was accused of causing her death. The register notes its two-colour moulded brick.
The Google reviews call it 'almost intact' after about 2,000 years; the name 'Mola della Caffarella' is also used for it.
Reviewers say it is hard to visit. Its portico columns were walled in during 1634. Inside, the frescoes of the life of Christ and a small crypt are said to be remarkable.

It began as a 2nd-century temple on the estate of Herodes Atticus in the Caffarella, usually said to be dedicated to Ceres and Faustina; it became a church in the 9th century. Urban VIII restored it in 1634 and walled in the four marble columns of the portico, which you can still see in the brick front.

Inside, a cycle of 11th-century frescoes with the life of Christ covers the walls. It is almost always closed: it opens only on rare special days (one was 13 June 2026 under the PNRR programme). Even shut, it is worth the climb for the view over the valley.
s-urbano-caffarella.s: it.wikipedia (Sant'Urbano alla Caffarella); Parco Appia Antica; KonMap Rome research notes (Nov 2026)

p: The galleries were dug for building material. Guides from 'Sotterranei di Roma' lead the tour, and reviewers mention bones and a Roman wine tasting at the end.
Since hours are confusing, call the number on the sign before you go.
The register describes a threshing floor of ancient columns. Reviewers say the cheese is made on site; others found it shut with no signs.

The farmhouse belonged to the Caffarelli family and is built around a medieval tower. Look for the threshing floor laid with ancient column drums, Roman stone reused for farm work. The farm keeps about 1,000 sheep and makes pecorino and ricotta on site.

It is a working farm, not a museum: the shop has no fixed hours and is sometimes shut with no notice. It sits in the middle of the Caffarella, so combine it with the Nymphaeum of Egeria and Sant'Urbano.
A grotto-fountain in the Caffarella valley, with a headless river-god lying in the back niche and water still running: the Romantic picture of ancient Rome that Grand Tour visitors came for.

It is a 2nd-century nymphaeum, a fountain-grotto cut into the hillside, built in brick and once faced with marble. In the back niche lies a headless statue of the river-god Almo, the stream of the valley; water still trickles through. It was part of the estate of Herodes Atticus.

The name is a Renaissance guess: the nymph Egeria, adviser of King Numa, had her spring near Porta Capena, not here. Later it held an osteria where Romans came to picnic, and Goethe and other Grand Tour visitors sketched it. Free and always open; PNRR maintenance in 2026 may fence parts.
ninfeo-egeria.s: Parco Appia Antica; it.wikipedia (Ninfeo di Egeria); Google Places

p: The water has free CO2 of about 580 mg/L and a pH near 6.35. Reviewers describe bubbly water, stalls and a small bar.
Bring bottles and a bag.
fonte-egeria.s: Register research (X1, X2, MB, MC, MD, OSE2); Google Places

p: The Acqua Felice (1585–87) was set into the arches of the older Claudian aqueducts; here it crosses the road. Sixtus V's arms are on the far side.
The fountain is an 18th-century addition. The pin is approximate; look for the viaduct itself.
porta-furba.s: Register research (OSE, OSE2, K2); pin: Google Places (Nov 2026)

p: Quadraro's murals began around 2010. The register lists Diavù's *Quadraro People* (Via dei Lentuli), Lucamaleonte's *Nido di vespe* (a reference to the 'nest of wasps' nickname) and Omino71's *Molti amici molto amore*.
Reviewers add Veks Van Hillik's 2014 *Frogs* on the stretch between Via dei Quintili and Via dei Pisoni.
A reviewer says it was built by Costantino Schneider in 1916 and enlarged by Paolo Stefani in 1955. Don Rey's name is linked to the list of those deported on 17 April 1944.

Find the bronze plaque of 1994 to Don Gioacchino Rey, the parish priest called "parroco delle trincee". On 17 April 1944, when German troops rounded up the men of Quadraro, he drew up the list of the deported that families later used to trace them.
The church is on Via Tuscolana 613, open mornings and late afternoons. It is one of the markers of the Quadraro round-up: Parco XVII Aprile and the M.U.Ro murals are a few minutes' walk.
buon-consiglio.s: Google Places; KonMap Rome research notes (Nov 2026)

p: Operazione Balena swept up men of the Quadraro quarter, which the Germans called a 'nest of wasps'. Don Rey drew up a list. Wreaths are laid every 17 April.
The park shares the hill with the mausoleum of Monte del Grano.
Coarelli argued in the Journal of Roman Archaeology (December 2025) that the Portland Vase came from this tomb. A lightning strike felled its tower in 1900.
Reviewers say it is far less known than the mausolea of Augustus and Hadrian but a landmark of Tuscolano.
monte-del-grano.s: Register research (OSE2, MB, MC); Google Places

p: The tower stands where the Claudia and Marcia aqueducts cross, with the Tepula and Iulia running through its base. The surrounding 'Campo Barbarico' marks the 537–539 Gothic siege.
A reviewer finds it hard to reach on foot from Parco degli Acquedotti and notes a cafe.
The park holds arches of the Aqua Claudia and Anio Novus built between AD 38 and 52, and a restored marrana channel with a waterfall (2023).
It also appears in *Mamma Roma*, where a motorbike rides under an arch on Via del Quadraro.
Reviewers call it a brutalist building and single out the ceiling. The brickwork runs at 45°.
It sits beside the Parco degli Acquedotti, so the two fit one walk.
The interior has Ranocchi's dream mosaics and Emilio Greco's red-granite font with dancing angels in the first chapel on the left. It appears unfinished in *Mamma Roma*.
Piazza San Giovanni Bosco's porticoes were designed with the church.
The studios held a refugee camp in 1944–50, and the Quadraro men were held here before deportation. Visitors report a museum of 1950s cinema and guided tours of the Rome set.
Reviewers say some tours rely on photographs and that you cannot enter working sets.
cinecitta.s: Register research (OSE, OSE2, MC); Google Places

p: Reviewers say it is often almost empty and good for a long walk. Take water and snacks.

The villa was the biggest in the Roman suburbs. It belonged to the brothers Quintilius, consuls in 151, until the emperor Commodus had them killed in 182 and took it for himself. From the Appia Nuova gate a long path crosses the fields to the ruins: baths, a nymphaeum and the remains of the residential rooms.
Enter from the Appia Nuova gate. One Appia park ticket covers the villa, the Tombs of Via Latina and the Villa of the Sette Bassi. Reviewers say it is often almost empty; take water and snacks.
Vietti Violi designed the 1926 stands. Reviewers report free entry on race days and concerts here in summer.

From the stands you look across the track to the arches of the Aqua Claudia, the best place in Rome to see a racecourse and an aqueduct in one frame. Vietti Violi's 1926 stands hosted the first Italian Derby here, won by Apelle. On the infield, cricket clubs play on summer weekends.
Racing resumed on 4 September 2026 with free entry; the calendar runs to 29 December. Hippotours (guided visits) are booked through 060608. Bus or train FL4 to Capannelle.
capannelle.s: Google Places; KonMap Rome research notes (Nov 2026)

p: The villa had a second period of splendour in the 4th century. Its façade fell in 1951 and a steel prop holds a wall.
Reviewers praise the guides.
sette-bassi.s: Register research (OSE, OSE2, MC); Google Places

p: The confiscated villa at no. 16 is now an autism day centre. The park has a library, a basketball court and old olive trees.

The park stands on the site of a Casamonica villa demolished in 2018: the city took the land from the clan and opened the park in 2019, at Via Roccabernarda 15 in Romanina. The name is the point: a public space where a symbol of criminal power stood.
It is a neighbourhood park, open 9:00–19:00. The nearby Vela of Calatrava and the Tor Vergata campus make it a stop on a south-east outer day rather than a trip of its own.
legalita.s: Google Places; RomaToday; KonMap Rome research notes (Nov 2026)

p: The register places *Mamma Roma* in the INA-Casa Tuscolano estates and in the nearby streets: the market stall scene is set on Via Lucio Sestio, with the aqueduct at the end of the street, and the film's screen address on Via dei Treviri is invented.
Libera's Unità orizzontale on Via Selinunte, in this district, is a separate stop in the Tiburtino-Tuscolano walk. The pin here is approximate.
tuscolano-ina.s: Register research (OSE, OSE2, D1, L1); Map pin approximate

p: Garbatella began with a first stone on 18 February 1920 and was planned as a quarter for the workers of the new Ostiense industrial and port zone. Its first lots are in the 'barocchetto' style, with stair towers, arched passages, loggias and inner gardens instead of straight blocks, so the suburb feels like a village that fell into Rome.

The best way to see it is to wander. Start at Piazza Brin (the first lots), go through the arches beside Dar Moschino into the courtyards, then drift towards Piazza Sauli and the school. Sabbatini's later 'alberghi suburbani' and the library in the old public baths show how the idea changed through the 1920s.
Practical: it is a lived-in neighbourhood, so keep voices low in the courtyards and do not photograph windows. This stop is the overview; the detail stops follow.
garbatella.s: Register research (X1, OS, OS2); Google Places

piazza-brin.t: Piazza Benedetto Brin: the first stone
p: A plaque in the arch records the first stone of 18 February 1920 and calls the place an 'aprico quartiere', a sunny quarter. Lots 1–4 around the square were drawn in barocchetto style by a team that included Giovannoni, Sabbatini and Nori.
