The arch beside Dar Moschino leads into the courtyards. In 1922 a Blackshirt squad burned the cooperative's shop here, a reminder that the 'garden suburb' was also a political place. Walk through before you eat at Dar Moschino.

alberghi-suburbani.t: Alberghi suburbani: the 'hotels' for the evicted
p: These blocks (lots 41–44) were called 'hotels' but were temporary housing for families displaced by the 1920s–30s demolitions in the centre. Sabbatini gave them 997 rooms, shared services and a plan shaped like a bottle in the 'Albergo Rosso'.

A clock on the Albergo Rosso is said to be stopped at 11:25, tied by local lore to the raid of 7 March 1944; the register treats that link as lore, not record. Gandhi is also said to have visited the Albergo Bianco's maternity ward in 1931.
Look from the street; the courtyards are private housing.
alberghi-suburbani.s: Register research (OS, OS2, MD); Google Places

p: Alongside the big lots, Trotta designed small cottages in 1925–27 on Via Massaia and Via De Nobili for families who had lived in shanties. They show the other face of Garbatella: single-family houses with gardens in a suburb that is mostly known for its blocks.
The pin is approximate (Google puts Viale Massaia 22 nearby); walk the two streets and look for the low houses.
Calza Bini built the church in 1931–33 at the heart of the quarter. In the right transept is the Madonna del Divino Amore, credited by parishioners with sparing Rome in the 1943 bombing.
A reviewer notes it was the first parish John Paul II visited, on 3 December 1978. Inside, the space is large and plain.

scuola-battisti.t: Scuola Cesare Battisti and the film squares
p: Nanni Moretti rides his Vespa past this school's pillars in Caro diario, and the building stands in for the 'Liceo Foscolo' in the TV series I Cesaroni. The arch at Piazza Sant'Eurosia and Luzzatti's 'Scoletta' also appear in Totò e Marcellino.

The 'Bar dei Cesaroni' is really the Roma Club Garbatella, Piazza Giovanni da Triora 6, with the Teatro Garbatella at no. 15. Fun for fans, not a monument: the neighbourhood is more interesting than the sets.
scuola-battisti.s: Register research (OS, OS2, MD); Google Places

p: A Garbatella institution since the 1970s, at the foot of the first lots. Horses are painted on the walls; the kitchen runs on a weekly rhythm (tripe on Tuesday, gnocchi on Thursday) and is closed on Sunday.
Book ahead. It is a good lunch stop between the first stone and the alberghi.

moby-dick.t: Biblioteca Moby Dick and Teatro Palladium
p: Sabbatini designed these 'bagni pubblici' in 1926–30 on the model of an Ostia Antica insula, for people without bathrooms at home. Gismondi's Casa di Diana is the reference. They are now a municipal library.
Teatro Palladium stands beside it. Opening hours are disputed in the sources, so check before a special trip.
moby-dick.s: Register research (X1, MB, OS); Google Places

p: During works in 2004 a bridge turned up about 7 m below street level, spanning a branch of the Almone. It is Roman, possibly reworked in the Middle Ages, and now shows through a plexiglass roof in the middle of the square.

The Almone itself, called the Acquataccio, runs in a tunnel 15–17 m under Circonvallazione Ostiense nearby. The river that gave Caffarella its water ends up here, underground and almost invisible. A good thing to show a non-archaeologist: a river and a bridge, buried in a residential square.
piazza-biffi-bridge.s: Register research (OS2, MD); Google Places; pin: Google Places (Nov 2026)

p: Gaius Cestius, a magistrate, built this tomb in a few hundred days around 12 BC in the Egyptian fashion. Aurelian then built it into the city wall, which is why it survives so well.

After works funded by the PNRR, new guided visits of the interior were announced for September 2026, but no regular schedule has been found. Google lists 9:00–16:30 daily for the surrounding site, and a reviewer says getting inside is possible only on specific events.
Stand by the Metro B station and look; the Non-Catholic Cemetery (Keats and Shelley) is next door.

Adalberto Libera and Mario De Renzi designed this for a Rome that was building modern public offices in the 1930s. The façade is a calm band of travertine with diamond-shaped windows at each end; a long portico runs the length of the street.
Inside, an elliptical skylight of glass blocks lights the main hall. Walk in as a customer. It is the best way to see a building that still works as designed.
A temporary station was put up fast for Hitler's arrival on 3 May 1938; the permanent building was inaugurated on 28 October 1940, with a marble atrium and mosaics.
It is the easiest place to feel the 1930s Rome behind the Pyramid. The old 'Ostiense' station is now a main interchange for the Roma–Lido and Metro B.
The wholesale markets closed in the 1990s and a 'City of Youth' project stalled. The listed fish pavilion's roof fell in in February 2026. A wetland has formed inside over the buried Almone.

Public meetings on a regeneration plan were scheduled for January–February 2026, and a reviewer says Hines funds are meant to build a student residence. Until then it is an urbex site; do not climb in.
ex-mercati-generali.s: Register research (X2, MD, OS, OS2); Google Places reviews

p: Roma Tre reused the industrial strip: the rectorate and law on the Bordoni glassworks (Via Ostiense 133 and 161), DAMS in the old Tommaseo school (139) and the humanities in the Alfa Romeo works, where Isotta added a round wing in 1961 (no. 234).

The Goa Club at Via Libetta 13 (1995–2021) and the 'Libetta Village' stood nearby; the site is slated for university classrooms. Walk past on a weekday and see what a former industrial zone looks like when students fill it.
roma-tre-ostiense.s: Register research (OS, OS2, MD); Google Places

sepolcreto-ostiense.t: Tombs of the San Paolo rock
p: The register dates the discovery to a 1953 collapse that exposed a frescoed chamber; a Google reviewer says it was found in 1898 during excavation of the rocky hill. The dates conflict, so treat both as unverified.

The tombs were used by freedmen's families and workers from the 1st century BC to the 3rd century AD. Life-size reproductions of the frescoes exist elsewhere. A visit was possible on 26 September 2026 through the Parco Archeologico (060608); no regular schedule has been found.

This is in Municipio VIII (the manual pass moved it from the south-west). The 1929 basin was where Italian ship hulls were tested as models. The campus also reuses the former OMI optics works and the 'Avorio' balloon works, now maths and physics.
Roma Tre tendered completion of the second lot in July 2026. The campus is open to walk around on weekdays.
A postwar public-housing quarter built by INA-Casa, in the same bend of the Tiber as the old gasworks and the university. It is in Municipio VIII, not the south-west.
Walk it as a contrast to Garbatella's 1920s picturesque: lower, plainer, planned for families rather than a garden-city idea.
valco-s-paolo.s: Register research (D1, MC, OSW); Google Places

p: The register lists an early graffito in vernacular Italian here, among the oldest known. The catacomb is run by the Pontifical Commission for Sacred Archaeology.
Access is the problem: Google reviews range from 'closed with no signage' to a good guided tour with a short wait. Phone first (PCAS, 06 446 5610) and do not travel on a hunch.
commodilla.s: Register research (C1, OS); Google Places reviews

p: Favini built this for the Society of St Paul in 1947–54. It is a Baroque plan executed in reinforced concrete.
The founder Alberione is buried in the crypt. A reviewer calls it little known but worth a look.

On 10 September 1943 the German advance met a mixed force of soldiers and civilians in the Montagnola. The register counts 53–59 dead; their names are in the parish crypt. At the Istituto Gaetano Giardino, Don Occelli raised a white sheet.
The monument is built around an ancient column. Pair it with the Fosse Ardeatine for the story of Rome's first days of occupation.
It is one of the forts of Rome's ring built after 1870. Its caponiers and Carnot wall survive in a 5.5 ha park. The Germans mined it in 1944.
The pin is Google's street address; the fort itself is fenced and 2021 works are unknown. Treat it as an exterior stop.

A valley with quarry faces and the open course of the Marrana. Campaigners stopped the building plan in 2002. The 'tower' is the Torre di San Tommaso; the name 'Marancia' is said to come from a freedman called Amaranthus.
Reviewers call it one of Rome's most rustic parks, with bike tracks and picnic tables.

The lot was built as basic housing in 1947–48 and called Shanghai by residents. In 2015 it became an open gallery: Mr Klevra's blessed 'Nostra Signora di Shanghai', Jaz's pilot wall and Caratoes' 'Welcome to Shanghai 35' over the old graffito are the best known.
A lift and a QR-code app help you find the murals. Be tactful: the courtyards are homes.
tor-marancia-murals.s: Register research (OS, OS2, MD); Google Places

p: The two sources disagree on the date (1938 or 1967), so its place in the church timeline is unsettled. It is listed for the church hunt with the other postwar parishes of the Ardeatino.
Go in only if you are already nearby.
The pair were left half-abandoned for years and earned the Beirut nickname. They were reclad and reopened on 12 October 2026.
They give a counterpoint to the marble 1930s EUR next door.
Gaetano Minnucci designed it for the E42 world fair that never happened. The fountain of 18 basins is decorated with mosaics by Gino Severini. In the atrium is the 1960 Olympic model of EUR.
Below the building is a 475 m² air-raid shelter, isolated from the structure by a 125 cm gap; it opens rarely. A reviewer praises the 90-year exhibition on EUR inside.

The archive is housed in a building planned for the 1942 fair. A small exhibition called 'Lo scrigno della memoria' shows treasures from the collections, including an original of the Italian Constitution.
Opening is limited to Tuesday–Thursday and guided requests go by email.

plastico.t: Gismondi's model of Rome (Museo della Civiltà Romana)
p: Italo Gismondi built the model of Rome as it was under Constantine, a plaster reconstruction of the city under Constantine. It sits in EUR's museum of Roman civilisation.
The museum has been under renovation for years. A reviewer says only part of the display is open; a reviewer who came on a Monday could not enter. The Spectre funeral scene was shot here.
plastico.s: Register research (X1, MB); Google Places reviews

fungo.t: Il Fungo, the EUR water tower
p: The mushroom-shaped tank holds about 2,500 m³ and stands on pillars that also carry pipes and stairs. It feeds the cascades of the EUR lake and the fire mains. The restaurant opened in 1964 and was bombed in 1978.
The tower appears in L'eclisse and The Last Man on Earth. Figures for height and wells are not verified.
fungo.s: Register research (OS, OS2, MD); Google Places

p: Tradition says Paul's head bounced three times and three springs rose; three churches mark the place. In 1868 monks planted eucalyptus trees to drain the malarial marsh, and the abbey now sells a eucalyptus liqueur and the Tre Fontane Tripel, the only Italian Trappist beer (the eleventh in the world).
Reviewers call it quiet and out of the way. Cross the road to the Marian apparition site.
tre-fontane.s: Register research (OS, OS2, MD); Google Places reviews

p: Palpacelli's tower (1986–90) is a piezometric tank that holds pressure for a large area, up to Testaccio. Google reviewers describe a circular restaurant at the top that was never opened and a project for a water-science park that was never completed.
Height is given as 85 m in the register and 95 m by reviewers; check on site. The tower can be seen from the public park beside it; the FAI opens it about once a year (24 Oct 2026 this year).
vigna-murata.s: Register research (MB, MD); Google Places reviews

p: Minnucci's workers' village for E42 became the home of exiles from 1947. A 1961 Karst boulder on Via Laurentina marks them.
The Archivio Museo storico di Fiume at Via Antonio Cippico 10 is nearby; a reviewer recommends it. The original fabric is mostly gone.

s-marco-laurentino.t: San Marco Evangelista in Agro Laurentino
p: A round plan with two huge columns carrying the roof over the sanctuary. A reviewer calls it small, circular and welcoming. It stands on the square of the exiles' quarter, so it pairs with the monument.

Canino and Rizzi built it in 1969–71; they also built SS. Redentore at Val Melaina in the north. Inside, look at the two great columns carrying the flat roof of the presbytery: the whole structure is shown, nothing hidden.

The quarter is the Villaggio Giuliano-Dalmata, Minnucci's E42 workers' village, given from 1947 to Italian exiles from Istria, Fiume and Dalmatia. A Karst boulder of 1961 on Via Laurentina marks it, and the Archivio Museo di Fiume is at Via Cippico 10 (afternoons except Thu).
s-marco-laurentino.s: Google Places; KonMap Rome research notes (Nov 2026)

p: The reserve contains an archaic settlement that may be Tellenae and the shell of a 1937 plant that bottled the local fizzy water. The settlement can only be glimpsed from the paths.
Reviewers note it is bigger than expected and in need of maintenance.
acqua-acetosa-laurentina.s: Register research (OS2, MD); Google Places reviews

p: The museum shows around 300 vehicles, including an Ansaldo M15/42 tank. It sits inside the Cecchignola military city (1937–43), which is closed to the public.
Google reviewers report being turned away without a booking and that photographing the outdoor exhibits is not allowed. Call first.
motorizzazione.s: Register research (OS, OS2, MD); Google Places reviews

p: Luigi Moretti's masterplan, with Libera, Cafiero and Guidi, laid out the quarter like a Roman castrum with two crossing axes, Viale Camillo Sabatini and Viale Sabato Martelli Castaldi/Via Romualdo Chiesa. Blocks stand on pilotis and low walls leave views open.
A reviewer who grew up there says the gardens are neglected and some social decay shows, but another calls it a rare gem. Walk it for the geometry.
incis-decima.s: Register research (OS, MD); Google Places reviews

mater-ecclesiae.t: Santa Maria Mater Ecclesiae al Torrino
p: The church uses a coffered ceiling and four box skylights to light the nave. Its foundation stone is said to come from the old St Peter's basilica.
It is a quiet extra for church-hunters already in Torrino.

The plan dates from 1965 and the quarter was built 1966–81 around one spine, with Chiarini's 'omnibus' blocks on it. Moretti visited and is quoted as saying 'pensavo peggio', 'I thought it'd be worse'.
Visit it with the church of San Giovanni Evangelista, at the end of the spine.
Julio Lafuente and Gaetano Rebecchini built it in tuff and travertine with curved volumes that almost vanish into the neighbouring buildings. A long canopy on tuff blocks leads in.
A reviewer calls it modern but warm. It is run by the Family of Merciful Love.
The Laurentino cemetery is huge and has its own internal bus stops. The Garden of Angels, built in 2012, has a round chapel with a copper roof by Testa.
Reviewers report neglect in places. Take it as a stop only for the chapel.

quattro-venti.t: Arco dei Quattro Venti and the Villa Corsini gate
p: Busiri Vici designed the arch in 1859 on the ruined Casino dei Quattro Venti, with four winds on top, and the date of the building is still disputed: guides say it was designed in 1859 and built in the following decades, a Comune text gives 1874–76 and a reviewer says it was rebuilt 1856–59 using parts of the 17th-century casino. The record is unsettled.

In June 1849 the French used this hill as their artillery base against Garibaldi's defence of the Roman Republic; the villa was ruined in the fighting. At Largo 3 Giugno 1849 by the Villa Corsini gate, French cannonballs still sit in the rockwork, and a 1949 bronze panel is no. 1 of the Garibaldi itinerary. A monument to the French dead is nearby.
A placard on the path tells the story. Expect fenced areas while the park is renovated.
quattro-venti.s: Register research (OSW, OSW2, MC); Google Places reviews

p: Plautilla Bricci, called 'Architettrice' in the building contract, designed the villa as a ship with a hanging garden. In 1849 Medici's legion held it against the French, and the façade was ruined. The ruin was kept and a plaque was added in 1897. Only part of the original structure survives.
The Grande Oriente d'Italia (Freemasons) has owned it since 1983. Visits are possible on FAI days; reviewers say the guides are excellent. Otherwise, look from the street.
vascello.s: Register research (OSW, OSW2, MD); Google Places reviews

p: The church stands by the Porta San Pancrazio where the 1849 battles were fought. A reviewer notes it is little known and that the catacombs were not open.
Pair it with the Quattro Venti arch and Villa Pamphilj.

The Casino del Bel Respiro by Algardi stands on a terrace; the Giardino Segreto has lily-and-dove hedges; Lago del Giglio has a bald cypress; and the one footbridge over the 1960 Via Olimpica cut links its halves.

The aqueduct arches on the park's north edge (Traiano-Paolo) feed the Fontanone on the Gianicolo, and a stretch fell in 2019. A reviewer says restoration is slow and the lakes and fountains are closed at times.
The ancient columbaria at Via Aurelia Antica 111 belong to this estate; see the next stop.
villa-pamphilj.s: Register research (OSW, OSW2); Google Places reviews

p: The Grande Colombario was found in 1838 and its frescoes are in Palazzo Massimo. The nearby columbarium of Scribonius Menophilus was found in 1984, with a white mosaic 'tabula ansata'.
MiC lists the site as not needing booking, but it is not an open walk-in site, so check before going. Map pin approximate.
scribonio-menofilo.s: Register research (OSW, MC); Heidelberg columbaria study

p: One of the forts built after 1870 to protect Rome. After a restoration begun in 2016 it reopened to visitors in 2026. An iron bridge crosses the moat to the entrance.
Reviewers call it a wonderfully restored fort and note that some parts were still under work.
forte-aurelia.s: Register research (MB, MD); Google Places reviews

p: Wurts's Lombard statues came from Brignano; the satyrs' fountain has the Visconti serpent. The park also holds an aviary, an exedra of the twelve months and the Castelletto. The 1932 plaque had Mussolini's name erased and rewritten.

The park is in Municipio I but belongs with this walk. PNRR works (belvedere loggia, Janiculum walls, fountains, statues, aviary, landslide work) were due to end in Q2 2026; some sectors may still be fenced.

The 1909 plan of Mayor Nathan produced a garden suburb of villini with turrets, gardens and linking stairs: Via Carini, Piazza Rosolino Pilo, Via Fratelli Bandiera, Via Saffi and Largo Ravizza (the old Villa Baldini fountain). A state employees' 'edificio rosso' stands near Via Cavalcanti 26.
Walk it slowly up and down; the stairs make the hill part of the design.
Pasolini lived at Via Fonteiana 86 from 1954 to 1959, then at Via Carini 45 until 1963; a plaque marks Via Carini.
Nearby are the bar of Moretti's Ecce bombo (Via Alberto Mario 20) and the Villino Cirini, Via Ugo Bassi 1, used in Romanzo criminale.
Caffè Faustini opened in 1935 and was reopened on 16 November 2025 as Bixio Caffè Bistrot under Frida Giannini. Reviewers like the service.

Monteverde Vecchio is the villa quarter on the hill above Trastevere, laid out under the 1909 Nathan plan; the café is on its main street, Via Alessandro Poerio, and has served it since 1935. The new owner, Frida Giannini, was Gucci's creative director.
Open daily from breakfast. Villa Sciarra is a few minutes' walk, and Pasolini's flat in Via Carini 45 (plaque) is close.
bixio-faustini.s: Google Places; KonMap Rome research notes (Nov 2026)

p: The family began with a small tobacco shop. Mario Vitali is a local historian who has written on Monteverde. The place trades as 'dal 1914'; the register's 1922 date is not confirmed.
Bar at the front, restaurant behind; a reviewer says come early on Thursdays for the gnocchi.

The catacomb is called 'ad ursum pileatum', 'at the bear with the cap'. Its baptistery is flooded by a spring, and in the war it was a shelter. Access is by appointment only and has not been confirmed for 2026.
Google gives Via Poerio 59; the register gives 55.
ponziano.s: Register research (OSW, OSW2, MD); Google Places

jewish-catacomb.t: Site of the Monteverde Jewish catacomb
p: The catacomb zone is bounded by Circonvallazione Gianicolense, Via Francesco Massi, Via Vincenzo Monti and the Rome–Viterbo railway. Small underground rooms and burials turned up during works in Via Vincenzo Monti, and a four-year study by Rossi and Di Mento was published in 2013.
Almost all of the roughly 200 inscriptions are in the Lapidario Ebraico in the Vatican. This is a 'site of' stop for completeness.
jewish-catacomb.s: Register research (OSW, MC); International Catacomb Society; Vatican Museums

p: The IFACP built these blocks in 1930–32, up to nine storeys and 534 flats, for families moved out of the centre. They sit above the covered Fosso di Tiradiavoli. Pasolini's 1955 novel Ragazzi di vita is set here; a 2005 plaque on Via Abate Ugone remembers him, and an antifascist epigraph is on the estate.
The idea that the plan spells DUX from above is unsourced and is left out.
grattacieli-olimpia.s: Register research (OSW, OSW2, MD); Google Places

p: The collapse of 17 March 1951 appears in Ragazzi di vita. A second Pasolini plaque is on the school, and a popular music school (founded 1976) works in the area.
Walk the hundred metres between this and the skyscrapers.

Traders will move to 70 temporary boxes at Piazza Madonna de La Salette. Just under 30 operators have already suspended trading. The €17M rebuild (105 stalls) starts in spring 2027 and lasts 2–3 years.
Reviewers say it is not a tourist market; some stalls were closed. See it before it changes.
san-giovanni-di-dio.s: Register research (OSW, OSW2, MC); Google Places reviews

p: Caniggia designed the pavilion hospital, opened on 28 October 1929. Its Puddu pavilion hosted Rome's first cardiac surgery. The ghost sanatorium of the Forlanini is just beyond.
Respect patients; look at the buildings, not the people.

forte-bravetta.t: Forte Bravetta and the Parco dei Martiri
p: A late-1960s monument opposite the entrance lists the patriots killed here. After the war the fort was used as a munitions depot and then became a public garden.
A reviewer finds it quiet and surprising for a place with that history. The parade ground can be visited by booking.
Six arches carry Viale Marconi over the Tiber. Work began in 1937 and the bridge opened in 1955. Viale Marconi is the commercial spine of the quarter.

It is 235.7 m long, Rome's longest Tiber bridge. Begun in 1937 for the E42 roads to the sea, it was halted by the war and opened on 26 February 1955. The best view is from the riverside cycle path, where the six arches line up.
Walk it to cross between Ostiense and Marconi; the quarter's market streets start at its west end.

pozzo-pantaleo.t: Drugstore Museum and the Portuense necropolis
p: Reviewers call it a fantastic small museum with burial remains, grotto tombs, mosaics and frescoes, in an unlikely place. One found it closed when it should have been open, so book.
The Pozzo Pantaleo, at Via Portuense × Via Campana, is a tomb turned cistern turned chapel of Saint Pantaleon.
pozzo-pantaleo.s: Register research (OSW2, MD); Google Places reviews

p: A reviewer calls it rather weird but enjoyable, a circular modern church. Mass is at 8, 9 and 18:30 on weekdays.
The register gives an elliptical plan and the coloured-steel campanile.

Pier Luigi Nervi used a thin ferrocement shell for the first time here, folded like paper and only 2.5 cm thick; he patented the material in April 1945 and later used it from the Turin Salone to the Palazzetto dello Sport. The Magliana lot was the base of his firm from 1936 to the end.
The ministry census (scheda 734) calls this the only survivor of the firm's prefabricated buildings. It now stands in a chaotic car park. A reviewer says you enter via the parking area.
nervi-shed.s: MiC Censimento, scheda 734; Claudio Greco; Google Places reviews

p: The quarter was built in the mid-1960s about 6.5 m below the river embankment, and an 'atto d'obbligo', a promise to the community, was never honoured. In the 1970s residents fought for housing. Piazza De André is its centre.
Visit it with the church of San Gregorio Magno and the pumping stations, which show what holds the water back.
magliana-nuova.s: Register research (OSW, OSW2); Map pin approximate

p: The gates close when the Tiber rises and the pumps lift storm water. The 1926 embankment ran from Santa Passera. The register has not confirmed the station's name or capacity.
The park offers a cycle path and river views.
magliana-pumps.s: Register research (OSW2, MD); Google Places reviews

s-gregorio-magliana.t: San Gregorio Magno alla Magliana Nuova
p: The parish dates to 1963; the church was built in 1975–77 on a central plan with a coffered flat roof on exposed beams. It is raised above the piazza and reached by a stair; Christ stands on the campanile.
Pope Francis visited in April 2014. The nearby Santa Maria del Rosario ai Martiri Portuensi (2007) was the site of a cancelled Siza project.
s-gregorio-magliana.s: BeWeB; GCatholic; Register research (OSW, MC); pin: Google Places (Nov 2026)

p: A large industrial ruin at the corner of Via della Magliana and Via dell'Imbrecciato. No 2025–26 news has been found, so its present state is unknown. View from outside.

It covers about 20,000 m² and burned in 2019. It is a reminder that Via della Magliana was an industrial road on the edge of the reclaimed river plain. Do not enter: roofs and floors are unsafe. Look from the street, and pin it on the spot if you go (pin approximate).
The catacomb was rediscovered in 1868. A ruined basilica of Pope Damasus stands above ground. The Arval Brothers' grove, Lucus Deae Diae, is invisible on private land nearby.
A Muri Lab guided walk covers the area by booking.

Innocent VIII's name appears over the court windows. Sangallo's palazzetto and Leo X's chapel are here; Raphael's Eterno Padre from the chapel is in the Louvre. Leo X got the news of Milan here on 24 November 1521.
It is now offices of the San Giovanni Battista hospital; visits are by the Comitato with ACISMOM.
The Poeti der Trullo write verses in erasable marker; the Pittori Anonimi del Trullo paint murals. A reviewer says the movement, led by Mario D'Amico, took off in 2015.
Via di Massa Marittima has the 'Nina' wall and the market corridor a mural.
The valley keeps the casali of old farms; Villa York, once of the Cardinal Duke of York, is private and used for events.
Visit with the Trullo walls for a western outer-Rome half day.

Ostia was a marsh until the 1880s drainage and a seaside resort only after the railway of 1924. This was the building that made it a town: Vincenzo Fasolo's headquarters of the Governatorato (1924–28), with a corner tower, reliefs of trophies and sgraffito decoration by Calzolari. It stands in the square of the old station, the first thing a visitor from Rome saw.

It was a film set as well as a town hall: the police station in the comedy Caccia al marito is this front. Today the offices of Municipio X work here. Start the Ostia walk here, then climb the short slope to the church at the highest point of the old dune.
A visitor review says the main door has opened onto the courtyard since the recent restoration; treat that as unconfirmed.

Giulio Magni built this between 1919 and the late 1920s on the highest dune of the new town, so that the church would face the sea and sit on the same line as the Governatorato. The ribbed vaults are shown on the outside, which makes it look like a fortified basilica from the beach side. It is seen from most of the town.
A visitor review praises the garden. Mass hours leave the church closed from about 12:00 to 15:30.

lido-centro-stele.t: Lido Centro station and the 1921 stele
p: The Roma–Lido railway made Ostia a bathing place for Romans. Marina di Ostia's first station was bombed in the war, and the stele that recorded its first stone, laid on 10 December 1921, was kept for the new Lido Centro building of 1951. It stands in the atrium.
The same line also has postwar stations of interest to architecture fans: Stella Polare (1948), Castel Fusano (1949) and Colombo (1960), all along the railway behind the seafront.

The 1936 fire station on Via Celli is a rationalist block from the years when Ostia was being rebuilt as a model seaside town. It is still working, so look from the pavement and do not block the gate.

Vincenzo Fasolo, who also designed the Governatorato and the Colonia Marina, is credited with the fire station; FAI dates it 1926, not 1936, so the year on the map is disputed. In July 2026 the union reported the Ostia station closed for weeks over the state of the building: it may not be working when you pass.
vvf-ostia.s: FAI (Palazzo del Governatorato); USB Vigili del Fuoco (Jul 2026); Google Places

p: Ostia needed workers as well as bathers, and the ICP built them housing in the same years as Garbatella on the other side of Rome. Camillo Palmerini's blocks on Corso Duca di Genova and Via della Paranzella (1926–29) use the same repertoire: courtyards, arches and warm plaster, scaled down to a seaside town.
Compare them with the rationalist fire station and the post office a few minutes away.

Built by the Fascist institute for local-government employees, designed by Benadusi in 1932–36 and opened by the king in May 1937, the college could hold about 400 pupils in primary, secondary and naval training. Its central tower, said to be 75 m high (the register also gives 59 m), was a landmark on the coast.

In 1943 the Germans blew it up as they withdrew, so it could not guide an Allied landing. The Guardia di Finanza now runs a school here. The pin is Google's point on Via delle Fiamme Gialle, further east than the register's old position.
collegio-iv-novembre.s: Register research (OL, MA); Google Places review; Map pin approximate

p: Angiolo Mazzoni, the state railways' architect, designed this in 1933–34 for a town that was meant to be a showcase. A curved colonnade wraps the square; inside is an impluvium, an ancient Roman pool in the hall, with sculpture by Napoleone Martinuzzi. It is the finest of the 1930s buildings in Ostia.
A reviewer notes it still works as a post office, and that Saturday afternoons and Sundays it is closed. Compare it with Libera's post office in Ostiense (walk 48).

The covered market of 1966 is where Ostia buys its fish. Reviewers praise the fish and the raw sandwiches to eat on the sand. The register notes a leaking roof and works that have stalled, so do not expect repairs.
Go in the morning, then walk down to the seafront.

anco-marzio.t: Piazza Anco Marzio and the Pappagallo
p: Piazza Anco Marzio is the heart of the bathing town. Marchi's Palazzo del Pappagallo (1929), with pointed balconies in red, yellow and green, faces Antonelli's ochre Villini Rossini (1927); the Stabilimento Battistini of 1919 (one of the first bathing establishments) is nearby, and Consagra's sculpture is a monument to Pasolini.

Pasolini, Fellini and Muhammad Ali were customers of the Bar Sisto here. It closed in March 2024 and the premises were for sale, so the register keeps it as a story. The square leads straight to the pier.
anco-marzio.s: Register research (OL, OL2, MA); Google Places

pontile.t: Pontile di Ostia and the Ravennati square
p: The pier was blown up in 1943 and rebuilt in 1953. A wind rose is set at the tip. At its foot, Piazzale dei Ravennati has a 1984 monument to the labourers who came from Romagna to drain the marsh from November 1884; roughly a fifth of them died of malaria in two years (see Ostia Antica, walk 62).
From the end you see the whole shore: the Pappagallo, the Kursaal's dome to the south-east and the coast of Fiumicino to the north-west.

villini-libera.t: Libera's villini and the Ostia villa quarter
p: The Società Tirrena held a competition in 1932–34 for the villas of Ostia Levante, and Libera's villini won. They have rounded corners and balconies like ship bridges. Only one of the seven is said to survive unaltered, so the Google pin may be one of the changed ones; look along Lungomare Caio Duilio and the side streets.

Luigi Moretti's own villa on Viale della Pineta di Ostia (1932–37) is in the same district, and the "Cento Villini" of the early 1920s, Liberty holiday villas of which about seven are still recognisable, stand closer to the centre. All are private.
Moretti built the beach establishment Duilio (now Il Capanno) in 1936–37 with a naval look. It is a beach club in summer, so the front can be seen from the seafront outside the season.

Luigi Moretti, who did the Casa delle Armi at the Foro Italico and later the Girasole and Washington's Watergate, gave this beach club the look of a ship: decks, rails, white walls. It belongs to the 1930s Ostia that the regime promoted as "Rome by the sea".
Seasonal; out of summer you see the front from the seafront path. The Villini Libera on Lungomare Caio Duilio are a short walk.
il-capanno.s: Google Places (Nov 2026); KonMap Rome research notes (Nov 2026)

canale-pescatori.t: Canale dei Pescatori and the groynes
p: The Canale dei Pescatori is a small fishing village on a canal with an armoured mouth. The T-shaped groynes built in 2020–21 give the beach a sawtooth outline behind them, and the dams far upstream on the Tiber have cut the sand supply, so every beach in Ostia is losing sand.
The canal also traces Paolo Orlando's 1890s port plan, which was never built and is the reason the Ostiense industrial quarter exists. A visitor says the water is sometimes dirty and shallow.

Built in 1950 by Lapadula with Nervi and Bartoli, the Kursaal had a ribbed ferrocement dome, the same material as Nervi's Magliana shed (walk 57). The tall "K" diving tower seen from the beach is a 1974 copy.

The sources disagree about access: the register says the dome building is closed, abandoned and fenced and can only be seen from the beach, while Google lists Kursaal Village open as a beach club and restaurant. Go in winter, when the club has free beach access, and look at the dome from the sand.
kursaal.s: Register research (OL, OL2, MA); Google Places

p: The red ATER blocks around Via della Corazzata and Via Baffigo are the Ostia of the people who live on the far side of the railway, not the seafront. Visit with discretion.

This is the big postwar public-housing estate of Nuova Ostia, built for the high-density housing plan of the 1960s–70s that also produced the competition church of Nostra Signora di Bonaria nearby. By 2021 the façades were crumbling; a €4.5 million façade job followed, with more works in 2024, so expect scaffolding or freshly painted blocks.
Nuova Ostia has a hard reputation in the press, and the estate is a home, not a set: look from the street, do not photograph people or doorways, and move on to Bonaria and the Idroscalo.

A competition of 1967 by the Pontifical Society for new churches in Rome picked four sites in the four quarters of the periphery, to rebuild with the new liturgy after Vatican II. Bonaria was the south-west church, finished in 1982. The altar sits where the plan of the assembly wants it, not at the end of a nave.
A reviewer says it is so unlike a church that it is fun. Pair it with Nuova Ostia's housing and the Idroscalo.

porto-turistico.t: Porto Turistico and the Morante library
p: The Porto Turistico di Roma, a yacht harbour of 2001, was built on the ground of the old Idroscalo, the seaplane base of the 1920s–30s. The public library named after Elsa Morante, the author of La Storia, now has its seat here, and on 15 January 2026 the Municipio voted to make that seat permanent.

The library moved here in 2025 when its historic home in the former Colonia, on Via Cozza, closed for energy works; it is a good place to sit with a coffee before the LIPU oasis and Tor San Michele, both a short walk away.

The marina has a murky side: its owner, Mauro Balini, was named in investigations into corruption and clan links. Nothing survives of the seaplane base, which the Germans wrecked in 1943; Balbo's 24 seaplanes landed on this reach of the river mouth on 12 August 1933.
porto-turistico.s: Radio Roma (Jan 2026); Canale Dieci (2025); en.wikipedia (Marina of Rome); it.wikipedia (Idroscalo di Ostia); pin: Google Places (Nov 2026)

idroscalo-base.t: The Idroscalo: seaplanes, shacks and Pasolini
p: The Idroscalo "Carlo Del Prete" was a seaplane base from 1926 to 1943. On 12 August 1933 Italo Balbo's 24 S.55X flying boats landed here after crossing the Atlantic, watched by about 75,000 people. After the war the base's huts became a borgata of shacks, the Idroborgo.

It is also where Pier Paolo Pasolini was killed in the night of 1–2 November 1975; the monument to him stands in the park. The place is the end of the film Caro diario and the setting of Amore tossico (1983) and of Citti's Ostia. Pin approximate.
idroscalo-base.s: Register research (OL, OL2); general history; Map pin approximate

p: A visitor review says that in the mid-1990s this was an illegal dump and that developers planned an oceanarium. LIPU, the bird-protection league, fought it and proposed a wetland instead; the register dates the lake to 2001. It has reed beds, purple herons and over 200 species recorded. A WWII bunker stands on the trail.
The reviewer's version of the 1990s history is not in the register; the lake itself is certain. The volunteers run the visitor centre, so bring cash for the entrance.
lipu-chm.s: Register research (OL, OL2, MA); Google Places

p: Built in 1559–69 and attributed to Michelangelo, the tower stands near the Idroscalo lighthouse. It was meant to watch a coast that was moving: the Tiber delta grows seaward, so what was a shoreline fort is now inland.
A visitor says it can be seen from the road but is locked; the register gives booking by email. Reviewers also report homeless camps and no pavement nearby, so go by bus or car and in daylight.
tor-san-michele.s: Register research (OL, OL2, MA); Google Places

p: Moretti built a villa for himself in the pines of Ostia Levante between 1932 and 1937, in the years he also designed the Il Capanno beach club. It is private, so this is a look from the road.

Moretti was the regime's favourite young architect: the Foro Italico's Casa delle Armi is his, and after the war he built the Girasole in Parioli and the Watergate in Washington. His own house in the pines shows the early, quieter Moretti, plain volumes under the trees.
Private; look from Viale della Pineta di Ostia and do not linger at the gate. Pin approximate.
villino-moretti.s: it.wikipedia (Luigi Moretti); KonMap Rome research notes (Nov 2026)

p: Before the rationalist buildings, the first holiday houses of Ostia were small Liberty (Italian Art Nouveau) villas of the early 1920s, the "Cento Villini" of what was then called Ostia Marittima. About seven are still recognisable among later blocks, mostly on the Ponente side behind the seafront.

Look for the giveaways of the style: curved window heads, small towers and loggias, iron railings with plant motifs and plaster friezes, on two-storey houses with gardens. They belong to the years when the land drainage of 1884 had made the coast habitable and the Roma–Lido railway, opened in 1924, made it a day trip from the city.

The name is a round number, not a count, and which villas are original is not documented in one place; the figure of about seven comes from a local architecture site and a visitor review. Treat it as a walk to spot them yourself, and pair it with the 1930s villas by Libera and Moretti a little further east.
cento-villini.s: lamiaostia.com; Musei in Comune (Ostia school sheets)

p: The Roma–Lido line opened in 1924 and was extended along the coast after the war with small modern stations: Stella Polare (1948), Castel Fusano (1949) and Cristoforo Colombo (1960), the last stop before the pine forest.

They are plain postwar buildings, worth a look from the platform for their flat roofs, canopies and the way they sit low among the 1930s villas. Between Castel Fusano and Colombo the line crosses the Canale dello Stagno on a single-span bridge. Use them as the way in and out of the Levante walk (Libera's villas, Il Capanno, the Kursaal) rather than as a sight on their own.

What each station looked like when new, and how much of it survives, is not well documented; the dates come from railway-history sites. The line itself is the old Società Tirrena route that made Ostia a Roman suburb by the sea.
tirrena-stations.s: ilmondodeitreni.it; it.wikipedia (Ferrovia Roma-Lido); pin: Google Places (Nov 2026)

p: A huge 1920s seaside holiday camp (colonia marina) on the Ostia front, built to send poor and sick Roman children to the sea, now shared by a theatre, a bookshop and social services.

Marcello Piacentini first planned it as a sea hospice for children with tuberculosis; Vincenzo Fasolo enlarged it to over 300 beds. Queen Elena opened it on 24 January 1932, and it was named after her husband, who gave it to the city on condition that it serve social purposes. It sent Roman children to the sea until the 1950s.

Today the vast complex at Lungomare Paolo Toscanelli 176 holds the Teatro del Lido, the Almayer bookshop, a hostel and a Caritas centre. The Elsa Morante library has been here, but a 2026 note says its permanent seat is now the Porto Turistico: check which building it is in.
colonia-ostia.s: visitostia.tv; Il Giornale; Turismo Roma (Teatro del Lido); In_Bo (Jul 2024); pin: Google Places, Teatro del Lido (Nov 2026)

p: Claudio Caligari's Amore tossico (1983) was shot among friends who were addicts, around the shacks and the beach of the Idroscalo. Citti's Ostia and the Macchie solari blocks of the seafront belong to the same Ostia of the margins.
Nothing is marked. Stand on the beach and read it as a set.

Giuliano della Rovere, later Pope Julius II, was cardinal-bishop of Ostia when he had Baccio Pontelli build this castle (1483–86); Pontelli's name is on the courtyard portal. A spiral ramp for horses climbs the keep, and a stair of the Peruzzi workshop is decorated with a Hercules.

The moat is dry because the river changed course in the flood of 1557 (see the Fiume Morto). The ticket includes the dig of the Constantinian basilica; Google's hours disagree with the register's, so confirm before the trip.
castello-giulio.s: Register research (OL, OL2, MA); Google Places

p: After the ancient port was abandoned, Pope Gregory IV founded Gregoriopoli here after 846 as a defence against Saracen raiders. Cardinal d'Estouteville rebuilt it in the 1400s with terraced houses, and Sant'Aurea and the Episcopio have frescoes by the Peruzzi circle in the Salone Riario.
Monica, mother of Augustine, died at Ostia in 387 and was buried in the borgo's church until her relics went to Rome in 1425.
borgo-ostia-antica.s: Register research (OL, OL2); Map pin approximate

p: From November 1884 gangs of labourers from Ravenna and Romagna arrived to dig the drainage channels of the Ostia marsh. About a fifth are said to have died of malaria within two years. The square has the 1904 bust of Andrea Costa, the socialist, and a stele of 1951.
This is the human side of the pumps at the idrovore (walk 62) and of the Ravennati monument at Ostia's pier.
sacrario-romagnoli.s: Register research (OL, OL2); pin: Google Places (Nov 2026)

p: The Monumento opened in 1884, the year of the first drainage gangs, and the Romagna cappelletti on the menu are the same dish those men brought. L'Alimentari next door dates from 1897.

The square is the drainage workers' square. In November 1884 a cooperative of about 500 labourers from Ravenna arrived to drain the Ostia marshes, and about a fifth of them died of malaria in the first two years. Across the piazza is their memorial: a 1904 plaque with a bust of Andrea Costa ("Pane e Lavoro", bread and work) and a 1951 stele to Nullo Baldini; wreaths are laid every late November.

The restaurant's "since 1884" and the family recipes are its own claims; the Alimentari's 1897 is also self-reported. Eat here after the castle and the excavations, which are a few minutes' walk away; booking is advised.
The tower of the 1200s stands on the round base of Ostia's lighthouse. It was on the shore then. The Tiber delta grows seaward by roughly 7.5–10 m a year, so it is now about a kilometre inland.
It is one of the plain's gauges of how fast the coast moves; the Fiume Morto and Tor San Michele tell the same story.

Between 14 and 15 September 1557 a flood made the Tiber cut across its last loop near Ostia, and the old bed was left as the Fiume Morto, the dead river: first a crescent-shaped lake, now fields. Julius II's castle, built to guard the river, was suddenly beside nothing.
There is nothing to enter. Look at the curve on a satellite view first, then walk the edge east of the castle: the line of field boundaries and lanes still follows the old bank.

The cut changed the whole coast. The papal customs moved to Tor Boacciana until 1568, and Tor San Michele was built because the river mouth had moved; the delta then kept growing seaward by several metres a year. How far the coast jumped in 1557 is disputed (about 1,000 m or 1,750 m, from local sources), so treat the figure as rough.

The pumps of 1889 lifted the water of the low land into the high channels so the drained marsh could be farmed. A visitor says the traces of the reclamation still stand among reeds and water birds. A working model and the channels are the main things to see.
When the pumps failed in 1988 the Longarina flooded. The Ecomuseo del Litorale Romano runs the visits; an anniversary event on 22 Nov was unconfirmed.
idrovore-ostia.s: Register research (OL, OL2, MA); Google Places

p: Salt was one of the first reasons for Ostia. Behind the town lay the stagni, shallow lagoons probably used as Roman salt works; in the Middle Ages salt was stored at the Casone del Sale, and the street names Via delle Saline and Via dei Monti del Sale keep the memory.

Ancient tradition ties Ostia's founding by King Ancus Marcius to the salt pans at the river mouth, and salt went up to Rome along the Via Campana on the right bank and then the Via Salaria inland. The lagoons survived until the drainage of 1884–91, when pumps and canals turned them into farmland.
There is little to see but flat land and the street names; the stop makes sense on the way between the pumping station and the castle, where the drainage story is told.

Castel Fusano is 916 hectares of mostly planted stone pines, the green lung of the coast. The Sacchetti family began planting in the 1700s to sell the pine nuts; the city bought the estate from Prince Francesco Chigi in 1932 and opened it on 21 April 1933.

Look for the regrowth from July 2008, when a series of arson fires burned at least 80 hectares, and for pines with black, sticky needles: an introduced scale insect is now killing stone pines across Rome. The paved avenue to Villa Chigi (Pietro da Cortona, 1624–29) and the Roman Via Severiana both run through the wood.
The forest became a city park in 1980 and part of the Litorale Romano reserve in 1996. It is free and open; the Severiana walk to the Villa della Palombara is the best route through it.
castel-fusano.s: it.wikipedia (Parco urbano Pineta di Castel Fusano); comune.roma.it; Abitarearoma

p: Pietro da Cortona remodelled the castle for the Chigi in 1624–29. The avenue to it is paved with stones taken from the Roman Via Severiana. Francesco Chigi, the register notes, was an early colour photographer.
The villa is mostly private; the visits listed are the only dates in the register.

severiana-palombara.t: Via Severiana and Villa della Palombara
p: The Via Severiana, built in 198–209 under Septimius Severus, ran along the coast from Ostia to Anzio. Basalt slabs and milestones survive here, beside the Villa della Palombara, which people call Pliny's villa; that attribution is wrong. A small Chiesola basilica stands near.
Visits are limited to 30 people and need a booking.
severiana-palombara.s: Register research (OL, OL2, MA); Google Places (approx.)

p: The Vicus Augustanus is a Roman roadside village of the age of Augustus, with a small forum and baths, on the coast road inside the presidential estate of Castelporziano. Visits run in a short autumn season; the 2026 season (3 October–15 November) is over.

It was the village of the ancient Laurentine shore, where rich Romans had seaside villas; Pliny the Younger described his Laurentine villa somewhere along this coast, though which ruin it was is still argued. The Via Severiana, which you can walk in Castel Fusano, ran past it.

The estate is a closed nature reserve, so the only way in is the booked season; look for next year's dates online in late summer. Without a booking, the Severiana and the Villa della Palombara give you the same landscape from the public side of the fence.

Wilma Montesi, 21, was found dead on the beach at Capocotta on 11 April 1953. Rumours of parties at the Marquis Ugo Montagna's estate drew in Piero Piccioni, son of a government minister, and the case was never solved.

It became Italy's first great media scandal, often called the birth of the paparazzi era; the trial ended in acquittals in 1957. Later the beach took another identity: in 1965 President Saragat opened gates onto the Castelporziano shore, and gaps cut in the fence gave Capocotta its nickname "il buco", the hole; it is also a long-standing naturist beach.
There is no marker. Come for the dunes and the story, and keep the facts to the record: the cause of Montesi's death is still disputed.

Valadier laid out the village in 1823–28 around the 1819 customs house and the church of Santa Maria Porto della Salute. The Torre dei Piloti of 1949 replaced the lost Torre Clementina. Old rail tracks and canal-side fish stalls remain.
A reviewer finds it charming but badly kept.

Grassi showed in 1898 that malaria is carried by Anopheles mosquitoes, and in 1918 he built an observatory here to study their flight, marking mosquitoes with paint. A clock and his marble effigy stand in the square.
It is the other half of the Ostia story: the labourers died before the cause was known.

Giovanni Battista Grassi, the zoologist who showed in 1898 that Anopheles mosquitoes carry human malaria, lies in the small cemetery of Fiumicino. He asked to be buried "modestly in the little cemetery of Fiumicino, where at least my bones will witness its redemption from malaria".

He worked here from 1918 at his malaria observatory in the town (now Palazzo Grassi), marking mosquitoes with paint to learn how far they flew. He lies with his wife and daughter; the Pro Loco looks after the tomb and holds a ceremony every 4 May, the anniversary of his death in 1925.
The Nobel Prize of 1902 went to Ronald Ross alone, and the quarrel over credit is part of Grassi's story. Pair the grave with Palazzo Grassi and Borgo Valadier.
grassi-tomb.s: fiumicino-online.it; Il Faro Online (May 2025); en.wikipedia (Giovanni Battista Grassi); Treccani; pin: Google Places (Nov 2026)

p: The lighthouse of 1946 is 32 m high with about 200 steps, and was declared unsafe in 1971. Street artists painted it. Dante's line about where the Tiber's water turns to salt is attached to this coast.
Reviews disagree: one says you can climb to the top, others that the road is gated and rubbish-strewn. Treat access as unverified.
faro-fiumicino.s: Register research (OL, OL2); Google Places reviews

p: The bilancioni are big stilted nets lowered into the sea from platforms. The new port's breakwater moved the sand, so many now stand stranded on the beach. A jersey-barrier wall about 500 m long has stood here since early March 2025; a cruise-port plan by the iCON fund is the reason.

Each platform carries a large square net on a frame, lowered and raised by a winch from a hut. Some are kept up by families who have fished from them for generations. Here, standing far from the water, they show how fast the coast moves when a breakwater is built.
See them from the end of Via del Faro by the old lighthouse. The jersey wall makes access awkward; do not climb onto the platforms.
bilancioni.s: Register research (OL2, MA); Map pin approximate

p: The hulls came out of the mud when the airport's works reached the old harbour basin. The museum shows the wooden remains of five ancient Roman ships, among them the boat with a well for live fish. Reviewers say it takes about 30 minutes.
A free shuttle runs from the airport, so it suits a layover.
museo-navi.s: Register research (OL, OL2, MA); Google Places

p: Claudius built the first harbour here and Trajan added a hexagonal basin, so that grain ships had a safe inner port connected to Ostia by canal. The hexagon, now a lake, is the sight the visitors come for, and several reviewers could not reach it.
The register says the hexagon is seen via the Oasi di Porto, by horse cart on Thursdays and Sundays in season; booking is needed. The two Google hours are Tue–Sun.
porti-imperiali.s: Register research (OL, OL2, MA); Google Places

p: The tombs of the port's freedmen and workers are small brick houses with terracotta reliefs showing what the dead did: a surgeon, Ulpius Amerimnus, a midwife, Scribonia Attice, and the work of the port. The paint on the walls is gone, and a reviewer notes the frescoes were stripped.
The site has a quiet, uncrowded feel, and a reviewer says the guide is personal. A ticket for Ostia Antica covers it for eight days.
Riccardo Morandi, the engineer of the Genoa bridge that fell in 2018, hung huge cantilevered roofs from concrete masts for the airline's hangars. They are airside, so look from the perimeter.

The early-1960s hangars have roofs that cantilever about 60 m with no support at the far end, held by cables over concrete masts about 15 m high. The two Boeing 747 halls of 1969–70 are bigger still, each about 74.5 by 78 m and 20–30 m high; the airport operator strengthened them in 2024.

They are inside the airside area. You can see them from the perimeter roads of the technical zone, or from the plane when landing; there is no visit. Morandi's other Roman work is the double ramp of the Mercato Metronio.
morandi-hangars.s: MiC Censimento architetture (ids 431, 996); EDIL CAM Sistemi (2024); structurae; Breng

p: Maccarese was a marsh and an estate until its reclamation in the early 1900s. The castle of San Giorgio is the heart of the borgo; the register mentions an altar inscription in the chapel, and a reviewer praises the garden and park.
The red farmhouses, the silo at the station and the milk centre show the working side. Reviewers warn about car break-ins at the castle car park.
The Maccarese branch of the Ecomuseo del Litorale Romano sits by the pumping plant on Piazza della Pace, next to the castle. It tells how the water is still kept off the reclaimed land.

Maccarese was a malarial marsh until the 1920s. In 1925 the Società Anonima Bonifiche drained it and turned it into one great farm, later owned by the state holding IRI and, since the 1990s, by the Benetton family; it still runs about 3,600 cows. Look for the red farmhouses scattered over the plain and the pumps that lift the water into the canals.

Visits are on event days or by booking with the Ecomuseo, whose main site is the pumping station at Ostia Antica. A reclamation museum by the castle is mentioned in one notice, but whether it is open is unconfirmed.
ecomuseo-maccarese.s: comune.fiumicino.rm.it; fiumicino-online.it; Fondazione Catalano; maccaresespa.com; pin: Google Places (Nov 2026)

p: The osteria is in the old estate store of the Castello San Giorgio, one of the castle's shops that stood empty for about 30 years and was restored in 2017.

The castle is recorded in 1254; the Mattei added bastions in 1569 and the Rospigliosi gave it its present form in 1756. In 1925 it became the headquarters of the drainage company, and the borgo around it, with school, post office and shops, was the farm's village. Eat here after the castle and the Ecomuseo.
Torre di Maccarese, also called Torre Primavera, is one of the watchtowers of the papal coast, built in 1574 by Ciriaco Mattei.

The towers were a chain of lookouts against raids by Barbary corsairs, each in sight of the next. This one did its job at least once: in 1748 it helped capture 26 Turks landed from a galley. It stands on estate land between Maccarese and Fregene and is seen only from outside.
torre-primavera.s: Fondazione Catalano; en.wikipedia (Maccarese); pin: Google Places (Nov 2026)

p: The LIPU reserve covers more than 180 hectares inside Castel di Guido, the large farm owned by the city of Rome on the Via Aurelia. Visits are by phone booking (328 5569123).

It is farmland managed for birds rather than a wilderness: fields, hedges and small woods on the edge of the coastal plain. Ask when booking what is about in the season; the register has no species list, so do not expect a hide-and-checklist site like the LIPU oasis at Ostia.
lipu-castel-guido.s: Manual pass (Nov 2026); LIPU; pin: Google Places (Nov 2026)

p: The Società Generale Immobiliare built Casal Palocco from 1961 to 1975 with architects including Libera, Luccichenti, Paniconi and Pediconi, Vaccaro. The plan has a ring parkway, houses in gardens, and a stepped centre called Le Terrazze.
Nanni Moretti rides his Vespa through it in Caro diario.
Bruno Bozzini's parish church, consecrated in 1997, in the new quarter of Dragoncello north of Acilia.

It is dedicated to the two brothers who took Christianity to the Slavs in the 9th century; Cyril died in Rome and is buried in San Clemente. The church is a titular church of a cardinal and is listed on the Italian bishops' itinerary of modern Roman churches (BeWeB). Its interior and details are unchecked, so judge it on the spot; it fits a church day with San Pier Damiani and Vitinia.
cirillo-metodio.s: en.wikipedia (Santi Cirillo e Metodio); BeWeB (Chiese moderne di Roma)

p: San Pier Damiani is a church of 1966–70 on a rise above Casal Bernocchi, between Acilia and Vitinia, reached by a flight of steps on the axis of the entrance.

The design is by Attilio Spaccarelli, co-author of Via della Conciliazione, with F. Bruno and F. Nespega: a central plan on a frame of steel sections. It opened in March 1970 and became a cardinal's titular church in 1973. It was so poorly built that it had to be rebuilt in 1998–2002; Pope Francis visited in 2017.
Casal Bernocchi began in 1960 as an INA-Casa village and takes its name from a farmhouse of the Bernocchi counts.
pier-damiani.s: BeWeB (Chiese moderne di Roma); Turismo Roma; en.wikipedia (San Pier Damiani ai Monti di San Paolo)

p: Acilia was the last of Rome's Fascist borgate, inaugurated on 21 April 1940, Rome's birthday. Its 150 small houses stood on a grid of plots of about 1,000 m², so the families could grow their own food.

The borgate ufficiali were the regime's answer to the people it moved out of the centre and to the shanty towns: low-cost settlements far out, without much else. Il Messaggero reported Acilia's "first baby" on 19 May 1940. Walk the grid near the station for the surviving small houses among later building.
Which houses are original is not mapped in the sources; look for single-storey cottages on large plots. The singer Franco Califano lived in Acilia.
acilia-borgata.s: BCC Roma; Le borgate del fascismo (Issuu); en.wikipedia (Acilia)

p: Tradition says King Ancus Marcius destroyed Ficana in the seventh century BC to take Rome to the sea. Excavation shows the town lived on.

The site on Monte Cugno, above the Tiber, was identified in 1971 by the archaeologists Lorenzo Quilici and Stefania Quilici Gigli. Livy says Ancus Marcius destroyed it before founding Ostia; the excavations show the town lived on and was even re-walled in the 4th–3rd century BC.
Nothing is visible: there is only the hill and the view over the river plain towards the sea. It is a stop for the story of myth against record, on the way between Acilia and Dragoncello.
ficana.s: riservalitoraleromano.it; Livy, Ab urbe condita I.33

p: The Acqua Vergine ran as a low channel on arches through this part of the city. Fifteen of them survive in the basement of the Rinascente on Via del Tritone, and the store shows them in a glass-walled area. Go in during shop hours.

The arches came to light during the rebuilding of the department store, which opened in 2017, and the store kept them on show in its lower floor. This is the Acqua Vergine of 19 BC, the aqueduct that still feeds the Trevi Fountain, here running on low arches because its water arrived with very little fall.

Two minutes away, at Via del Nazareno 14, three more arches carry Claudius's restoration inscription, and the Vicus Caprarius shows the distribution tank under the street: together they make the Vergine line visible from here to Trevi.
rinascente-arches.s: K2 thread research (en.wikipedia Acqua Vergine; Turismo Roma); La Rinascente; pin: Google Places (Nov 2026)

colonna-press.t: Palazzo Colonna: the Roman Holiday press conference
p: In William Wyler's Roman Holiday the press conference at the end is shot in the real Galleria Colonna. The same palace has a cannonball from 1849 on its stairs (see the Galleria Colonna cannonball stop).

In the scene, Hepburn's princess meets the press and finds Gregory Peck among the reporters. The hall is the Grand Gallery of Palazzo Colonna, finished in the early 1700s, still privately owned by the Colonna family; the film used the room as it is.
The Galleria Colonna opens to visitors on Saturday mornings (paid). On the stair to the hall a French cannonball of 1849 is still lodged where it landed during the siege of the Roman Republic.

conclave-barberini.t: Palazzo Barberini in the film Conclave
p: In the film Conclave the homily scene was shot in Palazzo Barberini, while the Sistine Chapel itself was a set at Cinecittà. The famous staircases of the palace are by Bernini and Borromini (see the Barberini stop).

Conclave (Edward Berger, 2024) could not film inside the Vatican, so it built the Sistine Chapel at Cinecittà and used Roman palaces for the rest. Palazzo Barberini, now the national gallery of old masters, was a natural choice: it is the palace of a papal family, built for Urban VIII from 1625.

Inside the gallery, look up at Pietro da Cortona's ceiling of Divine Providence in the great hall, the Barberini's own advertisement. The palace was built partly with travertine taken from the Colosseum, hence the Roman joke that what the barbarians did not do, the Barberini did.

A plaque on Piazza del Popolo remembers Angelo Targhini and Leonida Montanari, two Carbonari (members of the secret society fighting for a united, liberal Italy) beheaded in the square on 23 November 1825 by the papal state.

Targhini had stabbed and wounded a man the society suspected of betraying it; Montanari, a surgeon, was condemned with him. Both refused the last rites on the scaffold, which made them heroes of the anticlerical Risorgimento. The executioner was Mastro Titta, whose red cloak is in the Museo Criminologico.
The plaque is small and easy to miss: look along the house fronts rather than at the obelisk.
targhini.s: D2 report (rerumromanarum; romasegreta); it.wikipedia (Angelo Targhini); pin: Google Places (Nov 2026)

p: Piazza del Popolo has two long-standing cafés facing each other, Rosati and Canova. Canova was Federico Fellini's café: he lived round the corner on Via Margutta and is said to have kept an office at the back.
A small room of photographs and sketches from his life and films keeps the link. Sit outside with the twin churches and the obelisk in front of you, then compare with Rosati across the square.
Don't confuse it with the Caffè Canova Tadolini on Via del Babuino, a café in the sculptor Antonio Canova's old studio, which is a different place and worth a visit of its own.
canova.s: Fodor's; Culture Trip; Turismo Roma (Canova Tadolini)

p: On Piazza del Biscione, behind Campo de' Fiori, a painted "Beccheria" sign (butcher's shop) and iron meat hooks survive on the front of Palazzo Orsini Pio Righetti, from when butchers had their stalls here.

The palace itself is the bigger story. It was built around 1450 on the ruins of Pompey's Theatre, over the temple of Venus Victrix at the top of its seating, which is why the square curves: the houses follow the theatre's arc. The square is named after the snake (biscione) on the Orsini arms. A gilded bronze Hercules, now in the Vatican, was dug up under the courtyard in 1864.
Look for the Roman opus reticulatum in the basements of the restaurants around the square, then walk through the Passetto del Biscione into Via di Grotta Pinta, which traces the theatre's curve.
beccheria.s: D2 report; Turismo Roma (Palazzo Pio Righetti); it.wikipedia

p: La Campana, on the alley named after it between Via della Scrofa and Piazza Nicosia, claims to be the oldest restaurant in Rome: the owners date it to about 1518, from a tax receipt paid that year by one Pietro della Campana.

The claim is the house's own, though the city tourism site repeats it, and the restaurant also says Goethe ate here in 1787. Whatever the date, it is a good traditional trattoria with waiters in black waistcoats and Roman classics (artichokes, oxtail, saltimbocca). Book at weekends; it has usually closed on Mondays (check).
la-campana.s: Turismo Roma; Wanted in Rome; Airmail (2019)

p: The Carceri Nuove, the new prisons, were built for Innocent X and opened in 1655 on Via Giulia to replace the older papal jails. They were designed by Antonio Del Grande and counted as a model prison for their time.

The inscription over the door dedicates the building to justice and clemency, for a safer and gentler custody of the accused; inside, cells were separated by type of prisoner, which was new. The prison worked until Regina Coeli opened in the 1880s.

Today the building holds offices (the national anti-mafia directorate) and is not open; look at the long façade and the inscription from the street. The Museo Criminologico, round the corner on Via del Gonfalone, holds the instruments of papal justice.
carceri-nuove.s: X1 report; it.wikipedia (Carceri Nuove); pin: Google Places (Nov 2026)

p: The Accademia dei Lincei holds the Corsiniana library in Palazzo Corsini on Via della Lungara. It is a working scholars' library, opened to visitors only on special days.

The library was founded by Cardinal Neri Maria Corsini, nephew of Clement XII, and opened to the public in 1754, one of the first public libraries in Rome. When the state bought Palazzo Corsini in 1883 the collection passed to the Accademia dei Lincei, the scientific academy founded in 1603 that counted Galileo among its members.
The reading rooms keep their 18th-century shelving and globes. Watch the Lincei website for open days; otherwise visit the Galleria Corsini in the same palace and see the library only from the stair.

spezieria-scala.t: Spezieria di Santa Maria della Scala
p: The Carmelites' pharmacy at Santa Maria della Scala kept working until 1978. It is now under works, and no reopening date has been given. Look from the square at the church and its neighbours.
The pharmacy dates from the late 16th century. It kept its laboratory, distillery and pill room, and sold its own "Acqua della Scala"; it was known as a supplier to the papal court.

It has been closed for restoration since October 2024 (façade, laboratory roof, ceilings) and no reopening date has been given. Check before going; meanwhile the Museo Storico dell'Arte Sanitaria at Santo Spirito has a reconstructed 17th-century pharmacy you can visit.
spezieria-scala.s: X1 report (romaguida.com; it.wikipedia Spezieria di Santa Maria della Scala); manual pass B (Nov 2026); pin: Google Places (Nov 2026)

piazza-pia.t: Piazza Pia and Via della Conciliazione
p: Between 1936 and 1950 the Spina di Borgo, a block of old houses between Castel Sant'Angelo and St Peter's, was demolished to make a straight avenue; its tenants were moved to the borgate. The Piazza Pia of December 2024 is the new Jubilee square at the avenue's start.
Look back from the avenue's end to see the dome framed as planned.

A long stretch of the Servian Wall, Rome's first stone city wall, stands in front of Termini station as rows of large tuff blocks. Tradition gives it to King Servius Tullius; the wall you see was built in the 4th century BC, after the Gauls sacked Rome in 390 BC.

Look at the blocks: squared volcanic tuff, much of it from the quarries of Grotta Oscura near Veii, laid in alternating headers and stretchers. It is the geology of the city you can touch. Behind it, the station front of 1950 with its long wavy canopy, nicknamed "il dinosauro", is a landmark of postwar Roman architecture.
Further stretches of the same wall survive around the station area and on the Aventine; the line enclosed the seven hills and was overtaken by the Aurelian Walls in the 270s AD.
servian-wall.s: K2 and X2 reports; general history (Lacus Curtius; Coarelli, Guida archeologica di Roma); pin: Google Places (Nov 2026)

p: This obelisk comes from the Iseum, the Roman temple of Isis. It was moved to the front of the station in the 1880s to remember the Italian dead of Dogali in Eritrea.

It is one of three obelisks from the Iseum Campense, Domitian's temple of Isis near the Pantheon (the others stand at the Pantheon and on Bernini's elephant at the Minerva); it carries hieroglyphs of Ramesses II. It was set up in front of Termini in 1887 for the roughly 500 Italian soldiers killed at Dogali in Eritrea that January, and moved to this garden in 1925.
It is small and easily passed. Read the dedication on the base, then continue to the Baths of Diocletian next door.
The Acqua Felice, built in 1585–87 for Sixtus V (Felice Peretti) and named after him, enters the city on this arch, set into the Aurelian Wall near Porta Tiburtina.

Domenico Fontana gave the aqueduct monumental arches where it crossed the old roads, in the Roman manner, with Sixtus's inscriptions. It was the first new aqueduct since antiquity, 28.7 km from springs at Pantano Borghese, and it brought water to the hills for the first time since the Middle Ages.
From here follow the water: to the Moses fountain at Piazza San Bernardo, then down to the Quattro Fontane. Porta Furba on Via Tuscolana is the arch where the same aqueduct crosses outside the walls.
The Embassy beside Porta Pia is by Sir Basil Spence, the architect of Coventry Cathedral, built in 1968–71. Look at it from Via XX Settembre and from the gate.

The old embassy on this site, Villa Torlonia, was blown up by the Zionist group Irgun on 31 October 1946. Spence's building replaced it: a block raised on piers over a pool, clad in travertine and articulated to answer Michelangelo's gate next door. It was argued over when new; it is now listed among Rome's notable postwar buildings.
It is a working embassy: no visits, and be discreet with cameras at the gate.
british-embassy.s: D1 report; Ordine Architetti Roma; en.wikipedia (1946 British Embassy bombing in Rome)

p: The Museo Civico di Zoologia stands on the edge of Villa Borghese next to the Bioparco, the zoo, and has a gallery of animal skeletons among its displays.

Founded in 1932 from the university's collections, which go back to the Archiginnasio Pontificio, it holds about 5 million specimens, from shells of a few millimetres to a 16 m whale skeleton. The osteology gallery and the old collections are the reason to come; there are also modern habitat rooms for children.
It is a municipal museum: tickets for Rome residents €6 (€4.50 reduced), higher for others. Check opening days on the Musei in Comune site before going.
zoology.s: Musei in Comune; Turismo Roma; en.wikipedia (Museo Civico di Zoologia)

p: Rome's big flea market spreads from Porta Portese along Via Portuense and the side streets on Sunday mornings, selling everything from clothes and furniture to old books, records and junk.

It grew after the Second World War, when the black market moved here, next to the gate of 1644 that replaced the ancient Porta Portuensis and to the Ripa Grande, the river port of Trastevere. In Ladri di biciclette (1948) the father and son search the stalls here for the stolen bicycle.
Go early (from about 7:00); it winds down by early afternoon. Keep your wallet in a front pocket. The best second-hand finds are in the side streets away from the gate.
porta-portese-market.s: X2 report; L1 report; general history

p: The Arco di San Lazzaro on Via Marmorata is a surviving piece of an ancient arcaded building in the old Emporium district, the river harbour of imperial Rome at the foot of the Aventine.

Archaeologists read it as part of a warehouse (horreum) of the Emporium, where marble, grain and oil were landed; the street name Marmorata comes from the marble that was unloaded here. A small mithraeum has been recorded beside it.
It is a fragment to notice while walking between the Porticus Aemilia, Monte Testaccio and the river, not a sight to travel for.
arco-s-lazzaro.s: Pleiades (Arco di San Lazzaro); mithraeum.eu; X2 report; pin: Google Places (Nov 2026)

p: The nasone, the small iron fountain with a curved spout, appeared in 1874. The first examples were set at the foot of the Capitoline near Via delle Tre Cannelle, Via di San Teodoro and the Bocca della Verità. Block the spout with your finger and the water jets up like a drinking fountain.

The fountains were installed from 1874 by Luigi Pianciani, the first mayor of Rome as Italian capital, to bring free drinking water to the streets. The first model was a cast-iron column with three dragon-head spouts; the single curved spout, the "big nose", came later. Counts vary: Acea has recorded more than 5,000, the city says about 3,000.

Whether the column on Via delle Tre Cannelle is an original or a copy is disputed; the one on Via di San Teodoro may be the most intact. Since 19 March 2024 there are also three new nasoni inside the Colosseum park, the first in an archaeological area. Acea's app maps them all.

la-storia.t: Morante's La Storia in San Lorenzo
p: Elsa Morante's La Storia follows Ida Ramundo and her children through wartime Rome, and its San Lorenzo is real: Via dei Volsci and the Parco dei Caduti del 19 Luglio. See the neighbourhood's bombing stops for the history.

The novel came out in 1974. Its centre is the bombing of 19 July 1943, when the Allies hit the rail yards and San Lorenzo was devastated: Ida and her small son Useppe lose their home and end up in a refugee room in Pietralata. Morante set history in capitals against the lives of the poor, and the book was both a best-seller and a fight among critics.
Walk Via dei Volsci and the Parco dei Caduti, named for the dead of that day. The 1943 plaques and lists of the dead are within a few hundred metres.
Pasolini used the railwaymen's palazzo of Casal Bertone for Mamma Roma (1962). It is a real location, in a district of railway housing.

Casal Bertone grew up between the Tiburtina yards and the Prenestina as housing for railway staff, and the big railwaymen's block is the kind of sober, anonymous city housing the film's Mamma Roma wants for her son. The exact building is not pinned: treat this as a look at the quarter rather than a doorway. The film's other places are in the south-east, at Via dei Treviri and in Parco degli Acquedotti.
In Mamma Roma the flats stand along the new Tuscolano estates; the number on the screen is invented. Pair this stop with Parco degli Acquedotti and the INA-Casa Tuscolano blocks.

In the film the move to the Tuscolano is Mamma Roma's climb into respectability: new INA-Casa blocks, a fruit stall, a respectable job for her son. Walk the Tuscolano I–II estates and Libera's Unità orizzontale at Via Selinunte 49 to see the housing the film is set in. Her market stall was in Via Lucio Sestio, with the aqueduct at the end of the street.

On 17 April 1944 German troops rounded up about 700 men of Quadraro, which they called the nest of wasps, and deported them. The register gives at least 683. Other markers are at the park named for the date, at Buon Consiglio and in the Quadraro murals.

The round-up, Operazione Balena ("Whale"), was a reprisal after partisan attacks in the area, among them the Gobbo del Quarticciolo's attack at the Osteria da Gigetto. Men aged 16 to 60 were taken at dawn, held at Cinecittà and sent to labour camps in Germany; many did not return.

Look for Lucamaleonte's *Nido di vespe* mural (seven wasps) on Via del Monte del Grano, the memorial in Parco XVII Aprile 1944, and Don Rey's plaque at Buon Consiglio. Wreaths are laid every 17 April. The street markers are always visible.
quadraro-roundup.s: ANPI Roma; Museo della Liberazione; KonMap Rome research notes (Nov 2026)

p: The CAR wholesale market feeds Rome. Its fish hall runs at night, with a 560 m gallery and vets on the night shift. Public access is unconfirmed, so call first.

CAR is the Centro Agroalimentare Roma at Guidonia, just outside the ring road. It took over the wholesale trade of the old Mercati Generali in Ostiense, whose empty site is now a building site. Fish arrives through the night and is sold to restaurants and markets before dawn.

Practical: trade starts around 02:30, Tuesday to Saturday. A Saturday morning public opening (7:00–12:00) is reported once and not confirmed; call before you go, and expect a business site with lorries, not a market for tourists.
car-fish.s: KonMap Rome research notes (Nov 2026); pin: Google Places (Nov 2026)

p: The Peschiera springs gush from a karst cave and supply about 80% of Rome's drinking water through an aqueduct. A fountain stands at the source. The Capore and Salisano nodes join it; inside the works is for delegations only.
peschiera.s: Register research (X2, K2, D1); not Google-pinned

p: The 1902 hydroelectric plant at Tivoli stands where in 1892 the first long AC line carried power to Rome's Porta Pia (a plaque marks it there). Openings are rare, so ask Enel Green Power.
acquoria.s: Register research (X2, K2, D1); not Google-pinned

p: ENEA's Casaccia centre has a TRIGA research reactor, earthquake shake tables and solar plants. It opens to the public only on the European Researchers' Night in late September.
enea-casaccia.s: Register research (X2, K2, D1); not Google-pinned

p: The INFN laboratories at Frascati host the DAFNE collider and a visitor centre named for Bruno Touschek. Visits need booking; the OpenLabs days are in May.
infn-frascati.s: Register research (X2, K2, D1); not Google-pinned

cave-del-barco.t: Cava del Barco, Bagni di Tivoli
p: Travertine from here built the Colosseum and, centuries later, St Peter's and Bernini's colonnade. The quarry and the Montarozzo rise are visited on geo-walks during the Earth Week.
cave-del-barco.s: Register research (X2, K2, D1); not Google-pinned

acque-albule.t: Lago della Regina and the Acque Albule
p: The Acque Albule are sulphur springs that deposit the travertine of the quarries. The lake can be seen near the spa; access to the shore is unchecked.
acque-albule.s: Register research (X2, K2, D1); not Google-pinned

lago-albano.t: Lago Albano and its Roman emissario
