p: The crater lake is kept at its level by a Roman drain tunnel, which still works, as does the Valle Ariccia, a drained crater. The lake can be seen from the road or the shore.
lago-albano.s: Register research (X2, K2, D1); not Google-pinned

lago-nemi.t: Lago di Nemi and the Roman ships museum
p: Lake Nemi has a 1,650 m Roman emissario, and a museum for Caligula's ships. Some footpaths are closed.
lago-nemi.s: Register research (X2, K2, D1); not Google-pinned

p: The Commonwealth and American cemeteries at Anzio and Nettuno record the beachhead battle of 1944. Open; train to Anzio.
anzio.s: Register research (X2, K2, D1); not Google-pinned

routes.name: Capitol and the Forum
routes.summary: The Gesù and Via Caetani, the Theatre of Marcellus, the Capitoline Museums and the Aracoeli, the Vittoriano terrace, the Tullianum, the Forum, Trajan's Markets and the new underground library.

routes.name: Colosseum, Celio and Monti
routes.days: Best Sun, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri, Sat
routes.summary: The Colosseum, the Palatine houses and Santa Maria Antiqua, the Domus Aurea and Trajan's baths, San Pietro in Vincoli, San Clemente's three levels and the Celio churches.

routes.name: Navona and the Pantheon
routes.days: Best Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri
routes.summary: Domitian's stadium under Navona, Borromini's Sant'Ivo, Caravaggio in San Luigi and Sant'Agostino, the Angelica library, the Pantheon and the Minerva flood plaques.

routes.name: Campo de' Fiori and Via Giulia
routes.summary: Largo Argentina and Caesar's death, Bruno's pyre, Pasquino, the bones of Orazione e Morte, Chiesa Nuova and the Vallicelliana, the prisons and the crime museum on Via Giulia.

routes.name: Ghetto, Bocca della Verità and Testaccio
routes.days: Best Sun, Mon, Tue, Thu, Fri
routes.summary: The Ghetto and the Synagogue, the river-port temples and the Cloaca Maxima, the Circus Maximus, the Aventine keyhole, Monte Testaccio and the Mattatoio.

routes.name: Trevi and the Corso
routes.summary: The Acqua Vergine from its arches to Vicus Caprarius and the Trevi, Sant'Ignazio's flat dome, the Collegio Romano, the Doria and Colonna palaces, Via Rasella and the Quirinal.

routes.name: Piazza del Popolo, Via Margutta and the Ara Pacis
routes.summary: The Popolo churches and the Pincio, the old cafés, Goethe's flat, the rubbish edict of Via Margutta, the doll hospital, the Ripetta flood columns, the Ara Pacis and Augustus's tomb.

routes.name: Spanish Steps to Porta Pia
routes.summary: The Spanish Steps and the anamorphoses of Trinità dei Monti, the Hertziana's monster door, the Capuchin crypt, Palazzo Barberini, Bernini's Teresa, the Porta Pia breach and Galleria Borghese.

routes.name: Santa Maria Maggiore to the Quattro Fontane
routes.summary: Santa Maria Maggiore and its underground, Palazzo Massimo, Michelangelo's church in the baths, the Moses fountain, Borromini and Bernini at the Quattro Fontane, and Via Panisperna's physicists.

routes.name: Lateran and Porta Maggiore
routes.summary: St John Lateran and the Scala Santa, Santa Prassede, Via Tasso's SS prison, Santa Croce, Porta Maggiore's aqueducts and the Felice arch.

routes.name: Caracalla and the Appia gate
routes.summary: The Baths of Caracalla, Porta San Sebastiano and the wall museum, and the first miles of the Via Appia Antica.

routes.name: Trastevere south and the Tiber island
routes.summary: San Bartolomeo on the island, Ponte Sisto, the churches over Roman houses (San Crisogono, Santa Cecilia), Ludovica in San Francesco a Ripa, and the Porta Portese market.

routes.name: Trastevere north and the Gianicolo
routes.summary: The Farnesina's Raphael rooms and the Landsknecht graffito, two Trastevere churches, Bramante's Tempietto, the 1849 ossuary and the Acqua Paola, ending on the Gianicolo terrace.

routes.name: Vatican and Borgo
routes.summary: St Peter's Square and its meridian, the basilica and the Scavi, the Vatican Museums, the old hospital of Santo Spirito, and the executioner's house.

routes.name: Prati and Castel Sant'Angelo
routes.summary: The castle and its escape corridor, Piazza Pia, the Valdese temple and San Gioacchino's aluminium dome, the purgatory museum and Teresa Gullace's plaque.

routes.name: Flaminio: the 1960 Olympics to the Mosque
routes.days: Wed or Sat morning for the Mosque
routes.when: Mosque visits Wednesday and Saturday mornings only; GNAM closed Monday.
routes.summary: Nervi's stadium and dome, the Olympic village under the Corso Francia viaduct, Mussolini's marble stadium, Brasini's domeless church, the old mineral spring and Portoghesi's mosque.

routes.name: Nomentana: Porta Pia to Santa Costanza
routes.when: Villa Torlonia bunker visits are guided and booked (060608).
routes.summary: The 1870 breach, Mussolini's bunkers, a round postwar church and Constantine's daughter's mausoleum, with the national library on the way.

routes.name: Sapienza: the science campus
routes.when: The Sapienza Tour and the pathology museum are by booking; the chemistry museum opens Mon–Thu mornings.
routes.summary: Piacentini's campus with Sironi's uncovered mural, the Primo Levi chemistry museum and the Policlinico's pathology collection. Also the Neanderthal skulls of Saccopastore at the anthropology museum and the Istituto Superiore di Sanità's museum.

routes.name: Montesacro: garden city on the Aniene
routes.when: The ex-GIL gym is a working gym; the bunker-free walk is all street.
routes.summary: Giovannoni's and Sabbatini's garden-city square, the villini, the 1934 youth-movement gym, then the Aniene bridge and the hill of the plebs' secession and Bolívar's oath.

routes.name: Tufello and Val Melaina: the borgata
routes.when: Courtyards are private homes: stay on the public ways.
routes.summary: Sforza's comb blocks, the evictees' blocks from the Spina di Borgo, De Sica's labour office, and two 1970s churches.

routes.name: Trieste and Coppedè: market, fantasy and a devil's chair
routes.when: Mercato Nomentano shuts Sunday; Sant'Agnese closes about 12–15.
routes.summary: Luzzatto's market of 1928–29, Coppedè's fairy-tale quarter, a Roman tomb on a car-park island and the 7th-century mosaic of Sant'Agnese.

routes.name: Parioli and Villa Ada
routes.when: The royal bunker is by guided tour only: book first. Forte Antenne's opening is unknown after 31 Oct 2026.
routes.summary: Moretti's sunflower house, the Garibaldian battlefield of 1867 and the royal park where Mussolini was arrested, with the Savoy bunker.

routes.name: Flaminio north: sheds, concert halls and Ponte Milvio
routes.when: The Guido Reni sheds are not yet demolished; the Auditorium museum is free and open daily.
routes.summary: The army works due for demolition, Piano's halls built round a Roman farm, Rome's oldest bridge and a drum-plan church in Vigna Clara.

routes.name: North Tiber: dam, airfield and the cut of Fidenae
routes.when: Needs a car, the Roma–Nord railway or buses; the Rocca and the airfield cannot be entered.
routes.summary: The 1951 dam, the hill where an amphitheatre fell in AD 27 and Rome's 1928 airfield.

routes.name: Via Flaminia north: Prima Porta and Malborghetto
routes.when: Villa di Livia's regular days are unconfirmed; Malborghetto opens on a monthly calendar.
routes.summary: A Roman kiln and road beside the RAI, Livia's painted garden villa and Constantine's four-way arch in a farmhouse.

routes.name: Prati, Della Vittoria and Trionfale
routes.when: Mercato Trionfale shuts Sunday; check Antico Falcone's closing day (Tuesday per Google).
routes.summary: The law courts on their concrete raft, a record concrete bridge, the Della Vittoria quarter, the covered market and a 15th-century posting inn.

routes.name: Monte Mario: observatory, meridian and fossil sands
routes.when: The observatory is by booking; the French cemetery is shut Sunday.
routes.summary: Italy's old zero meridian and the observatory with its globes, the Pleistocene shells, the Zodiaco view and the hill's 1960s hotel.

routes.name: Valle Aurelia and the Vatican railway
routes.when: Mostly outdoors; the greenway has a steep climb.
routes.summary: The last brick kiln of the valley, the viaduct and path beside St Peter's station, and the old rail line turned into a greenway.

routes.name: Primavalle and Torrevecchia: borgata and towers
routes.when: Far from the centre: allow time and take a bus.
routes.summary: The 1930s comb-plan borgata and its church, the fort that houses the spies, and four towers on a deck.

routes.name: Ottavia and Insugherata: the north-west edge
routes.when: The Ipogeo degli Ottavi must be booked (06 47788343).
routes.summary: A 3rd-century painted tomb, a wild reserve of cork oaks and, on the way, a Paola-fed wash-house.

routes.name: San Lorenzo: pasta mill, first Montessori school, 1943
routes.when: The Pastificio's gallery opens Tue–Sat 15:00–19:00; Bar Marani is closed Monday.
routes.summary: The 1905 pasta mill turned artists' studios, the building of Montessori's first school, the traces of the July 1943 bombing and a 1928 bar with a pergola.

routes.name: Pigneto and Torpignattara: tomb, film street, Banglatown
routes.when: The Torrione's interior opens only on set days; Banglatown's prayer rooms are private.
routes.summary: An Augustan mausoleum in a park, the street of Pasolini's Accattone, Rome's Bengali quarter and an aqueduct with the scars of the shacks.

routes.name: Gordiani and Centocelle: quarries, airfield and aqueduct
routes.when: Quarry tours need booking; the airfield park is still being cleaned in parts.
routes.summary: Pozzolana quarries under a park, a domed Roman tomb, a 1960s estate, Wright's 1909 airfield and the tallest arches of the Alexandrine aqueduct.

routes.name: Pietralata to Rebibbia: the elephant and Pasolini's flat
routes.when: Casa Pasolini opens Thu–Sun by app booking; Casal de' Pazzi needs booking (060608).
routes.summary: A veterans' borgata, a 1930s church, a library in a dairy, the museum of the 200,000-year-old riverbed and the flat where Pasolini wrote Ragazzi di vita.

routes.name: Tor Sapienza and San Basilio: racetrack estate and revolt
routes.when: Needs a bus; the Cervelletta is exterior only.
routes.summary: The racetrack-shaped Morandi estate, a closed medieval tower in a reserve and the village of the 1974 revolt.

routes.name: Far east: Trevi's springs, a Republican bridge and Gabii
routes.when: Needs a car or buses; Gabii's opening is uncertain, so confirm first.
routes.summary: The springs that feed the Trevi, a castle on a tufa crag, a seven-arch bridge, a Latin city older than Rome and a 1939 workers' church.

routes.name: Appio Latino: Ridolfi's houses, the tram depot, Via Latina tombs
routes.when: Check the Via Latina tombs' ticket; Alberone market moves around 2027.
routes.summary: Two Ridolfi apartment houses, a revival church, the old tram depot and the Roman tombs on the Via Latina.

routes.name: Caffarella: tomb, quarry, farm and the fizzy spring
routes.when: The quarry runs weekend tours only; Sant'Urbano is closed except for special openings.
routes.summary: A Roman wife's tomb, a temple-church, quarry galleries, a sheep farm, the nymphaeum and the spring where you fill your own bottle.

routes.name: Quadraro to Tor Fiscale: murals, round-up and aqueducts
routes.when: Monte del Grano opens on set days; avoid the aqueduct park after dark.
routes.summary: An aqueduct arch on the Tuscolana, the quarter's murals, the memorial for the 1944 round-up, a giant mound, Tor Fiscale and the aqueduct park.

routes.name: Tuscolano: INA housing, Don Bosco and Cinecittà
routes.when: Cinecittà is closed Tuesday and Monday per Google; book a tour.
routes.summary: Postwar housing from Mamma Roma, the big Salesian basilica and the film studios.

routes.name: Appia Nuova and Anagnina: villa, racecourse and a Casamonica lot
routes.when: Sette Bassi runs weekend guided tours; a bus is needed between stops.
routes.summary: A Roman villa on the Appia, a 1926 racecourse, the villa of Sette Bassi and a park on a demolished mafia villa.

routes.name: Garbatella: the 1920 garden suburb
routes.days: Any day; Dar Moschino closed Sunday
routes.when: Courtyards are semi-public, so keep quiet; Dar Moschino needs a booking.
routes.summary: From the first stone of 1920 through barocchetto courtyards to the workers' 'hotels', the old baths turned library and a Roman bridge under a square.

routes.name: Ostiense and San Paolo: pyramid, post office and a university in factories
routes.days: Any day; the Pyramid interior only on guided dates
routes.when: Long distances: Metro B and a short bus. Sepolcreto and the Pyramid interior open only on special dates.
routes.summary: A pyramid in the wall, a 1930s post office and station, the gasholder, a ruined wholesale market, Roma Tre in old factories, then St Paul's, the INA estate and the ship-model tank.

routes.name: Montagnola, Tor Marancia and the Ardeatina
routes.days: Any day; the catacomb by phone
routes.when: Commodilla needs a call; the Fosse Ardeatine close mid-afternoon.
routes.summary: A catacomb with early Italian writing, a concrete Baroque church, the 10 September 1943 memorial, a fort, a rustic park, the 'Shanghai' murals and the Fosse Ardeatine.

routes.name: EUR beyond the icons: offices, a mushroom and a saucer
routes.days: Tue–Thu for the Archive; any day otherwise
routes.when: The Archive is open Tue–Thu mornings; the model museum is mostly closed.
routes.summary: The Beirut towers, Minnucci's fountain and shelter, the state archive, Gismondi's model, the water mushroom, the abbey of three fountains and the saucer-topped tower.

routes.name: Laurentina and Decima: exiles, a fizzy-water reserve and Moretti's camp
routes.days: Any day; the military museum Sat by booking
routes.when: A bus or car is needed between stops; the military museum needs a booking.
routes.summary: The exiles' village, a round church, a reserve around an archaic settlement, Moretti's INCIS quarter and a tiny church with a stone from old St Peter's.

routes.name: Spinaceto: a spine, a church and a cemetery
routes.when: Bus from EUR Fermi; the cemetery has internal buses on some days.
routes.summary: A 1960s estate on one spine road, Lafuente's concrete cylinders and the Garden of Angels at the Laurentino cemetery.

routes.name: Gianicolo west and Villa Pamphilj: 1849, Plautilla and the park
routes.days: Any day; Villa del Vascello only on FAI days
routes.when: Parts of the park and the arch are fenced for works; Forte Aurelia is a bus ride away.
routes.summary: A ship-shaped villa, the arch on a battlefield, a basilica, Rome's biggest villa park, the columbaria on its edge and a restored fort.

routes.name: Monteverde Vecchio: villini, Pasolini and a lost catacomb
routes.when: Villa Sciarra may be partly fenced; the Ponziano catacomb is by appointment.
routes.summary: A hill park, turreted villini, Pasolini's flats, two old bars and the site of a vanished Jewish catacomb.

routes.name: Donna Olimpia and Monteverde Nuovo: the skyscraper estate
routes.when: The market works Mon–Sat to early afternoon; it moves to temporary boxes from about 2 Dec 2026.
routes.summary: Nine-storey 1930s blocks, the school of Pasolini's novel, a market about to move, a hospital city, the Forlanini and a fort of martyrs.

routes.name: Marconi and Portuense
routes.days: Any day; the museum by booking
routes.when: A bus ride between the stops; the museum should be booked.
routes.summary: Rome's longest bridge, a small museum of tombs on the Via Portuense and a round 1978 church.

routes.name: Magliana: Nervi's shed, a flood-plain estate and a papal castle
routes.days: Any day; Castello visits are monthly on Saturday
routes.when: A bus or car; the castle and the catacomb open only on arranged visits.
routes.summary: Nervi's first ferrocement building in a car park, the Magliana churches old and new, an estate below the river, the pumps that guard it and Leo X's castle.

routes.name: Trullo and Valle dei Casali: outer west
routes.when: A half day needing a bus or car; the Casa del Parco is open 9–17.
routes.summary: A borgata whose walls carry poems, Corviale's long block and a nature reserve of old farmhouses.

routes.name: Ostia centro: town hall, post office and the pier
routes.when: Roma–Lido train from Piramide to Lido Centro. Post office closes Saturday afternoon and Sunday; the market is Mon–Sat mornings.
routes.summary: Ostia's 1920s–30s new town: Fasolo's tower, Mazzoni's post office, the Pappagallo and the pier.

routes.name: Ostia Levante: villini, groynes and the Kursaal
routes.when: Bus or bike along the seafront; the beach club side is quieter outside summer.
routes.summary: Libera's and Moretti's villas, the 1936 college tower site, the fishing canal and Nervi's Kursaal dome.

routes.name: Nuova Ostia and the Idroscalo: church, birds and a tower
routes.when: Bus or car; the road to the Idroscalo is desolate, so go in daylight.
routes.summary: Post-Council Bonaria, the seaplane base, Pasolini's last place, a bird reserve on a dump and Tor San Michele.

routes.name: Ostia Antica village: castle, drainage men and the pumps
routes.when: Train from Porta San Paolo to Ostia Antica; the pumps are 2 km away, so bike or taxi.
routes.summary: A papal fortress, the village of Gregoriopoli, the Romagna labourers who drained the marsh and the river that moved.

routes.name: Castel Fusano: pines, Chigi villa and the Severan road
routes.when: Car or bike; the villa is open only on set days and the palombara needs a booking.
routes.summary: A burned and regrowing pine wood, Pietro da Cortona's villa, the Via Severiana and the estate's Roman village.

routes.name: Fiumicino town: the malaria man and the old lighthouse
routes.when: Train to Fiumicino Aeroporto then bus; the lighthouse road is rough.
routes.summary: Valadier's customs village, Grassi's mosquito observatory and tomb, the 1946 lighthouse and the stranded fishing platforms.

routes.name: Porto and Isola Sacra: ships, harbour and tombs
routes.when: The museum has a free shuttle from the airport; the harbour and tomb sites each want a taxi or a bike.
routes.summary: The airport's Roman hulls, Trajan's hexagonal harbour, a harbour-workers' cemetery and Morandi's hangars.

routes.name: Maccarese: reclamation estate
routes.when: Train to Maccarese-Fregene station; farms are seen from the road.
routes.summary: A reclaimed marsh turned dairy estate, with a castle borgo, an ecomuseum and a bird reserve.

routes.name: Palocco, Acilia and Malafede: a suburb, a borgata and a church
routes.when: Car recommended; buses are infrequent.
routes.summary: Casal Palocco's 1960s plan, Acilia's last borgata, two late churches and the legend of Ficana.

tours.name: Church day: modern religious buildings
tours.intro: Rome's most daring religious buildings since 1890, from an aluminium dome to Meier's sails, with a mosque and a Buddhist temple. The main church day; three more modern days follow (south-west, south-east, north).
tours.how: Metro, train and bus; 7–9 stops. Best on Wednesday or Saturday (Mosque). Catholic churches close about 12–16, so the midday stops are the ones open all day: San Gaspare, the Jubilee Church, Hua Yi Si.
story: After 1870 the new Italian state and the papacy competed in stone: the Church answered the Protestant and Jewish buildings that were suddenly allowed inside the walls, and later raced to put parishes into the housing estates spreading over the Campagna. That race produced Rome's best concrete churches: Busiri Vici, Nervi, Spadolini, and finally Meier for the Jubilee of 2000.
The tour runs in the order of the city, not the calendar: Prati and Parioli in the morning, the eastern estates in the afternoon. Each stop has one thing to find.

stops.note: 1911–14: the first reinforced-concrete church in Rome, built by Protestants. Find the candelabrum lunette.
1897: the aluminium dome with crystal stars.
1920–34: Piacentini's halfway modern.
1923–51: the 100 m dome that never was; its model stands in a pier.
1984–95: columns that branch like palms (Wed/Sat mornings).
1976–81: Nervi's last church, entered at a corner. Open all day.
1998–2003: Meier's sails, self-cleaning white cement. Open all day.
2013: a pagoda behind warehouse walls. Open 10:30–15.
1985–87: the cross made of sunlight between two pinnacles.
1965–71: the rawest concrete church in Rome (from 16:30).
1989–93: a hyperbolic-paraboloid vault, 900 m from the Visitazione.

tours.name: Church hunt through the ages: one day, 1,500 years
tours.intro: The strangest church of each era, oldest first, in one long day: a Byzantine-painted hall, temples under a church, a cannonball, a drilled column, Borromini, Pozzo, a synagogue, Nervi and Meier.
tours.how: Mon, Tue, Thu or Fri only (Sant'Ivo is weekday mornings, San Nicola shuts Wednesday, the Synagogue Saturday). Start 9:30 at the Forum; Sant'Ivo before 13:30; metro east after the Synagogue.
story: Rome is the one city where you can walk the whole history of church building in a day, because almost nothing was ever thrown away: temples became churches, churches were buried under churches, and every age added its own experiment.

stops.note: 6th–9th c.: painted layer on layer, buried by an earthquake.
A medieval church eating three Republican temples.
998: Asclepius' island, and a cannonball of 1849.
Medieval: the drilled column that was probably not a sundial.
1642–60: Borromini's star and spiral.
1685: Pozzo's painted dome.
1901–04: the square aluminium dome.
1976–81: Nervi's pyramid.
2003: Meier's sails.

tours.name: Modern churches of the south-west
tours.intro: A second modern day: tent roofs and ovals of the 1950s–60s, a then-and-now pair in Magliana with a brutalist neighbour, the EUR basilica, Spinaceto's cylinders and the tilted arches of Malafede.
tours.how: Bus and tram, then the Roma–Lido train to Vitinia; a car makes it easy.
story: These are the churches of the southern and western estates, from Fagnoni's 'church of work' to the arches of a parish founded the year Padre Pio was beatified.

stops.note: 1957–65: the tent roof that breaks light into cones.
1955–60: the bell tower is the front door.
2006: the artists' church…
1975–77: raw prefabricated panels and a coffered flat roof, up a stair from the piazza.
…and, across the road, a medieval church on a Roman tomb.
1939–58: the dome that closes EUR.
1975–79: concrete cylinders that cut into each other; glass-block lunettes where roof meets wall.
1955: Avetta's church, said to be one of the best of its time.
2007–10: three arches that touch the ground only at their ends.

tours.name: Modern churches of the south-east: a star, a dome, a pyramid
tours.intro: A third modern day, on the Tuscolana side: the retro church that ignored modernism, Nervi's pyramid, a roof floating on four piers, Nicolosi's concrete star, the third-largest dome in Rome, and Meier's sails to finish.
tours.how: Metro A (Furio Camillo, Cinecittà) and buses; about 7 stops. Catholic churches close about 12–16: do San Gaspare and the Jubilee Church (open all day) in the middle of the day. Cafasso is closed on Monday.
story: These are the parishes the Vicariate raced to build as the eastern estates went up in the 1950s–70s, and they show every answer the Church tried: copy the past (Piazza Asti), let an engineer shape the roof (Nervi), or let the structure become the sign (Nicolosi's star, Rapisardi's dome).
Go in the order of the Metro A line, west to east, and look up in every one: the roof is the point here.

stops.note: 1955–66: a 1950s copy of Bolsena's Romanesque church in travertine. The contrarian start.
1976–81: Nervi's pyramid, entered at a corner. Open all day.
1966–68: a roof that floats on four piers, and a four-pier concrete bell frame. Closed Mon.
1964–67: six beams meet as a star under the lantern; the brick is laid at 45°.
1952–59: a dome of about 40 m. Find Emilio Greco's red-granite font, first chapel left.
1998–2003: Meier's three white sails. Open all day.
1985–87: the cross made of light between two pinnacles.

tours.name: Modern churches of the north: drums, strata and a dome that never was
tours.intro: A fourth modern day across the northern estates: a concrete cylinder, a borgata's travertine tower, Ressa's two churches, the unbuilt 100 m dome, a tent roof, pillars striped like rock layers and a fan-shaped theatre church.
tours.how: Bus from Torrevecchia across Monte Mario, then Vigna Clara, Parioli and Talenti; a car or bike helps. Most are parish churches open mornings and late afternoons only, so start at 8:00 and pause at midday.
story: North Rome's parishes were built for the new middle-class quarters and the borgate alike, and the same few architects keep coming back: Giuseppe Ressa twice, the Canino and Rizzi pair, Giorgio Guidi in Talenti.
Run it west to east and compare how each solves the same problem: a big room, cheap, that still reads as a church from the street.

stops.note: Gresleri's concrete cylinder; find the cross hung like a stalactite.
Consecrated 1960: closes the Primavalle borgata's axis; the 35 m campanile is clad in travertine.
1957–61 (Ressa): Morbiducci's crucifix; the octagonal crypt opens from the piazza.
1960–62 (Ressa): two drums set off-centre; the windows are grouped into three crosses.
1923–51: the 100 m dome that was never built; its model stands in a pier.
A tent roof; Nervi's models for a Via Crucis.
1975–78: travertine and peperino pillars alternate like rock strata.
1970–73 (Guidi): a fan-shaped 'theatre' plan; the campanile is the landmark.

tours.name: Under the churches
tours.intro: Go down: houses, temples, tombs and whole basilicas under today's churches, and two catacombs.
tours.how: Most need a small ticket; catacombs are guided and close at midday.
story: In Rome the ground rose by metres over the centuries, and builders reused what was below. These are the places where you can stand inside the earlier city.

stops.note: Three levels down to a Mithraeum.
A shrine painted into a Roman stairwell.
Alleys between temple podiums.
A whole basilica under the trams.
Roman basins: tannery or dye works?
Frescoed galleries and an empress's tomb.
A three-storey stack to a Roman tomb.
A basilica sunk into the catacomb.
Pilgrims' scratched prayers to Peter and Paul.

tours.name: Bones, executioners and the condemned
tours.intro: Rome's relationship with death: the brotherhood that buried the drowned, the friars' bone chapels, the pyre of Bruno, the executioner's house, the baby hatch and the Purgatory museum.
tours.how: Central and walkable; Orazione e Morte may be closed for restoration.
story: The papal city made death public: executions on squares and bridges, confraternities to comfort the condemned and bury the unclaimed, crypts arranged as sermons in bone.

stops.note: Skulls labelled with the cause of death.
3,700 friars arranged as decoration.
Mastro Titta's red cloak, in a museum shut for years.
Giordano Bruno burned, 1600.
Over 500 executions, and umbrellas.
The wheel for abandoned babies.
Scorch marks said to come from Purgatory.
335 men shot in 1944.

tours.name: The Tiber's record: floods, gauges and the great sewer
tours.intro: Rome wrote down its floods on its walls. Follow the plaques from 1277 to the gauge that still measures the river, and the sewer that has drained it for 2,100 years.
tours.how: Central, about 4 km on foot.
story: Until the embankment walls of the 1880s, the Tiber regularly filled the city: 19.56 m on the Ripetta gauge in 1598. Rome has more than a hundred flood plaques; this is a hydrologist's walk.

stops.note: The oldest flood mark still in the street.
The 1598 mark under the hospital portico.
The gauge that is still Rome's zero.
A ladder of floods, 1422–1870.
The sewer's 2,100-year-old mouth.
The island's well over the sacred spring.

tours.name: Science in the street
tours.intro: Sundials, meridians, an observatory on a church's piers, the lab that opened the nuclear age, a penicillin factory and an accidental lake.
tours.how: Centre on foot, then the outer stops by public transport.
story: Rome was a city of astronomers and calendar-makers long before it was a city of physicists. The trail ends with the chemistry of the 20th century: viscose, antibiotics, and what they left behind.

stops.note: Augustus' sundial pointer.
The 1702 meridian that checked the calendar.
A sighting hole, perhaps.
Secchi's observatory and the time-ball.
Fermi's slow neutrons, 1934.
A mineral spring closed for pollution.
A rayon factory and an accidental lake.
Italy's first penicillin plant, opened by Fleming.

tours.name: 1849: the cannonballs of the Roman Republic
tours.intro: The Roman Republic lasted five months. The French guns that ended it left balls in walls and on altars, and the dead got a Fascist-era crypt.
tours.how: Gianicolo and centre, on foot.
story: In 1849 Garibaldi and Mazzini defended a republic in Rome against the French army sent to restore Pius IX. The siege of June left its marks across the city.

stops.note: A ball in the church wall.
A ball that stopped on the altar.
A ball left on the palace stairs.
The dead, with Mameli's tomb.

tours.name: Occupied Rome, 1943–44
tours.intro: Nine months of German occupation: the bombs on San Lorenzo, the round-up of the Ghetto, the partisan bomb and its reprisal, the SS prison and the women shot at barracks and bakeries.
tours.how: Centre on foot; Verano, Pigneto and the Fosse Ardeatine by public transport.
story: Rome was bombed in July 1943, occupied in September and liberated on 4 June 1944. The places are small, mostly plaques and marks, but they are exact.

stops.note: The bombing of 19 July 1943.
The round-up of 16 October 1943.
The GAP bomb of 23 March 1944, and the bullet holes.
The reprisal, the next day.
The SS prison.
A mother shot outside a barracks.
Rossellini's version of her death.
A massacre now doubted by historians.

tours.name: Political murder: Matteotti to the Magliana gang
tours.intro: The exact spots of the killings that shaped modern Italy: Matteotti in 1924, Moro in 1978, a student on a bridge in 1977, a gang boss in 1990.
tours.how: All central, on foot or by tram.
story: Each marker records a turning point: the murder that made Mussolini a dictator, the kidnapping that ended the historic compromise, the 'Years of Lead' and the criminal Rome that grew in their shadow.

stops.note: Seized here on 10 June 1924.
Found here on 9 May 1978.
Shot here on 12 May 1977; no one convicted.
Shot here on 2 February 1990.

tours.name: Rome on screen: real spots and fakes
tours.intro: Stand where the scene was shot, and learn what was faked: neorealism's real streets, Hollywood's replicas, Cinecittà's rebuilt Via Veneto.
tours.how: Centre on foot; Pigneto and EUR by metro.
story: Rossellini and De Sica shot on streets still full of rubble; Fellini rebuilt the city in the studio; Hollywood built St Peter's Square in California and the Spanish Steps in England. This tour separates the real from the set.

stops.note: Roma città aperta (1945): really here.
Ladri di biciclette (1948): the theft spot.
Roman Holiday (1953): the hand.
Roman Holiday: Joe's courtyard at no. 51.
Roman Holiday: the press conference.
La dolce vita (1960): really here; Via Veneto was a set.
John Wick 2 (2017): the stair fight.
John Wick 2: the Continental.
John Wick 2: Rome playing New York.
John Wick 2: the map shop.
Spectre (2015): a museum playing a cemetery.
Mission: Impossible (2023): the yellow Fiat.
Ripley (2024): the coin lights.
Angels & Demons (2009): exterior real, interior a set.
Angels & Demons: the 'Vatican archive'.

tours.name: Rome in books
tours.intro: Real places behind Goethe, Hawthorne, Henry James, Gadda and Morante.
tours.how: Centre on foot; Via Merulana and the Verano by tram.
story: Foreign writers came for the ruins and the Catholic strangeness; Italian writers wrote the modern city of crime and bombs.

stops.note: Italian Journey: his flat.
The Marble Faun: Hilda's tower.
The Marble Faun: the dead Capuchin.
Daisy Miller's grave 'in an angle of the wall'.
Gadda's Pasticciaccio.
Morante's La Storia: the bombing.

tours.name: Built for an event, then left
tours.intro: A world's fair that never opened, the 1960 Olympics, the 1990 World Cup, the 2009 swimming championships: what Rome built, and what it did with it afterwards.
tours.how: Flaminio on foot, EUR by metro, Tor Vergata by bus.
story: Rome keeps building for events and then leaving the buildings: a stadium closed since 2011, a velodrome blown up, a racecourse rotting, a sail that stood unfinished for fifteen years.

stops.note: 1942: the world's fair that never opened.
1960: the athletes' village and Nervi's viaduct.
1960: still in use.
1960: closed since 2011.
1960: blown up in 2008.
1959–2013: the grandstand left to rot.
2005–: the unfinished sail, reused in 2025.

tours.name: Housing the poor: from borgate to megablocks
tours.intro: How Rome housed the people it pushed out of the centre: the Fascist borgate, the INA-Casa 'village', a walled kasbah, a kilometre-long slab and a ring of bridges.
tours.how: Outer districts; a day by metro and bus, or a bike.
story: From the 1930s the regime moved the poor from the demolished centre to borgate on the edge; after the war INA-Casa built humane villages; in the 1970s–80s the city went for megastructures that promised everything and delivered little.

stops.note: 1940–43: the last Fascist borgata.
1950–54: Libera's kasbah inside INA-Casa.
1970s–80s: a kilometre of concrete.
1970s–80s: the bridge-buildings.
1985–87: Tor Bella Monaca's landmark church.

tours.name: Saints you can see: bodies, skulls and a forearm
tours.intro: Rome keeps its saints on show: a martyr in wax over bone, a skeleton in a nun's habit, three popes behind glass, a flower-crowned skull, a severed forearm, a foot, a finger. Where the story is legend, the stop says so.
tours.how: Two half-days. West: St Peter's (early), Chiesa Nuova, Sant'Agnese, the Gesù and Sant'Ignazio, then Trastevere. East: Santa Francesca Romana, Cosmedin, Santa Croce, Santa Maria Maggiore, Santa Maria della Vittoria. Churches close about 12–16; Sant'Agnese is shut Mondays.
story: From the 4th century Romans built their churches over the graves of martyrs, and from the 1500s, when the catacombs were rediscovered, bones went out of them by the thousand, named, dressed and given wax faces. Showing a body made the saint present; a body that did not rot was read as a sign of holiness, which is why so many are 'incorrupt' with help from wax, silver masks and embalming.
Read each stop as two things at once: a real object you can stand in front of, and a story that may or may not be true. The tour keeps the two apart.

stops.note: Pius X under silver, John XXIII under wax, Innocent XI: three popes in glass.
The bones claimed as Peter's, behind a wall at the end of a Roman street of tombs (booking).
Philip Neri under a silver mask.
Agnes's head, given in 1900, on the site of her martyrdom.
The forearm that baptised Asia, cut off in 1614.
Robert Bellarmine in cardinal's red, behind glass.
Anna Maria Taigi: a wax face from her death mask over the bones.
Teresa of Ávila's right foot (check it is back from Spain).
A skeleton in a habit, holding her prayer book; Peter's kneeprints upstairs.
A skull with a flower crown and a name on its forehead; ten places claim him.
Thomas's finger, thorns, a nail, and a Title of the Cross carbon-dated to about 1000.
Pius V in a crystal coffin.
Victoria: a catacomb martyr built back into a person with wax. The best one in Rome.

tours.name: Marble Death: Baroque skeletons and dying saints
tours.intro: In the 1600s Death became a sculpture: a skeleton writing a pope's name, flying with a portrait, gaping as a soul escapes. And Bernini and his followers carved saints at the moment of dying. One walk through the centre, plus Trastevere and the Vatican.
tours.how: Central walk from Piazza del Popolo south to Campo de' Fiori and Via Giulia, then across to Trastevere; St Peter's and the Esquiline as add-ons. Mornings: Gesù e Maria and Monterone keep short hours, Santa Maria del Popolo shuts at midday.
story: Counter-Reformation Rome made death a public sermon. The skeleton on a tomb is not a horror prop: it is a reminder (memento mori) and often a joke at Death's expense, because the dead man's fame, soul or portrait gets away.

Bernini set the pattern with Urban VIII's tomb (Death writing the name) and his workshop's flying skeletons; Guidi, Legros and others made it a Roman genre. The dying saints, Ludovica and Kostka, are the other side of the same idea: a good death as a work of art.

stops.note: Gisleni's shrouded skeleton between a chrysalis and a butterfly; Death on the Chigi floor.
A robed, grinning skeleton with an hourglass (Guidi).
Death gapes as Fame opens Cardinal Imperiali's coffin (Guidi).
A winged skeleton guarding an empty tomb.
Bernini's workshop: a feathered skeleton flies up with Valtrini's portrait.
Real bones this time: the burial brotherhood's skulls, labelled (by appointment).
Bernini's last great statue: a saint dying on marble cushions.
Where it started: Death writing Urban VIII's name; Death with an hourglass under Alexander VII.
Kostka on his deathbed in coloured marble (Legros).
The reaper with scythe and hourglass over the Aldobrandini tomb; two skeletons for Vecchiarelli.

tours.name: Water lines: Vergine, Felice and Paola
tours.intro: Three lines carry Rome's water: the Vergine, the Felice and the Paola, plus the fixes for floods and swamps.
tours.how: Centre on foot. The outer stops need transport.
story: The Acqua Vergine (19 BC) comes from springs east of the city and feeds the Trevi. The Felice (1587) climbs the hills for Sixtus V, and the Paola serves the west bank from the Gianicolo. Between them run the arches, the fountains and the pumps.

stops.note: A castellum of the Vergine 8–9 m under the street.
Vergine arches with Claudius's inscription.
Fifteen arches in a shop basement.
The end of the Vergine.
The Felice's mostra.
The Paola's mostra, which also drove Rome's first hydro plant.
Paola pipes inside the bridge.
Where the aqueducts cross twice.

tours.name: Marsh to coast: drainage, malaria and a moving shore
tours.intro: From the river that moved in 1557 to the Romagna labourers who drained the marsh, the scientist who found the mosquito and the shore that keeps shifting.
tours.how: Train to Ostia Antica, then bike; Fiumicino by bus.
story: The coast of Rome was a marsh and a malaria zone for centuries. The Tiber cut a new course in 1557, the port moved, the delta grew seaward, and in 1884 labourers from Romagna came to drain it with pumps. Giovanni Battista Grassi's work on mosquitoes explained the disease; the sea resorts followed.

stops.note: The meander cut in 1557.
A dry moat left by the river's move.
The labourers' memorial.
The 1889 pumps.
A lighthouse base now a km inland.
The Ravennati monument at the pier.
Grassi's mosquito observatory.
Groynes against a shore losing sand.
